CHAPTER–I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
I.  KEY INITIATIVES 
Recommendation 
1.1 The Committee takes cognizance of the myriad functional areas of the Ministry of 
AYUSH, its key initiatives and the emergence of AYUSH in public healthcare system. The 
Committee is appreciative of the work done by the  Ministry for management of Covid 19. The 
efforts have not only generated genuine interest but also a lot of trust in the Indian Systems of 
medicine. Renewed interest in AYUSH system of medicine had led the country on the path of 
rediscovery of glorious pa st. The Committee is of the firm belief that even though Covid -19 
pandemic has caused havoc world over, it has provided a golden opportunity for the AYUSH 
Systems to emerge as a strong alternative system of medicine.  
(Para 1.8 of 128th Report) 
Action Taken 
Budget Section 
1.2 The observation of the Committee has been noted.  This Ministry will continue to strive 
hard to achieve further glory in providing AYUSH system. 
Recommendation 
1.3 The Committee takes note of the efforts being made by the Ministry to increase the 
presence of AYUSH systems in public health which includes creating AYUSH departments in 
defense and railway hospitals; granting soft loans and subsidies for the establishment of private 
AYUSH hospitals and clinics; building world -class institutes for both teaching and research in 
AYUSH systems; building digital infrastructure like AYUSH GRID for better access and reach 
etc. by the Ministry to promote and popularize the AYUSH system at district level. The 
Committee believes that it is high ti me the AYUSH system is encouraged by recognizing its 
importance and allocating adequate funds for its development and strengthening to enable it to 
regain its lost glory. 
(Para 1.9) 
Action Taken 
Budget Section 
1.4 The Ministry is grateful to the Committee for taking note of various initiatives taken by 
this Ministry to provide public health through AYUSH System of Medicine. 
1.5 Further, to explore the possibilities of higher grants in the AYUSH sector, adequate 
Budgetary provision is a pre -requisite.  There fore, as advised by the Committee, Ministry of 
Finance has been suitably apprised of the Committee‘s concern for allocating adequate Budget to 

3 
 
AYUSH Ministry to achieve its mandate in letter and spirit, vide Secretary (AYUSH)‘s D.O. 
letter No.H-11013/9/2021-Budget dated29.04.2021. 
NAM 
1.6 Ministry is implementing Centrally Sponsored Scheme of National AYUSH Mission 
(NAM) through States/UTs and supporting their efforts to increase the presence of AYUSH 
system in public health through different activities of NAM guideline and providing financ ial 
assistance to the respective State/UT Governments as per the proposals received in their State 
Annual Action Plans (SAAPs). Under NAM, Ministry has supported 104 units of setting up of 
upto 50 bedded integrated AYUSH hospitals in different State/UT Gov ernments and also 
assisted 4448 numbers of Dispensaries & Sub -centres for upgrading as AYUSH Health & 
Wellness Centres (HWCs). So that public may avail the AYUSH health facilities from these 
established hospitals as well as AYUSH HWCs. 
ADS  
1.7 Ministry of AYUSH has taken initiatives for the integration of AYUSH under the health 
establishments of Ministry of Railways. Defence and Home Affairs as detailed below:  
1.  Ministry of Railways: Ministry of AYUSH and Ministry of Railways signed a MoU for 
the establishment of AYUSH wings at 05 zonal railways Hospitals. Ministry of Railways has 
promised to create 25 contractual posts of Ayurveda, Unani Siddha and Homoeopathy Medical 
Officers.  
2.  Ministry of Defence:  
i.  Ministry of AYUSH and Ministry of Defence sig ned a MoU to start Ayurveda units at 
the Palliative care centre, Base Hospital Delhi Cantt, Research & referral Hospital. Delhi 
Cantt, Air force Hospital Hindon and 05 ECHS polyclinics in Delhi —NCR.  
ii.  Hon'ble Prime Minister during the meeting on 21.08 .2020 regarding Reforms in Medical 
education desired inter -alia to explore desirability of utilization of AYUSH systems of 
Medicine in health care services of Armed Forces. Accordingly, Ministry of AYUSH has 
proposed following:- 
a.  Ayurveda units may be e stablished in all major health establishments of Ministry 
of Defence including Hospitals/ Rehabilitation Centres/ palliative Care Centres 
etc.  
b.  A permanent mechanism for procurement of Ayurveda medicines may be 
developed to ensure uninterrupted supply of Ayurveda Medicines for all the 
Ayurveda units under the Health Establishments of Ministry of Defence.  
c.  Ayurveda doctors and supporting staff such as Pharmacists, Masseurs, therapists 
etc. may be recruited by the Ministry of Defence.  
d.  Ayurveda ho spitals may be empanelled to provide healthcare facilities to the 
troops and their families.  

4 
 
e.  On the line of 19 AIIMS established by the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare and in line with the directions of Hon'ble Prime Minister during the 
meeting on 21.08.2020 regarding Reforms in Medical education, department of 
Ayurveda may be started in Armed Forces Medical College, Pune and Army 
college of Medical Science, Delhi Cantt., with the provisions of Professors/ 
Associate Professors and Assistant Professors in different subjects of Ayurveda.  
iii.  A meeting between Defence Secretary and Secretary AYUSH is scheduled on 16.04.2021 
to discuss the methodology of the integration of AYUSH under the health establishments 
of Ministry of Defence.  
3.  Ministry of Home affairs : Ministry has taken up the matter with Ministry of Home 
Affairs for the integration of Ayurveda and other traditional systems of medicine. Ministry has 
provided all the technical know -how sought by the Ministry of Home Affairs from time to time. 
However. matter is still pending with Ministry of Home Affairs.  
Champion Services Sector Scheme for Medical value Travel:- 
1. Under the scheme Ministry has invited proposals for the establishment of AYUSH Super 
Specialty hospitals and Day care centers and Skill Development in AYUSH Sector.  
2.  Financial assistance has been provided to the autonomous bodies under the aegis of 
Ministry of AYUSH to develop their digital infrastructure under establishment of 
AYUSH Grid component of the scheme. 
 
II.    MACRO ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
Recommendation 
1.8 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the sharp shortfall in allocation of the 
Ministry as compared to the projected demand, despite its repeated recommendation for 
increasing the budgetary allocation of the Ministry, keeping in view the scope, reach and value 
AYUSH can add to the health of the people. Given its indigenous/traditional element, cost 
effectiveness and a safe alternative to modern system of medicine, the Ministry of AY USH, 
through its schemes and strategies, can help AYUSH system of healthcare to emerge as a 
valuable system of medicine in healthcare delivery. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that 
budgetary constraints should not be allowed to act as a stumbling block to achieve the mission

I. KEY  INITIATIVES 
3.1 The Committee takes note of the efforts made by Ministry in achieving its objective of 
“Health for all” during 2020 -21 under NAM and Information, Education and Communication 
Schemes by way of providing cost  effective AYUSH services and also to strengthen and 
popularize AYUSH systems at the grass root level. The Committee, however, feels much more 
needs to be done towards making AYUSH healthcare facilities accessible to all and making its 
presence felt in rur al and remote areas of the country. There have however, been doubts and 
questions regarding the efficacy of Indian systems of medicine. Even though the popularity and 
presence of AYUSH systems is increasing, the need of the hour is to lay focus on standard ization 
of academic courses and scientific validation of AYUSH system. The Committee desires the 
Ministry to focus on standardization of quality of AYUSH healthcare services, quality control of 
AYUSH drugs, strengthening of drug testing laboratories, pharm acies and improving the quality 
of AYUSH education in the country so as to position AYUSH as a true alternative system of 
medicine.  
(Para 1.13)

3.43 The Committee is appreciative of the achievements of the Ministry; however, it feels that

of these medicines. Instances of side -effects of AYUSH medicines and other products have also 
come to light. The Committee believes that a solid and robust quality control mechanism i s the 
only way to ensure credibility and safety of AYUSH drugs. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends that in order to have scientific validation, more and more clinical trials need to be 
done to fill up the gap due to lack of evidence based medicines. Gi ven the growing popularity of

documentation. The role of Central Drug Controller becomes very important in approval of 
drugs which have undergone pre -clinical trials , clinical trials etc. The Committee, further, 
believes that publication of peer-reviewed papers in reputed international journals will go a long 
way in establishing the credibility and authenticity of AYUSH systems of medicine. The 
Committee is also of th e view that there should be separate and adequate funding for clinical 
trials and scientific research which should stand international scrutiny so that AYUSH drug get 
the global recognition and acceptability.

IV. MAINSTREAMING OF AYUSH SYSTEM 
Recommendation 
3.91 The Committee acknowledges the initiatives taken by the Ministry of AYUSH through its 
various institutes in mainstreaming AYUSH systems of medicine. However, the Committee is of 
the opinion that the maj ority of the work done is preventive in nature and recommends that the 
Ministry should encourage and create a detailed roadmap for establishing AYUSH systems of 
medicine as a curative alternative to the Allopathic system. The Committee believes that the 
Ministry should do more than organizing seminars, conferences, meetings, workshops, road 
shows etc. to bring some tangible progress in the adoption of Indian traditional systems. The 
Committee notes the main reason behind the poor export of Indian traditiona l drugs is their 
failure to meet global norms on safety and efficacy. The Committee also notes that licensing of 
Ayurvedic drugs is a State subject, so there is a lack of uniformity in the approach of different 
States.

Further Recommendation 
3.119 The Committee takes into account the significant R&D and public health initiatives 
undertaken by various C ouncils of AYUSH to harness the potential of AYUSH systems.  
The Committee appreciates that c ollaborative research studies with different countries 
would help in establishing the system as the credible and scientific system of medicine 
which may emerge as a curative alternative to modern medicines.   The Committee, 
however, is disappointed to note that the Ministry has not given any information about 
reasons for poor export of ASU&H drugs. The Commit tee's concerns about ASU drugs 
failing to meet global norms on safety and efficacy have not been addresse d.  The 
Committee is also surprised that the Ministry has not paid attention to the point 
highlighted by it regarding lack of uniformity in the approac h of different States with 
respect to ASU Drugs as Health is a State subject.  The Committee emphasise s that given 
the increasing popularity of AYUSH systems especially during pandemic Covid -19, it is 
high time to showcase the effectiveness of ASU&H drugs in domestic market as well as 
global arena . The Committee recommends the Ministry to have a standard licensing 
process based on uniform parameters across all the States so that the drug formulations do 
not vary in different States and also conform to global norms of safety and efficacy. This 

65 
 
would go a long way in establishing Indian System of Medicine as an alternative system  of 
medicine.

3.120 The Committee believes that misleading and unfounded advertisements particularly by 
ASU drug makers will force people to gradually desist from consuming such ASU formulations. 
The Committee recommends that provisions of both the Drugs & Cosmetics Act Rules & Magical 
Remedies Act should be made more stringent to tackle the problem of misleading and unfounded 
advertisements. The Committee desires the Ministry to revisit both the period of imprisonment 
and the fine amount under these rules to regulate and cont rol the violation of the provisions of 
the said Acts. The licensing authorities and drug controllers at the State level must also take 
prompt actions against any such misconduct.

Recommendation 
3.123 The Committee observes that the trend of dis eases as well as severity of illnesses has 
undergone a substantial change in the modern age. Advancement in modern science has brought 
out a revolution in the way one identifies, diagnoses and treats illnesses now -a-days. The 
Committee believes that AYUSH with its traditional/classic knowledge has immense potential in 
devising a holistic approach against the ever changing challenges in the health sector and 
ensuring good health of the masses. However, AYUSH has remained neglected and modern 
system of medicine, with a scientific evidence base, has overshadowed AYUSH's popularity and 
growth. Nevertheless, the Committee observes that with the formation of a separate Ministry for 
AYUSH, various efforts have been made for the revival of AYUSH over the years. The Committee 
appreciates the Schemes and Programmes implemented by the Ministry of AYUSH for 
mainstreaming of AYUSH services and acknowledges its satisfactory trend of budgetary 
utilization. The Committee also believes that it is high time to make AYUSH more competitive 
and expand its outreach across States as well as in the international market. The Committee 
believes that for strengthening AYUSH research, education institutes, its industry and the quality 
of AYUSH healthcare, a substantial enhancement in budgetary allocation is the need of the hour. 
AYUSH must also collaborate and coordinate with other scientific disciplines as well as the 
modern system of medicine. Integration of AYUSH with modern advances will enhance its 
reliability and scientifically validate the ancient AYUSH traditions.

Further Recommendation 
 
3.126 The Committee appreciates the various initiatives of the Ministry of AYUSH to 
promote and develop Indian system of Medicine.  Given the vast potential of Indian System 
of Medicine in contemporary times and especially during pandemic Covid -19, the 
Committee believes that Indian System of Medicine has huge capacity to position itself as 
an effective and economic al system of medicine as an  alternative to modern system of 
medicine. This will help  reduce out of pocket expenditure on health .  The Committee 
recommends the Ministry to identify the 'Key Concern Areas'  especially with regard to 
quality of education and research, drugs and overall healthcare delivery systems in 
AYUSH institutions. The Committee recognizes the importance of collaborative researches 
as well as clinical trials for better research outcomes. Since Ayurveda is the valued heritage 
of the glorious past of our country, it needs proper propagation at the grass-root and global 
level. The Committee, in this regard,  recommends the Ministry to lay special focus on the 
regulation and control over safety and efficacy of Ayurveda drugs and products to enable 
the market of the  AYUSH products grow internationally and stand to any scientific 
scrutiny.  Keeping in view the vast arena of  AYUSH systems, the Committee recommends 
the Ministry to chalk out specific course of action to combat the challenges ahead for 
strengthening the infrastructure, education and practice of AYUSH systems and expand 
the reach of these systems across the country and abroad.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS - AT A GLANCE 
 
KEY  INITIATIVES 
 The Committee is pleased to note Ministry's plan to introduce a restructured 
Central Sector Scheme of “Ayush Oushadhi Gunvattaevum Uttapadan Samvardhan 
Yojana” (AOGUSY) during 15 th Finance Commission 2021-22 to 2025-26 with components 
like strengthening and upgradation of Ayush Pharmaceuticals and Drug Testing 
laboratories, pharmacovigilance of ASU&H drugs etc.  The Committee, however, would 
like the Ministry to keep a close track o f the challenges and Key Areas of Concern in 
respect of the implementation of AOGUSY component.  The Committee also recommends 
the Ministry to ensure efficient macro and micro planning and execution of the components 
of the scheme so as to strengthen the A YUSH system of medicine. The Committee observes 
that the role of the Pharmacopeia Commission of Indian Medicine for maintaining 
standards of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani & Homeopathy drugs need to be strictly monitored 
for assured standardization of ASU&H drugs .  The Committee, in this connection, 
recommends that States/UTs must be motivated and incentivized to ensure standardization 
of AYUSH education and quality healthcare delivery system in general and on quality 
control of ASU&H drugs in particular.  
(Para 3.14)  
 The Committee appreciates the role of All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA) in 
Covid-19 mitigation management. The Committee desires that AIIA needs to popularize 
AYURAKSHA project amongst common masses for attracting more and more people 
towards A yush system. The Committee believes that the clinical studies of CCRAS, 
intending to scientifically validate the efficacy and safety of classical Ayurvedic 
formulations to generate tangible evidence would not only yield in scientifically validated 
new drug  development but would also instill public faith in quality assured Ayurvedic 
treatment. The Committee, therefore, recommends that CCRAS should adopt a targeted 
approach and chalk out an action plan to achieve the same.  
(Para 3.15)  
 The Committee is of t he opinion that merely by writing to States Governments to 
check the practice of AYUSH System by quacks, the Ministry of AYUSH should not 
absolve itself of its responsibility to stop this menace as it not only brings disrepute to the 
AYUSH system of medici ne but also discourages people to have trust in this system. The 
Ministry, therefore, must think of devising certain code under which stern legal action 
could be taken against the quacks. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of 
Health & Family W elfare must examine and consider the regulatory amendments under 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1947 as suggested by the Ministry of AYUSH without delay to 
improve the quality, efficacy and safety of ASU drugs. The Ministry of AYUSH must take 
up this matter with  the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare on priority basis and inform 
the Committee on the action taken on the matter. 
(Para 3.17)  
 

73 
 
MACRO ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 The Committee takes note of the status of construction of the projects of National 
Institutes and finds that except for National Institute of Homoeopathy, Phase -II, Kolkata, 
all the Institutes are lagging behind with respect to their physical and financial progress. 
The Committee understands that given the prevailing pandemic Covid -19 si tuation, it is 
but natural that the deadline for physical completion of construction work at all Institutes 
would certainly not be met.  The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry must 
make all out efforts to complete the ongoing projects at the earliest so that all the institutes 
could be made operational for the benefit of the people. 
(Para 3.22)  
 
 The Committee is disappointed to note that as of now, 20 -23 States/UT 
Governments have submitted their State Annual Action Plans ( SAAP), 2 States/UT  
Governments have submitted UCs through the NAM web portal and the remaining 
States/UTs are under process.  The Committee apprehends that the NAM web portal is not 
popular amongst States/UTs for prompt submission of UCs despite imparting necessary 
training to officials of States/UTs on submission of SAAP, physical and financial report, 
UCs, etc. The Committee is surprised that the States which have submitted their SAAP 
through NAM web portal also have not submitted UCs through the same portal.  The 
Committee believes that such reluctance reeks of evasion of responsibility and 
accountability of funds given.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
persuade all States/UTs to submit not only their SAAP but also pending UCs through the 
web portal. 
(Para 3.25)  
 
SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY 
  The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry of AYUSH in extending the 
co-location of AYUSH facilities at PHCs, CHCs and District Hospitals and thus providing 
choice to the patients for different systems of medicines under single window. The 
Committee, however, finds such facilities lacking in Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, 
Daman & Diu and Delhi, etc. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
States/UTs need to be continuously persuaded for sending  proposals through their SAAPS 
for setting up co -location of AYUSH facilities under NHM.  The measures so undertaken 
would not only ensure preferred choice to the patients for different system of medicine 
under single system but also facilitate  mainstreaming of AYUSH services at the grass root 
level.  The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare would share 
requisite responsibilities in engagement of AYUSH doctors/paramedical staff and their 
training for enhancing the quality of human resource of each AYUSH centre. 
(Para 3.28)  
 
 The Committee expresses its concern that only 835 AYUSH HWCs against the 
target of 4436 HWCs could be made functional in 12 States which indicates the inadequacy 

74 
 
of steps taken by the Ministry.  The Committee i s utterly disappointed to note such tardy 
progress in operationalisation of HWCs. The Committee underlines the need of a 
streamlined procedure to ensure the completion of setting up of AYUSH HWCs within a 
specified time with adequate manpower and infrastru cture and provision of operational 
cost. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to engage the remaining States/UTs 
which have not yet started the process of making AYUSH HWCs functional so that 
equitable distribution of AYUSH HWCs, keeping in view the geographical extent and 
population of States/UTs, is assured.    
(Para 3.31)  
 The Committee is not convinced with the response and justification given by the 
Ministry on the mismatch between the target of setting up of AYUSH HWCs and actual 
operationalisation during a stipulated time frame.  The Committee, in this connection, 
reiterates its recommendation made in para 3.16 that a demarcation in physical targets 
with respect to approval of HWCs and targets for its operationalisation needs to be clearly 
spelt out.  The Committee recommends that a realistic timeline must be determined to 
make HWCs functional with requisite infrastructure and human resource. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry should work in tandem with States/UTs 
Governments on the operationalisation of all the approved HWCs. The Committee believes 
that proper monitoring and field visits will be of immense help in expediting the 
operationalisation process of HWCs.  
(Para 3.34)  
 The Committee is disappointed that the  Ministry has not shared any information 
about its effort undertaken to tap the full potential of the North East Regions with respect 
to the rich biodiversity in the NER.  The Committee firmly believes that NER with its rich 
bio-diversity and region specif ic plants of medicinal values must be focused upon for 
exploration, collection, documentation for sustainable and optimal utilization of medicinal 
plants.  The Committee, accordingly, reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must 
focus on North East  Regions and also liaise with Ministry of Environment and Forests for 
conservation and maintenance of potential utilization of hubs and medicinal plants. 
(Para 3.39)  
   The Committee acknowledges the efforts put in by the Ministry for encouraging 
farmers to cultivate medicinal plants. However, the Ministry has  not been able to take this 
scheme to the length and breadth of the country as a result of which majority of farmers 
are deprived of its benefits.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates is recommendat ion to 
make the presence of this scheme felt throughout the country in a time bound manner.  
(Para 3.42)  
The Committee takes into account that although it is mandatory for all Ayurvedic 
medicine manufacturers to comply with the standards prescribed under Ayurvedic 
Pharmacopeia of India (API) which includes Pharmacopeial standards for heavy metals 
content, microbiological limits, aflatoxines, etc., it is, however, skeptical about the 
adherence to these prescribed standards in the absence of proper monitorin g and 
supervision.  The Committee, time and again, has been emphasizing upon quality control of 
ASU&H drugs with the purpose of popularizing its domestic use and global acceptance.  

75 
 
The Committee hopes that all components of the new scheme outlined for the  duration of 
15th Finance Commission would be implemented effectively to strengthen the whole regime 
of standardization, scientific validation, Pharmacovigilance, etc.  The Committee reiterates 
its recommendation regarding increasing the credibility of AYU SH system to meet 
scientific global scrutiny and scientific validation of new Ayush drugs development 
including pre-clinical and clinical trials to showcase its evidence based products.     
(Para 3.44)  
 The Committee is constrained to observe that the rec ruitment process for filling up 
of 09 posts regulatory posts for creation of a vertical structure in CDSCO is progressing at 
a snail's pace.  The Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends that the creation 
of vertical structure for AYUSH under CDS CO should be expedited and the recruitment 
process be completed at the earliest.   
(Para 3.47)  
  The Committee notes that W.H.O Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) has been 
given to 21 Ayurvedic  Drug manufacturers to export their products as per standards and 
other requirements of importing countries. The Committee expects the Ministry to monitor 
whether these 21 manufacturers have in house quality control section and drug testing 
laboratory as p er the schedule 'T' of prescribed Good Manufacturing Practices. The 
Committee would like to be apprised whether any complaints with respect to sub -standard 
or inferior products has/have been received against existing licensed manufacturers in the 
last two years and the action taken against the manufacturers violating the Drugs and

effectively operationalise the E -Aushadhi portal by activating new application process for

(Para 3.51)  
  The Committee observes that during 2021 -22, an amount to the tune of Rs. 4.10 
crore has been allotted to further strengthen the Pharmacovigilance network and reporting 
mechanism by establishing more peripheral Pharmacovigilance centers i.e. upto 100 by 
ensuring adequate manpower for Pharmacovigilance Centres across the country. The 
Committee would like the Ministry to make an assessment of the operat ional cost of each 
Pharmacovigilance Centre along with the number of workforce required to run it smoothly 
and accordingly project its fund requirement for the scheme.  The Committee recommends 
the Ministry to comply with the findings and observations of t he Comprehensive Impact 
Assessment of the Pharmacovigilance Scheme for its effective execution and actual 
achievement of set objectives on the ground level.  
(Para 3.54)  
 The Committee notes that the various Councils of AYUSH and their institutes are in 
the process of obtaining their NABH accreditation.  The Committee, however, reiterates 
that a timeframe for completing NABH accreditation must be fixed by the Ministry and 
desired the Ministry to keep a close watch to ensure the compliance of NABH standards  by 
those who have been accredited. 
(Para 3.79)

AYUSH Mission under the component of Quality Control of ASU&H Drugs to State

  The Committee expresses its pleasure that various research institutes are 
undertaking clinical trials for making their research scientific and evidence based.  Such 
clinical trials help to reach a firm conclusion that a par ticular drug is both safe and

would get a big boost if quality and evidence based scientific research is carried out.  The

better ways to utilize each other research outcomes and thus create a platform for sharing

however, is disappointed to note that the Ministry has not given any information about 
reasons for poor export of ASU&H drugs. The Committee's concerns about ASU drugs 
failing to meet global norms on safety and efficacy have not been addressed.  The 
Committee is  also surprised that the Ministry has not paid attention to the point

global arena. The Committee recommends the Ministry to have a standard licensing 
process based on uniform parameters across all the States so that the drug formulations do 
not vary in different States and also conform to global norms of safety and efficacy. This 
would go a long way in establishing Indian System of Medicine as an alternative system o f 
medicine.

and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Thirty -Second Report of the Committee on Action Taken by 
the Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in the 127 th Report on on 
Demands for Grants 2021 -22 (Demand No. 45) of the Department of Health Research (DHR),

CHAPTER–I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
Recommendation 
1.1 The Committee observes that the Covid -19 pandemic has created the need for 
transformation of the allocation of budgetary resources for research and innovation in the health 
sector. The Department of Health Research being the nodal department for medical re search 
needs to reorient its focus in strengthening research capabilities and infrastructure and 
reinvigorating interest in medical research amongst the youth. Availability of up -to-date, 
sophisticated, state of the art research infrastructure will provide  impetus to research and 
innovation. These insights help in formulating group or population -specific policies. 
Technologically backed, swift and accurate testing & diagnostic services will effectively counter 
existing and emerging viral diseases. Incorpora ting niche technologies like ML and AI in 
understanding human behaviour and tendencies can generate qualitative insights into issues like 
how human behaviour impacts the transmission of diseases. The Covid -19 pandemic has made 
us realize that there is an u rgent need for improving infrastructure for enhancing bio -security in 
the country by strengthening testing and research facilities. The Department of Health Research 
needs to ramp up its resources and strategic research priorities. 
(Para 1.6) 
Action Taken 
1.2 Important initiatives taken by the Department of Health Research (DHR) and ICMR for 
improving infrastructure, strengthening bio -security as well as improving innovations are as 
follows: 
 Creating National Network for Clinical Trials utilizing the services of Multi -Disciplinary 
Research Units (MRUs) in Government Medical Colleges and Model Rural Health 
Research Units (MRHRUs).   
 Establishment of 30 MRUs and 11 MRHRUs during the 15th Finance  Commission 
period (2021 -22 to 2025 -26) in addition to 85 MRUs and 28 MRHRUs already 
established upto 31.03.2021. 
 Establishment of 42 more Viral Research & Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) during the 
15th Finance Commission period (2021 -22 to 2025 -26) in ad dition to 124 VRDLs 
already established upto 31.03.2021.  
 Establishment of 15 new „DHR -ICMR Advanced Molecular Oncology Diagnostic 
Services‟ (DiaMonds) Centres in addition to 9 existing Centers under the scheme of 
Human Resource & Capacity Development Scheme.  
 About 2800 Laboratories in medical colleges/ institutes/ private sector for COVID testing 
have been made functional. 
 Need- based custom platforms developed for COVID -19 testing (RT -PCR, True NAT, 
CBNAAT, Antigen testing, mobile vans, home testing). 
 Developed COVID KAWACH Elisa, first indigenous human IgG ELISA kit for SARS -
CoV-2 antibodies diagnosis. 
 Developed fully indigenous COVID -19 vaccine, Covaxin in collaboration with Bharat 
Biotech. Has been rolled out. 

3 
 
 With a view to ramp up and prioritize the research activities, following additional 
initiatives are proposed: 
 Establishment of Regional Research Platform for South East Asian Region Countries for 
collaboration in health research in partnership with WHO and 10 countries of SE Asia to 
combat emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases in SE Asia Region. 
 Establishment of Centre for One Health at Nagpur. 
 Setting up of 4 Zonal Institutes of Virology for North -East, North, South and Central 
Zones.  
 Setting up of National Centre for Assistive Health Technology at AIIMs/IITs.  
1.3 Setting up of ICMR -Centres of Excellence at the IITs for boosting innovation and 
product development in the domain of medical devices and diagnostics. 
 
II. Macro-Analysis of Budgetary Allocation to the DHR 
Recommendation 
1.4 The Secretary, DHR in his deposition before the Committee submitted that ideally, the 
overall public expenditure on health research should be at least 5% of the budget of the  
Department of Health & Family Welfare. The current allocation of 3.74% is thus short by 
1.26%. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should make all -out efforts 
to allocate 5percent of the budget of the Department of Health & Family Welfare to DHR at the 
R.E. stage. 
  
       (Para 2.5) 
Action Taken 
1.5 This aspect will be brought out to the notice of the Ministry of Finance during the 
forthcoming pre-budgetary discussions for finalizing the RE for 2021-22 and BE for 2022-23. 
 
III. ICMR 
Recommendation 
1.6 The Committee appreciates the ICMR’s track record with respect to the utilization of 
funds. Barring the year 2020 -21, the ICMR has a near -perfect track -record of utilizing the 
budgeted funds. The Committee, however, is surprised to note that the grant that ICMR receives 
is less than the actual allocation that the DHR get s in the name of ICMR. It is quite intriguing to 
the Committee that while on the one hand the Ministry of Finance does not allocate the fund as 
per the projected demand and even the allocated fund is not released in totality to the ICMR. The 
Committee opines that the role of ICMR is very crucial considering the current and future health 
challenges; inadequacy of funds to ICMR can undermine the desired outcomes in the health 
sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient funds must be released to ICMR 
including additional funds, at the RE stage. 
(Para 3.4) 
 

4 
 
Action Taken 
1.7 The recommendation of the Committee is appreciated. The need for enhancing the 
budgetary allocations for the ICMR would be emphasized at the RE stage.  
Recommendation 
1.8 The Committee recommends that the ICMR must formulate proper Recruitment 
Rules/guidelines to complete the recruitment process within a definite time frame. The schedule 
(date-wise) for the complete recruitment process should be notified well in time to help b oth the 
probable applicants and the recruitment conducting authorities. 
(Para 3.7) 
Action Taken 
1.9 Recruitment rules are framed with the approval of Executive Council/ Governing Council 
and efforts are being taken to fill up the vacancies within a definite time frame. 
Recommendation 
1.10 The Committee observes with concern a significant shortfall against the project demand 
to ICMR. The Committee understands the key role played by the ICMR and its associated 
organisations in fighting the Covid -19 pandemic. It is needless to mention; health research 
activities need to be promoted and encouraged to tackle future health care challenges/diseases. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Expenditure should pr ovide the 
additional funds to the tune of Rs. 599.33 crores for FY-22 at the RE stage for ICMR.  
(Para 3.10) 
Action Taken 
1.11 The recommendation of the Committee is appreciated. Ministry of Finance has already 
allocated an additional amount of Rs.526.28 crores to the ICMR in 2021 -22 through First Batch 
of Supplementary Grant for Covid -19 Emergency Response. The need for further enhancing the 
budgetary allocations for the ICMR would be emphasized at the RE stage. 
Recommendation 
1.12 The Committee expects the ICMR to formulate a long term vision document, comprising 
of its long term goals and objectives, technological interventions required to undertake action 
plans for improving the efficiency of the country’s health systems and   how it intends to provide  
quality, easily accessible and affordable healthcare to every citizen. The vision document should 
spell out the roadmap for the ICMR with which the schemes would be conceived, improvised, 
implemented and evaluated to overcome the health challenges encount ered by mankind in 
general and India in particular. 
(Para 3.11) 
Action Taken 
1.13 ICMR has released a new Health Research Strategy document, ICMR Strategy Plan: 
Agenda 2030, for next seven years designed to improve health outcome in India. It is based on 5  

5 
 
major pillars with 15 target -oriented goals. The strategy will revolve around 5 major elements 
which are capacity building, data management, leveraging traditional medicine, evidence to 
policy and strengthening program implementation through research. 
Recommendation 
1.14 The Committee is pleased to know that the ICMR is an equal partner in its MoU with 
Bharat Biotech. The Committee strongly recommends that the 5% royalty from Bharat Biotech 
be given to the ICMR exclusively for research and development. 
(Para 3.17) 
Action Taken 
1.15 ICMR is entitled to receive a royalty of 5% on net sales of Covaxin as per the MoU 
executed between ICMR and Bharat Biotech (India) Limited. 
Recommendation 
1.16 The Committee appreciates ICMR for publishing 779 research papers  /research 
documents, filing 16 patents and 34 tech developments in FY 2020 -21 (till December 2020). The 
ICMR had similar achievements in FY 2019 -20 too. The Committee hopes that these researches 
once scientifically validated and approved would be translat ed into technology and benefit the 
common man. 
(3.19) 
Action Taken 
1.17 The recommendation and observation of the Committee is appreciated. During last three 
years, through in house efforts various/diagnostic technologies developed through intramural and 
extramural supported research have been commercialized. A transparent process for transfer of 
technologies through website advertisement has been adopted to provide equal opportunities to 
all applicant companies. Advertisement for technologies has been plac ed on ICMR website and 
expression of interest received from companies has been evaluated as per company selection 
criteria set by the ICMR and examined through technology transfer committee.  
 
1.18 The technologies related to diagnosis & vaccine developmen t against Corona virus has 
been developed and commercialized despite of the constraints of the pandemic. The technologies 
viz. Development of anti ‐SARS CoV ‐2‐IgG antibody detection ELISA for screening human 
serum samples; Equine Anti Serum against SARS CoV -2 Covid-19 rapid antibody detection kit, 
RT-LAMP assay for detection of SARS -CoV-2 and development of TaqMan SARS CoV ‐2 
multiplex RT PCR has been transferred to companies on non-exclusive basis.   
 
1.19 Other technologies viz. ELISA based technologies i.e. Anti -CCHF Human IgM Elisa 
assay, technology for testing water for presence of Water -borne Viruses, Rotavirus Antigen 
Capture ELISA, Multiplex real time PCR for Dengue and Chikungunya, Anti-KFDV IgG ELISA 
assay; LAMP based technology viz. Loop mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay for 
reliable and rapid diagnosis of Leishmania infection has been transferred to companies on non -
exclusive basis.    
 
 

6 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.20 The Committee recommends that the ICMR should carry out comparative studies of 
mechanisms/ processes that similar organisations of other countries have put in place to spur 
professional, social, personal and thus holistic development o f their workforce particularly 
scientists. 
(3.25) 
Action Taken  
 
1.21 ICMR regularly explore  such possibilities and collaborate with international agencies to 
develop and nurture the talent pipeline in health research. For example, ICMR has signed a 
Declaration of Intent (DoI) with the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases 
(NIAID) of the National Institutes of Health, USA and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation 
(BMGF). This Declaration builds on an ongoing collaborative research and training programme 
between India and the U.S., including enhancement of research capacity. 
 
Recommendation 
1.22 The Committee also recommends ICMR to conduct regular training and workshops of its 
scientists and researchers to keep them abreast with the latest developments and findings in 
medical research. The Committee believes that most of the times the re is the protracted threat of 
research being limited to thesis and journals. Thus, such workshops will help researchers and 
scientists gain valuable insights into how research can be done keeping in view the ultimate goal 
i.e. betterment of public health. 
(Para 3.26) 
Action Taken 
1.23 ICMR regularly conducts training programmes/ workshops/ webinar for capacity 
building in different areas of health research like bio-ethics, vector borne diseases, nutrition etc. 
Recommendation 
1.24 The Committee is pleased to note that the ICMR is planning to establish the country’s 
first-of-its-kind Centre of One Health on the campus of Maharashtra Animal and Fishery 
Sciences University (MAFSU), Nagpur to view human health not in isolation but in co njunction 
with biotic and abiotic elements like plant life, animal life, the physical environment is a step 
forward in the right direction. The Committee believes that the concept of One Health must be 
effectively implemented for reducing the incidence of emerging zoonotic threats like COVID -19. 
The Committee recommends that the Department must promote One Health research for 
developing a sustainable disease control system that uses real -time health analytics and highly 
advanced data management tools for ac curate results. Further, such a model must be scaled up 
across the country. 
(Para 3.35) 
 
 

7 
 
Action Taken 
1.25 COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the risks of zoonoses  i.e. diseases or infections that 
can be transmitted between humans and animals. This has underlined the need to build effective 
mechanisms to avoid as well as to deal with such future pandemics. In pursuant to these 
directions, ICMR has already started th e preparatory activities for establishment of National 
Institute of One Health at Nagpur, which will also house a BSL -IV laboratory. Necessary land 
for establishment of the Centre has already been provided by the Maharashtra Animal and 
Fishery Sciences University (MAFSU), Nagpur.  This proposal to set up the One Health Centre 
forms part of the PM -ASBY package and the implementation of the project will be commenced 
immediately on approval.  
1.26 An International Workshop on One Health was organized on 12 th April, 2021 with all the 
stakeholders and their views/suggestions will be taken into consideration for achieving the best 
outcome of the project.  
Recommendation 
1.27 The Committee further recommends ICMR to establish meaningful research 
collaborations acro ss the world. Moreover, medical, veterinary, paramedical sectors and 
bioscience researchers must be integrated to form a task force to address the emergent issues. 
The Committee recommends that the ICMR should collaborate with health, veterinary, 
agriculture and life science research institutions and universities to broad base its R&D. 
(Para 3.36) 
Action Taken 
1.28 In order to adopt a holistic and integrated approach to solve health issues, a high level 
Inter-Ministerial Steering Committee has been constituted on Eco Health, including the subject 
of One Health.  The committee has members from Department of Health and  Family Welfare, 
Department of Health Research, Department of Defense Research and Development, Ministry of 
Environment, Forests and Climate Change, Department of Agriculture Research and Education, 
Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairy and Fisheries, Depa rtment of Biotechnology, 
Department of Science and Technology and other experts from WHO -South-East Asia Region 
Office, National Centre of Disease Control, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Indian 
Council of Medical Research and Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, etc to broad base the research.  
Recommendation 
1.29 The Committee appreciates ICMR’s vision of incorporating modern technologies like AI 
for the detection and diagnosis of serious contagious diseases like TB. The Committee notes that 
the ICMR’s role in this collaboration is primarily data generation and validation of the tool. The 
Committee, however, recommends that the ICMR must use high quality annotated training data 
sets to train this AI tool. The ICMR must generate exhaustive and large dataset s to train this 
model for various exigencies involved during the testing and screening of patients for TB. The 
Committee would like to further recommend that the Department must carry out studies 
concerning the readiness of health centres, the skillset of healthcare personnel and the suitability 
of overall infrastructure areas to ascertain the effectiveness of such a model. 
(Para 3.39) 

8 
 
Action Taken 
1.30 The proposal for development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool for screening and 
detection of TB has been initiated in collaboration with Institute of Plasma Research, Department 
of Atomic Energy, Ahmadabad. The focus is on generating high quality annotated data sets 
which would be used for training and testing of the tool. 
Recommendation 
1.31 While appreciating the initiatives of ICMR to combat malnutrition, the problem of 
fluorosis, IDD and menace of Vitamin-A deficiency, the Committee is of the considered view that 
given the mandate of ICMR with regard to medical and health research, a lot mo re needs to be 
done. The Committee recommends that the DHR must complete the studies on the prevalence of 
fluorosis, Vitamin A deficiency and IDD and finalise the report as soon as possible. The 
Committee would like to be updated on the findings of the stu dies and the actions taken by DHR 
thereon.  
1.32 The Committee also recommends the Department to promote such studies in other 
regions of the country and incorporate findings of such studies in the National Health Policy. 
(Para 3.41) 
Action Taken 
1.33 Following actions have been taken by the ICMR to promote studies in this regard: 
i. Prevalence of fluorosis in the community of selected districts of India and development 
of an appropriate intervention model for prevention and control of fluorosis‟ was a Task 
Force Study under the Centre for Promotion of Nutrition Research and Training (CNRT) 
– ICMR HQ. ICMR-NIN, Hyderabad conducted the study in Prakasam district of Andhra 
Pradesh. Dental fluorosis screening was done in 60,000 population from 30 villages and 
the data was shared with ICMR for analysis 
ii. Similarly, Vitamin -A Deficiencies data was collected as part of the ICMR Task Force 
Study led by NCRT, ICMR -HQ. Of the eight states in which the study was being carried 
out, ICMR -NIN led the data collection in Medak district of Telangana.  The data was 
collected and sent to the ICMR in March 2020 and report is awaited 
iii. The ICMR Task Force Study on Assessment of Iodine Status Among Pregnant Women in 
Selected Districts of India” has been initiated in April 2017 in ten di stricts, that is, one 
district from each of the ten states of India. ICMR -NIN is one of the participating centers 
for the longitudinal study and coordinated and implemented the same in Telangana State. 
The data collection (demographic, health, WASH, releva nt pregnancy, child birth and 
lactation related data, diet and anthropometry) and sample collection (blood, urine and 
household salt samples for relevant biomarker estimations) from 200 pregnant women 
recruited from 100 villages from the district of Yadadr i/Bhuvanagiri has been completed 
(including data scrutiny) during all the six study time points (2017 to 2020). The data and 
samples have been shared with the Centre for Promotion of Nutrition Research and 
Training – (CNRT), ICMR, New Delhi and analysis is in progress. 
1.34 ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition agrees with the recommendation of the committee 
and would take up such studies in future on a continuous basis in regular time intervals so as to 

9 
 
contribute in building data at different time points for taking appropriate measures to control the 
prevalence of these deficiency disorders. 
IV. Schemes/ Projects of Department of Health Research (DHR) 
Recommendation 
1.35 The Committee acknowledges that outbreak of pandemic Covid -19 has put extra  burden 
on the available resources. The Committee however, appreciates the efforts of DHR  for 
strengthening the network of Viral Research & Diagnostic Laboratories for managing  epidemics 
and national calamities. The Committee notes that the Department managed toset up 118 VRDLs 
against the target of setting up 125 VRDLs in 2020 -21. Also, 3 more  VRDLs are expected to be 
established by 31.03.2021. 
(Para 4.5) 
Action Taken 
1.36 Now 124 VRDLs have been set up against the target of 125.  Hence the target set for the 
period of 14 th Finance Commission has almost been achieved.  The scheme has been further 
continued for the 15 th Finance Commission period (2021 -22 to 2025 -26) with the target to 
establish another 42 VRDLs, bringing the total number to 166 VRDLs upto 2021-26.   
Recommendation 
1.37 The Committee understands that the financial year 2020 -21 was unique as Covid -19 
pandemic made it difficult to accomplish the set targets. The Committee, however, feels that 
DHR should take up the matter with the State Governments to expedite their proposa ls for 
establishing VRDLs. The Committee hopes that DHR, put every possible effort in achieving its 
set target of establishing VRDLs. 
(Para 4.6) 
Action Taken 
1.38 As already mentioned in para 4.5 above, 124 VRDLs have been set up against the target 
of 125.   Hence the target set for the period of 14th Finance Commission has almost been 
achieved. The scheme has been further continued for the 15th Finance Commission period 
(2021-22 to 2025-26) with the target to establish another 42 VRDLs, bringing the total number to 
166 VRDLs upto 2021-26. 
 
Recommendation 
1.39 The Committee observes that as against the projected demand of Rs. 90.00 crores, the 
scheme has been allocated only Rs. 82.00 crores  for the year 2021 -22. It is however a matter of 
concern that for 2020 -21, the actual expenditure as on 19.02.2021 is Rs. 57.08 crores only as 
against the allocation of Rs. 83.00 crores at both BE & RE stages. The Committee was informed 
that though in 2021-22, the Department is aiming to establish 8 new VRDLs but the provision of 
Rs. 82.00 crore (BE 2021 -22) will suffice the requirement of setting up these new VRDLs and to 
strengthen the existing network of VRDLs. The Committee recommends that the DHR may 
project its demand for the scheme considering the length and breadth of the country, size of 
population, vulnerable sections of the society and frequency of incidence of epidemics and 

10 
 
calamities for efficient management and control of the health emergencies . and effective control 
for optimum utilisation of funds allocated. 
(Para 4.8) 
Action Taken 
1.40 The expenditure under the scheme for establishment of Viral Diagnostic & Research 
Laboratories (VRDLs) during the year 2020 -21 is Rs. 81.90 crores, which is 98 .68% of the 
allocated budget for the Schemes in BE/RE. Thus, there is substantial utilization of funds under 
this scheme, during the year, against the allotted funds.  The department has proposed to 
establish 42 more VRDLs across the country during the nex t five years keeping to strengthen the 
existing network of VRDLs in the country.  
1.41 The allocation in 2021 -22 is Rs. 82.00 Crores and more funds will be sought, if 
necessary, at the RE stage. 
Recommendation 
1.42 The Committee recommends that to enhance its performance in disease surveillance and 
monitoring the Department must focus on the following priority areas: - 
 Network of laboratories should be equipped with the latest tool and technology and 
increase of testing capabilities; 
 Expeditious detection of viruses so as to initiate timely and effective health interventions; 
 Training in handling high risk pathogens; 
 Testing labs in under-served and difficult terrains; 
 Strengthening of laboratory quality systems through quality control quality assurance; 
 Capacity building of health care facilities etc. 
(Para 4.12) 
Action Taken 
1.43     The network has 124 Virus Research and Diagnosis laboratories (10 Regional, 25 State 
Level, 89 Medical College level) established across the country. The laboratories have state -of-
art infrastructure and are equipped with modern machinery required for  virus research and 
diagnosis. All the VRDLs have notable testing capacities for all viruses of public health 
importance. 
 All VRDLs have trained manpower and equipped with requisite infrastructure needed for 
detection of early diagnosis of viruses. The VRD Ls are now capable to diagnose the 
viruses within 12-48 hour depending on the complexity of the tests. 
 Trainings on handling High Risk pathogen and Biosafety & Biosecurity are routinely 
being conducted at National Institute of Virology, Pune and other equi pped Regional & 
State level VRDLs 
 Geographical coverage for virus diagnosis has already been taken care while site 
selection. Furthermore, efforts will be taken care to cover difficult terrains if some left 
untouched. 

11 
 
 Various QA/QC, EQA programmes for diff erent viruses are already under 
implementation. 
 VRDL resource center (NIV -Pune and NIE Chennai) as well as the Regional VRDLs 
organizes training programs for capacity building in lab diagnosis, outbreak investigation, 
reporting etc.  
Recommendation 
1.44 The Committee is of the view that a full proof surveillance system of DHR can help in 
timely identification of viruses and timely health intervention for the same. Further, the 
Committee believes that the DHR along with Department of Health and Family welfar e should 
formulate a concrete contingent plan to control infections before turning into pandemics/ 
epidemics. The level of preparedness must be resilient enough to contain the outbreak of 
epidemics and calamities so that precious human lives could be saved. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends establishing a robust and highly advance surveillance system for high -risk 
pathogens for early detection, response and research on an immediate call. In addition to this, 
the DHR should also create a trained workforce  for handling infectious disease pathogens of 
public health importance. 
1.45 To further strengthen the contingent plan for managing epidemic and National 
calamities, VRDLs must be trained in Good Clinical Laboratory Practices (GCLP). 
(Para 4.15) 
Action Taken 
1.46 Now 124 VRDLs have been set up against the target of 125.  Hence the target set for the 
14th Finance Commission period has almost been achieved. 
1.47 The scheme has been further continued for the 15th Finance Commission period (2021 -
22 to 2025 -26) with the target to establish another 42 VRDLs (1 Regional, 2 State Level, 39 
Medical College), bringing the total number to 166 VRDLs upto 2021 -26. This will expand the 
coverage to the entire country and will definitely help in future Epidemic and National 
Calamities and for fast tracking of viral outbreaks/surveillance.  
1.48 Good Clinical Laboratory Practices (GCLP) training is a regular component for this 
activity. More trainings in GCLP will be conducted in future. 
 
Recommendation 
1.49 Keeping in view the pandemic Covid -19 and the response time of the concerned  
Departments/agencies, the Committee underlines the need for establishment of more 
sophisticated labs in different parts of the country. The Committee has been given to  understand 
as of now only one such lab is  functioning at Pune, and 2 more labs are  proposed to be 
established. The Committee recommended that in order to cater to the  testing needs of the 
different zones of the country, at least one lab of BSL -IV category in  each zone should be 
established. 
(Para 4.16) 
 

12 
 
Action Taken 
1.50 In addition to establishment of Centre of One Health at Nagpur (BSL -IV), four Zonal 
Institutes of NIV, Pune  in the North East Zone (BSL -IV), North Zone, South Zone and Central 
Zone have been proposed under the PM-ASBY Scheme.  
 
IV. Schemes/ Projects of Department of Health Research (DHR) 
Recommendation 
1.51 The Committee takes serious note of the fact that not a single MRU has been established 
this financial year. The Committee also notes with concern that out of the total approved 80 
MRUs for establishment, research work has commenced only in 47 MRUs. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that DHR should speed u p the processes to attain the target of 
establishing 10 MRUs in the current financial year. The Committee also recommends that the 
Government should expedite approvals for MRUs that are at various stages of consideration. In 
addition to this, the Committee also recommends that research work in remaining 33 established 
MRUs must commence at the earliest. 
(Para 4.21) 
Action Taken 
1.52 Five new MRUs were established before the close of the year 2020 -21, taking the total 
number of sanctioned MRUs to 85.  During  2020-21, the resources and manpower of most 
MRUs were diverted to managing the COVID -19 pandemic related functions.  The matter is, 
however, being pursued with the MRUs to increase the pace of research related functions and it 
is expected that the research work would soon commence in all the remaining MRUs. 
1.53 The target for financial year 2021 -22 is to set up 6 MRUs and constant efforts are being 
made to achieve that target. 
 
Recommendation 
1.54 The Committee notes that under Health Technology Assessmen t in India (HTAIn) 
scheme/activities to analyze evidence related cost -effectiveness and clinical effectiveness for the 
deployment of health technologies covering medicines, devices and health programmes, are 
undertaken, which in turn ensures effective and optimal utilization of health budget and easy 
access to quality healthcare at the minimum cost. Its main objective is to reduce out of pocket 
expenditure and address inequality. The Committee, therefore, recommends optimal utilization 
of allocated funds to  minimize the cost for quality healthcare, especially in rural, urban slums 
and tribal areas. 
(Para 4.42) 
 
 

13 
 
Action Taken 
1.55 An allocation of Rs.15.00 crores was made in RE 2020 -21 for Health Technology 
Assessment in India (HTAIn ) and the utilization was Rs.13.66 crores (about 93.4%).  Budget 
allocated for HTAIn for the year 2021-22 is about Rs. 23 crores. 
1.56 Studies have been undertaken under HTAIn for optimal utilization of allocated funds to 
minimize the cost for quality healthcare, in rural as well as urban areas, as follows:   
1. Safety Engineered syringes for therapeutic care in India has supported the allocation of 
funds to interventions that will help save budget by preventing needle prick blood borne 
infection like Hepatitis and HIV 
2. Early Screening for cervical cancer study will help in early diagnosis of the disease and 
reduce mortality 
3. Neonatal Screening for identifying hearing impairment in infants will help in precise 
treatment during infant development 
4. Other studies have been undertaken to identify safer long -term contraceptives for family 
planning, precise treatment modalities for Preventing post -partum hemorrhage in women 
after delivery, etc where mortality is very high in rural areas, etc. 
 
Recommendation 
1.57 The Committee understands that due to problems posed by Covid -19, the funds could not 
be utilised fully. The Committee, however, is of the view that despite certain restriction due to the 
Covid-19 pandemic, academic research work could have progressed. Th e Committee 
recommends to the Department to ensure proper supervision and monitoring of the work being 
done under these schemes during the year so that the time lost is compensated and the allocated 
funds are not left idle. The Committee would like to emph asise that unless there is adequate 
budgetary allocation followed by optimal utilization of allocated fund, the DHR would find it 
very difficult to constitute a pool of talented, knowledgeable and trained medical researchers. At 
the same time, the Committe e further underlines the importance of capacity building by 
providing financial assistance and other social security measures to health researchers to build 
a dedicated pool of researchers. 
(4.44) 
Action Taken 
1.58 After the easing out of Covid-19 pandemic in the last two quarters of 2020-12, substantial 
progress of expenditure was achieved under the Scheme of Human Resource & Capacity 
Development, amounting to Rs.50.68 crores as against the expenditure of Rs. 26.22 reported to 
the Committee. This was 88.86 % of the RE allocation. The Covid -19 pandemic had maximum 
impact of the implementation of sub -schemes of Human Resource Development for grant of 
fellowships for training in Indian and foreign research institutions due to travel restrictions. 
Similarly, the  faculty/researchers in medical colleges could not submit any fresh research 
proposals for funding due to their deployment on Covid -19 related work. The suggestions of the 
Committee for capacity building by providing financial assistance and other social s ecurity 
measures to health researchers to build a dedicated pool of researchers have been noted for due 
consideration.

3.58 None of the indicators used in Global Hunger Index (GHI) specifically measures 
„Hunger‟. The methodology is flawed and data used are of sub -optimal accuracy. The Index 
intended to assess the status for entire population is giving excessive weightage to under -five 
children. There is a need to develop a robust and acceptable country specific methodology to 
measure hunger on priority and avoid using proxy indicators for hunger.  
3.59 In order to do so, the data on the actual diets and consumpti on of foods along with the 
indicators like population undernutrition, and child mortality etc need to be available from time 
to time. While CNNS data is the latest on children‟s nutrition status, there is hardly any data on 
national level prevalence of pop ulation undernutrition and dietary intakes. The most recent data 
available is from NNMB-NIN reported in the year 2012 for rural population (10 states) and 2016 
for urban population (16 districts).  
3.60 Such large-scale data collection should be taken up o n continuous basis for developing 
robust methodologies and datasets for ascertaining hunger status and development of country -
specific hunger index. ICMR -NIN can certainly take lead in doing it on a project basis from

Recommendations/Observations 
1.1 The Committee agrees that Nutrition, safe drinking water and clean sanitary conditions are 
fundamental in paving the way towards holistic health. The Government in encompassing all 
these parameters under the head, "Health and Well Being" has attempted to adopt the much 
needed multi-sectoral approach to hea lth. However, the Committee observes that the 137 percent 
increase in the health outlay from Rs. 94,452 crore in 2020 - 21 to Rs. 2,23,846 crore in 2021 -22 
does not compensate the inadequate funds allocated to both the Departments of Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of AYUSH. This Rs. 2,23,846 crore outlay on Health 
and Well Being includes the budget for the Department of Health and Family Welfare, 
Department of Health Research, Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation, Ministry of 
AYUSH, Package for Vaccination, Nutrition and Finance Commission(FC) Grants for Water and 
Sanitation and FC Grants for Health. Thus effectively, the budgetary allocation for health is just 
32 percent of the much hyped Rs. 2,23,846 crore funds. 
1.2 The Committee notes the observations of the Economic Survey that quotes the data from 
World Bank and WHO (Global Health Expenditure DataBase) which ranks India at 179th 
position out of 189 countries in prioritization accorded to health in its Government Budgets. The 
Committee is dismayed to note that in 2018, when the Government Health Expenditure (GHE) as 
percentage of GDP was as high as 9.27% and 9.21% in developed economies of Sweden and 
Japan, the same was just 1.4% in 2018 -19 of India. Even for developing economi es such as 
Maldives, Argentina and Colombia the GHE as % of GDP amounted to 6.65, 5.91, and 5.47 % 
respectively. 
(Para 2.8 & 2.15 of 126th Report) 
Action Taken  
1.3 The Government of India is committed to increasing health expenditure. The National 
Health Policy of 2017 is geared up towards increasing government health expenditure. The policy 
document recognizes the role of government health expenditure to ensure univ ersal health 
coverage to all. As per the NHA estimates between 2013 -14 and 2017 -18 Government health 
expenditure as a share of GDP has increased from 1.15% to 1.35%. 
 
Recommendation/Observations 
1.4 The Committee is of the view that this mismatch in alloca tion and actual expenditure is a 
sign of poor financial management and subsequently results into slashing of funds in the next 
year. The Committee understands that funds under some schemes remained unspent in view of the 
unprecedented situation due to the pandemic, however the Ministry must now take charge of the 
situation and work towards prudent budgetary allocation under different schemes. 
(Para 2.23)

had to be reallocated to cater the emergency activities. The recommendation of the Committee is 
well taken and in view of felt need of Programme Divisions prudent budgetary allocation under 
different schemes would be done. 
 
Recommendation

1.12 The Committee takes note that PMSSY scheme is financed through two sources, CRIF and 
GBS. PMSSY encompasses two components viz. setting up of new AIIMS and up gradation of 
Govt. Medical Colleges (GMCs). So far, setting up of 22 new AIIMS and 75 up -gradation projects 
of GMCs have been sanctioned under PMSSY. The Committee observes that keeping in view the 
past experience, there is a need to strictly monitor the execution of the PMSSY Scheme in order to 
ensure the completion of the project within the scheduled time. In order to achieve the set 
objectives, the Department also requires to have effective monitoring mechanism to cont rol the 
financial progress and to co -ordinate with the implementing agencies for ensuring timely 
implementation of the projects undertaken on setting up of new AIIMS and up -gradation of 
Government Medical Colleges (GMCs). The management of the 16 AIIMS and  GMCs must have 
Always Better Control (ABC) in order to keep the implementing agencies on the alert mode. 
 
(Para 3.69) 
Action Taken  
1.13 The Ministry has been closely monitoring the progress of PMSSY Projects in the matter of 
construction, procurement &  installation of medical equipment and recruitments of faculty and 
non-faculty personnel on a regular basis. Project monitoring and resolution of any problems in 
execution of projects happens at multiple levels.  
1.14 New AIIMS and GMC up -gradation projects in Phase III/IV onwards are being executed 
in EPC mode under which Executing Agencies (EA) are appointed for each of the Projects, who 
are empowered to take all contractual decisions. For procurement of medical equipment, HITES, 
which is a PSU of the Min istry of Health and Family Welfare, acts as the Procurement Support 
Agency (PSA). Progress of the projects, both in terms of civil works and procurement of medical 
equipment is regularly reviewed with EA and PSA, wherein all components of the project are 
reviewed in detail so as to ensure their time bound completion. A review committee as per rule 
141 of GFR 2017, has also been constituted in the Ministry to review the progress of the work of 
the projects. Recently, the Ministry has also started use of done  technology for a near real time 
and comprehensive review of projects.  
1.15 All State specific issues / hindrances with respect PMSSY projects are resolved through 
continuous and intensive engagement with concerned State Governments, through 
communications at various levels, one-to-one interaction and review meetings. 
Recommendation

course of action to achieve the objectives of the programme i.e. (i) prevention, (ii) taking care, 
support and treatment to people living with HIV/AIDS, (iii) capacity building, (iv) Strategic 
information management: - 
(i) Since only 76% of  the PLHIV know their HIV status, therefore, augmenting contact 
tracing and index testing promoting early detection of undiagnosed infections as index 
testing could link HIV -positive individuals to life -saving treatment, break chains of

(ii) The Committee has been given to understand that NACO developed client -centric IT 
enabled integrated monitoring, evaluation & surveillance system with embedded supply 
chain information system as the next gene ration of MIS. Since system is to be rolled out by 
31st March 2021, therefore, IT -enabled client -centric integrated strategic information 
management system with embedded supply chain management would be quite useful, not

(iii) Though the National Strategic Plan (2017 -24) aims to achieve, inter alia, the elimination

(iv) Endeavours be made to mitigate linkage loss across screening -confirmation-treatment-

(vi) Prioritize sexual and reproductive health services for women at increased risk of HIV

(vii) Adapting new approaches viz, by outsourcing the services under PPP model and by

services 
(viii) Considering the fact that 29% of estimated pregnant women seek delivery services in the

to optimize the resources.

services as well as enable  online programme management. The best practices developed

services under NACP 
(x) Enhancement of community support through community system strengthening through 
formal and infor mal engagement with an emphasis on the decentralized model of district -

(xi) The reach of National AIDS response has a potential to increase multi -fold across

(xii) Anchoring the response through focussed and strategic programme management and 
review.

1.89 The Committee takes note of the fact that as against the global MMR decline of 45% 
between 1990 to 2017, MMR de cline in India has been almost double, i.e, 80% during the same 
period. Five States have already attained SDG targets. However, the Committee finds that the 
overall Maternal Mortality Ratio in 2018 -19 was 113 whereas the 2030 Sustainable Development 
Goals Target is 70. The Committee believes that ensuring easily accessible and better quality 
healthcare for pregnant women is fundamental to reducing MMR. India still lags behind the 
envisaged target for MMR and the Ministry will have to make concerted efforts to reduce the 
MMR in the country to bring it below the SDG target. The Committee is of the view that 
increasing the number of institutional deliveries alongwith ensuring regular checkups and proper 
nutrition for the mother has to be pursued vigorously. The  Committee notes that ASHA and ANM 
act as a link between the Government and the pregnant women. Their role as a facilitator in 
providing adequate antenatal, natal and postnatal care can substantially improve health 
outcomes on various indicators. The Commi ttee also recommends the Ministry and the States to 
increase the outreach of the healthcare services under NHM especially in the backward and 
remote areas. 
(Para 4.14) 
Action Taken 
1.90 The Department of Health and Family Welfare acknowledges the observations and 
recommendations of the Committee to increase number of institutional deliveries alongwith 
ensuring regular check-ups and proper nutrition for the mother.  
1.91 National Family Health Surveys (NFHS) shows that institutional deliveries have risen 
from 38.7% in 2005 -06 (NFHS -3) to 78.9% in 2015 -16 (NFHS -4) and more importantly, 
institutional births in public facilities have increased from 18% to 52% during this peri od. 
Recently released first phase of NFHS -5 data available for 22 States/UTs has reflected that there 
has been a rise in institutional deliveries in 14 States/UTs with more than 90%  of institutional 
births in health facilities.  
1.92 Further, s everal i nitiatives under National Health Mission  have been taken to increase 
institutional deliveries:  
Existing initiatives:  
 Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY),  a promotion scheme launched in April, 2005 with the 
objective of reducing maternal and infant mortality. This is a conditional cash transfer 
scheme for pregnant women coming into the institutional fold for delivery.  JSY promotes 

18 
 
institutional delivery among pregnant women especially with weak socio -economic status 
i.e. women from Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and BPL households. It has been 
lauded as a successful scheme bringing about a surge in institutional deliveries since its 
launch. O n an average, around 1 Crore number of JSY beneficiaries are availing JSY 
benefits annually.  
 Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK): JSSK launched in 2011 entitles all 
pregnant women delivering in public health institutions  to absolutely free and no expe nse 
delivery, including for Caesarean Section. The entitlements include free drugs and 
consumables, free diet, free diagnostics, free blood and free transport between home to 
institution & back and between facilities in case of a referral. Similar entitlem ents also 
cover complications during ante-natal and post-natal period and also sick infants upto one 
year. All the 36 States/UTs are implementing JSSK. During FY 2020 -21, around 1.17 
crore beneficiaries availed the benefits under JSSK.  
Recent initiatives:  
 Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN),  a comprehensive multipronged and 
coordinated approach aims to provide assured, dignified, respectful and quality healthcare 
at no cost and zero tolerance for denial of services to every woman and new -born visiting 
public health facilities in order to end all preventable maternal and new -born deaths and 
morbidities and provide positive birthing experience. Under SUMAN, all existing schemes 
for maternal and neonatal health have been brought under one umbrella in order to create a 
comprehensive and cohesive  initiative which goes beyond entitlements and provides a 
service guarantee for the entitlements.  
All State/UTs are in process of notification of SUMAN CEmONC/ BEmONC/ BASIC 
facilities. Total 7,665 facilities have alre ady been identified across the country under 
SUMAN i.e. CEmONC -1029, BEmONC-2540 and Basic -4096. Budgetary provision has 
been made under National Health Mission‘s Programme Implementation Plan based on 
proposals received from States/UTs on generation of awareness. 
 Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA): Under PMSMA, all pregnant 
women in the country are provided fixed day, free of cost, assured quality Antenatal Care 
on the 9th day of every month. Since inception during the year 2016, more than 2.84 Crore 
antenatal check -ups have been conducted at PMSMA sites for comprehensive services 
under the programme and more than 22.98 lakhs high risk pregnant women have been 
detected. 
 LaQshya - LaQshya programme launched in  December 2017 is to improve the quality of 
care in Labour Room (LR) and Maternity Operation Theatres (OT) to ensure that pregnant 
women receive respectful and quality care during delivery and immediate post -partum 
period.Till 30 th June 2021, States/UTs have identified 2805 LRs and 1905 OTs facilities 
for certification of LaQshya. Out of which, total 1480 LRs / OTs (801 LRs & 679 OTs) are 
certified at State level and 727 LRs / OTs (404 LRs & 323 OTs) are certified at Nati onal 
level under this initiative.

B.  HEALTH SYSTEM STRENGTHENING UNDER NRHM 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.114 The Committee finds that Health System Strengthening under NRHM is the bedrock of 
NHM under its five major components, namely, Ayushman Bharat -Health and Wellness Centres, 
ASHAs & HRH, Free essential Drugs and Diagnostics, National Ambulance Services and M obile 
Medical Units (NAS & MMUs) and Quality Infrastructure Untied Funds. The Committee is of the 
view that there is a substantial scope for increasing the absorption capacity under this head. As 
per data furnished by the Ministry, over 70%of OOPE is on Ou t-Patient care (of which 60% is on 
medicines and 10% is on diagnostic services). In a scenario when medical emergencies have the 
potential of driving people to poverty, availability of free essential drugs and diagnostic services 
can go a long way in easin g the financial hardships of a common man. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Government should pay serious attention to this issue and provide financial 
protection against health risks. 
(Para 4.33) 
Action Taken 
 
1.115 Government has taken many steps under the National Health Mission (NHM) to enhance 
the access to affordable health care and thereby reducing the out of pocket expenditure (OOPE) by 

26 
 
households. These include supplementing the efforts of the States for provi ding a host of free 
services related to mental health, child health, adolescent health, family planning, universal 
immunization, free drugs and diagnostics services initiative, Prime Minister National Dialysis 
Programme, major diseases like Tuberculosis, V ector Borne Diseases, and Non -Communicable 
Diseases, etc.  
1.116 The Government has launched Ayushman Bharat to mitigate financial hardships caused by 
high OOPE. It has two components – Ayushman Bharat Health & Wellness Centers (AB -HWC) 
and Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM -JAY). While AB -HWC provides comprehensive 
primary health care, PM-JAY aims to provide health coverage of Rs. 5.00 lakh per family per year 
to around 10.74 Crore poor and vulnerable families for secondary and tertiary hospitalization. 
1.117 The National Health Policy, 2017 envisages achievement of Universal Health Coverage in 
progressive manner. The Government is committed to setting up of 1.5 lakh AB -HWCs by 
December, 2022. 
1.118 The National Health Policy, 2017 also envisages to incre ase public health expenditure to 
2.5% of GDP in a time bound manner. An increase in expenditure on health by both the Central 
and State Governments would also lower the OOPE.
