1.132 The Committee intends to highlight that according to the World Health Organisation 
(WHO), Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs) kills 41 million people each year globally. Almost 
5.8 million people die from NCDs (Heart and Lung diseases, Stroke, Cancer and Diabetes) every 
year. (WHO report 2015). The Committee takes note of the fact that while 71% of global deaths 
and about 65% of deaths in  India are caused by non -communicable diseases. Between 1990 and 
2016, the contribution of NCDs increased 37% to 61% of all deaths. The Committee is concerned 
at the increasing cases of Non -Communicable Diseases in the country and recommends the 
Ministry to conduct state specific surveys regarding its incidence so that targeted policies can be 
framed for containing NCDs. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to launch life style 
awareness programs that focus on healthy eating and healthy living. The Mi nistry must also 
include lifestyle modification programme especially for controlling obesity amongst adolescents.

Recommendations/Observations 
1.173 The Committee, in its 117th Report, has deliberated upon the need for streamlining  Human 
Resources for Health (HRH). The Committee is of the view that advancement in  technology in 
recent times demands trained individuals who can provide reliable results in  conjunction with 
patient safety. However, there is a huge dearth of trained technologists/technicians in the system. 
The Report of the Public Health Foundation of  India (PHFI) has indicated a supply -demand gap 
allied health professionals when demand  was calculated using basic international norms.  The 
Human Resources for Health (HRH)  shortfalls have resulted in the uneven distribution of a ll 
cadres of health workers. The  uneven distribution of professional colleges and schools has led to 
a severe health system  imbalance across the states, both in the production capacity and in the 
quality of education  and training, leading to poor health ou tcomes. The Committee is in the 
agreement with the  views of the National Knowledge Commission that recommended for 
producing more Healthcare Professional including AHPs by improving the quality and orientation 
of service provision towards better meeting th e health needs of the people stipulating that,  „there 
is a dire need to focus on increasing the quantum and quality of human resources for  nursing and 
paramedical/allied health services. The Committee believes that Healthcare can only be improved 
if human resources for nursing and allied health services are developed, nurtured and enhanced in 
a systematic and planned manner. The Committee  hopes that the Department would streamline 
the stewardship and oversight and provide  HRM strategic framework for rational deployment of 
skilled manpower, performance management system, task shifting and associated career 
development pathways for allied and health care professionals. 
1.174 The Committee believes that recent modernisation of healthcare has initiated a team -
based healthcare delivery model as medical teams are usually „action teams‟ due to their dynamic 

38 
 
work conditions, wherein teamwork and collaboration are the pre -requisites for patient safety. 
The Committee is of the view that not only the team approach is in strumental for safe patient 
outcomes but critical for efficient, cost -effective operations. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Department must pay attention to generate the spirit of team work in the health 
sector reflecting inter disciplinary appro ach, requiring a division of labour among the medical, 
nursing and allied and healthcare professionals on equal footing, although the doctors being the 
captain of the team, for better and faster and much more holistic decision-making. 
1.175 The Committee f eels that courses should follow international standards so that they are 
widely accepted and receive worldwide recognition. Course delivery, practical training and 
assessments should be standardised. Standardisation should incorporate the demonstration of 
learning as well. Strategies should be developed to create flexibility in course delivery through 
alternative delivery modes, multiple locations and timings. Students passing out from colleges 
should be in great demand and get good jobs. The educational me thods should produce such 
healthcare professionals as worthy of recruitment in domestic as well as global health care 
sector. In this regard, it is also pertinent to keep them abreast of knowledge and maintain good 
liaison with the industry in search of em ployment. The Committee is of the view that for each 
course, centres of excellence and globally recognized institutions should be identified alongwith 
hospitals with known good practices, which may become possible training sites. 
1.176 The Committee also recommends that the allied and healthcare professionals must  play its 
pivotal role in providing community healthcare services and be the part and parcel  of all the 
healthcare schemes especially, Pradhan Mantri Jan Aarogya Yojana – Ayushman Bharat. The 
Committee also desires that the government should plug policy gaps and  ensure generation of 
adequate and effective human resource for health to provide quality  care at primary, secondary 
and tertiary level of health delivery in the country. The Committee, in this regard, recommends for 
synchronizing and strengthening the allied  health sciences into articulate policies that help in 
capacity building and value realization of allied health professionals in  the health care delivery 
system. 
(Para 5.16, 5.17, 5.18 & 5.19)

trend by improving the ratio of doctor, as ratio of nurses to  population is low as compared to the 
norm set by the World Health Organisation. The  Committee also feels that State-wise variation in 
availability of doctors/nurses must be  adequately addressed. The Committee appreciates that the 
Government has initiated several programmes to augment the supply of healthcare professionals 
including doctors  and nurses which encompasses Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana 
(PMSSY) under which setting up of 22 AIIMS and up gradation of 75 government medical 
colleges have been sanctioned. Further setting up of 157 medical colleges in States have been 
approved in three phases, of which, 47 are functional. T he Committee recommends the  
Department to step up concerted efforts in this direction with a holistic and integrated approach. 
(Para 5.24) 
Action Taken 
 
1.184 The doctor-population ratio as per WHO recommendation is 1:1000. There are 13,01,319  
allopathic doctors registered with the State Medical Councils and the National Medical 
Commission (NMC) as on November, 2021 in the country. The doctor -population ratio is 1:834 
in the country assuming 80% availability of registered allopathic doctors and  5.65 lakh AYUSH 
doctors. Further, the Government has taken several steps to further increase the availability of 
doctors in the country. The numbers of PG seats have increased by 78% from 31,185 seats 
before 2014 to 55,595 seats including DNB and CPS seat s. The number of UG seats have 
increased from 51,348 before 2014 to 88,120 seats as of date which is an increase of 72%. 
Further, the Medical Education Division is administering a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for 
Establishment of new medical colleges attache d with district/referral hospitals. Under three 
phases of this scheme, 157 new medical colleges have been approved in the Country. As on date, 
70 medical colleges have become functional. As per the scheme guidelines, the State/UT 
Government is the implemen ting agency and the planning, execution and commissioning of the 
project is to be done by the State Government. However, frequent review meetings with the 
States/UTs concerned, are being conducted at various levels to monitor the progress in the 
remaining projects so that these colleges become operational as soon as possible. 
 
 The total  health workforce captured as part of the National Health Workforce Account 
submission for WHO in 2020 indicated the availability of approximately active stock of 

41 
 
8.1 million qualified workers, (excluding ASHAs, leading to a ratio of 49.8 HRH/10,000 
vis-à-vis the WHO norm of 44.1/10,000. This has already surpassed the WHO norm. 
 India proposed that the list of 57 countries with HRH crisis, should be revised and India 
must be removed from the list, to enable recruitment of health workers from India by other 
countries, especially considering the fact that India is at par with WHO norms for 
healthcare workforce and has annual production capacity of around 85,000 doctors, 0.3 
million nurses and midwives and 0.39 million pharmacists and other allied and healthcare 
professionals. 
 Accordingly, the revised list has been released (the Health Workforce Support and 
Safeguard List,2020) comprising of 47 countries and India has been removed  from the 
same. It is also pertinent to indicate that there is no reference to a one per 1000 ratio of 
doctors rather the countries with health workforce shortages are identified based on the 
UHC Service Coverage Index that is lower than 50 and density of doctors, nurses and 
midwives that is below than the global median.  
 It is also critical to factor in AYUSH practitioner (0.56 million), Allied and healthcare 
professionals (~1.3 million) and Community health workers such as ASHAs (~1 million) 
who have potential contribution in the system in rural as well as hard to reach areas of the 
country, which cannot be ignored.  
 Human resources for health availability is more a case of gross mal -distribution in India 
with dense concentration of workforce in Urban areas and poor concentration in rural areas 
causing challenges of inequity and inaccessibility of services and may not be related to the 
case of not having adequate number of practitioners in the system.  
 Several concerted efforts have been done in the recent past, including major regulatory 
reform for several unregulated allied and healthcare workers- the National Commission for 
Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021, which also provides for mechanisms of task -
shifting and sharing across professions.  
 Continuing with the reforms the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Bill is also 
being introduced in the Parliament. 
 In the light of ongoing pandemic, the Government has also reconstituted Empowered 
Groups (EG), the EG -3 with a mandate to oversee augmen tation of human resources and 
capacity building has two subgroups. The subgroups in the report have also defined 
facility based specific roles of professionals enabling task shifting and task sharing across 
different professions to ensure better care deliv ery. This has not only helped in mitigating 
the surge during pandemic, but will also help in ensuring services through 
multidisciplinary team based approach.  
 In addition, a Committee has been set up to look into the skewed distribution of nurses 
between t he rural and urban area and appropriate action will be taken upon receipt of 
their Report.

Child Health (R CH) services and Communicable Diseases services and by including services 
related to Non -Communicable Diseases (NCD) such as, Hypertension, Diabetes and common 
cancers of Oral, Breast and Cervix.  
3.3 AB-PMJAY provides health insurance coverage up to Rs. 5 .00 lakh per family per year to 
around 10.74 crore poor and vulnerable families (nearly 50 crore individuals) identified based on 
Socio Economic Caste Census (SECC) data.

tertiary care will lead to reduced OOPE. 
Further Recommendations 
3.5 The Committee understands that Ayushman Bharat aims to provide free access to 
health insurance coverage for the poor and improve accessibility of health services in the 
country. However, the Committee notes that there are administrative and implementation 
related loopholes under the scheme that need to be addressed  so as to provide universal 
coverage to the poor and the needy . The Committee, in this connection, wishes to flag the 
constraints related to non-updation of the list of beneficiaries, fraud ulent practices at 
empanelled hospitals, incomplete operationalization of the Health and Wellness Centres .  
The Committee desires the Ministry to address these issues besides giving imp etus to 
increasing the pace of implementation of the Scheme for the overall well being and good 
health of the economically weaker sections of the society.

as percentage of total expenditure (as per 2018 -19 Actual) of Meghalaya, NCT of Delhi and

Health Policy's target of health expenditure to 8 pe rcent of the State's budget. However the 
Committee is dismayed to note that most States have not allocated the stipulated percentage of 
their budget to the health sector. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that all the 
States and UTs must spend at least 8 percent of their total budget for the health sector as 
envisaged in the National Health Policy.

efficiently.

poor healthcare delivery system. The Committee desires that the States must be incentivized

Recommendation 
3.67 The Committee recommends the Department to make concerted efforts to upgrade the 
education standard of nursing in the country to global standard and fill up vacant posts of various 
cadres of Nursing in various hospitals in  the country so as to enhance the Nurse patient ratio in 
general. The present nurse patient ratio in the country is 1.7 nurses per 1000 population, is 
indicative of the shortage of nurses in the country. The Committee also desires that the issue of 
skewed distribution of nurses between rural and urban are needs to be addressed, suitably as per 
the recommendation of the Committee of Experts constituted under the chairpersonship of Dr. 
Bimla Kapoor. 
(Para 3.115)

of the Country are filled up by the respective State Governments. The Committee set up by this 
Ministry to look into skewed distribution of nurses between rural and urban area has begun their 
work and appropriate action will be taken upon receipt of their Report. 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
3.69 The Committee , in 126 th Report, had highlighted the shortage of nurses in the 
country which remains a grave concern; however the response of the Ministry, thereto, in its 
ATNs, is not tenable. The recruitment rules may vary from States to States but the Union 
Government must play a guid ing role in ensuring that the nurse and patient ratio in the 
country is improved. The Committee observes that while the nursing sector is in need of 
reforms, the issues like poor career progression, low remuneration, high workload etc 
plague the sector. Th e Ministry in consultation with the States must make efforts to ensure 
that the working conditions of the nurses are improved and the profession gets the respect it 
deserves. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to take appropriate action on the 
recommendations of the Committee of Experts constituted under the chairpersonship of Dr. 
Bimla Kapoor.

Recommendation 
3.70 The Committee fails to understand the rationale behind making provision for Rs. 35000.00 
crore for Covid-19 vaccination in Demand for Grants No. 40 transfer to the States during 2021 -
22. The Committee feels that the devolution of funds to States should have appropriately been 
through the Ministry of Health and Family  Welfare, being the Nodal Ministry involved in the 
implementation of the Covid -19 Vaccination Programmes. Even the release of fund to the States 
could have been better monitored by the Nodal Ministry keeping in view the progress of 
programme for Covid-19 Vaccination. 
(Para 3.142) 
Action Taken 
3.71 In the current financial year i.e. 2021 -22, INR 35,000 crore has been budgeted for 
procurement of COVID -19 Vaccin e. As on 27 th November 2021, an expenditure of INR 
19,675.46 crore has been incurred against this allocation which has been utilized for procurement 
of COVID -19 vaccine for free of cost supply to State/UTs. No separate expenses have been 
allocated for fuel. 
3.72 Further, an additional budget of Rs.4500 crore from Ministry of Finance has been sought 
for ensuring uninterrupted supply of vaccines and to protect the country. 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
3.73 The Committee observes that out of Rs. 35,000 crores  earmarked in 2021 -22 for 
procurement of COVID vaccine, an expenditure of Rs. 19,675.46 crores has been incurred as 
on 27th November, 2021 and funds to the tune of Rs. 15324.54 crores remain unspent  despite 
due and cry for vaccine doses . The Committee takes into account the concerns regarding 
issues of shortage of vaccines , raised by many States in the past few months rather some 
States claiming downsizing of the vaccines supply. Although, the Committee notes that the 
supply of vaccine doses to States is calculated on a formula that weighs all the factors like 
population, efficiency, active case -load, etc. the Committee recommends that vaccine equity 
must be ensured for mitigation of Covid -19 on ground level.  The Committee also desires 
strict monitoring over proper utilization of the funds budgeted for procurement of Covid -19 
vaccine doses. With the threat of Omicorn variant looming large and the rising concerns 
around omicron variant escaping immunity, calls of administering the booster doses of 
vaccines have drawn the attention of all. Moreover, with the start of vaccination programme 
for children between the age group of 15 -18 years, the Ministry must accordingly assess the 
additional budgetary requirements to ensure uninterrupted procurement and supply of  
vaccines to all the sections of the country.  The Committee also desires that issue of 
administering booster dose/precaution dose to all must be estimated without delay and 
adequate availability of vaccines must be ensured.

National Mental Health Programme 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.99 The Committee observes that Rs.50.00 crore was allotted at BE 2018 -19 under the NMHP 
and the same was reduced to Rs. 40 crore in BE 2019 -20 and BE 2020 -21. However to make 
things worse, the actual expenditure was Rs. 2.01 crore, Rs. 2.51 crore and Rs. 9.07crore in 2018-
19, 2019 -20, 2020 -21, respectively. The Committee expres ses its deep concerns over the gross 
under utilization of funds under National Mental Health Programme followed by dwindling trend 
of allocation of funds.The Committee is of the view that a constant under utilization over the years 
under this head clearly points towards the Ministry's inability to comprehend the magnitude of 
mental health burden in the country. Various studies have highlighted the high prevalence of 
mental illness in the country but no substantial progress has been achieved to facilitate a robust 
mechanism for delivery of mental healthcare services. 
(Para 4.82) 
Action Taken 
3.100 The approval for continuation of tertiary care programmers during 2019 -20 provided that 
no new activity could be supported under the programme and further release of funds to already 
supported Institutions will be on reimbursement basis. This Ministry had requested the Institutions 
already supported under NMHP to submit proposals for further release of funds as per the revised 
funding mechanism. However, funds alloc ated under the tertiary care component of NMHP could 
not be utilized due to lack of proposals from States/UTs for release of funds on reimbursement 
basis, despite regular follow up. The actual expenditure was Rs.2.01 Crores, Rs.2.50 Crores and 
Rs. 20.43 Crores in the years 2018-19, 2019-20 & 2020-2021 respectively. 
Further Recommendations/Observations  
3.101 The factors of poor utilization of budget under the Scheme and the lack of proposals 
from the States /UTs jointly contribute to the prevalence of mental health issues in the 
country. Despite reports citing the prevalence of mental health illness among the Indian 
population, the very indifference shown by the States reflects the continuing trivialization of 
the issue. Lack of awa reness about the importance of redressal /treatment of mental health 
issues is one of the major hindrances in implementation of the Scheme.  
3.102 The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to incentivize the Institutes in 
carrying out activities un der the revised funding mechanism and ensure that there is no 
delay in reimbursements to the Institutes. The Committee believes that the need of the hour 
is to launch a awareness campaign based on a systematic understanding of the magnitude of 
mental health burden and assessing the trends and its prevalence for all the States/UTs. The 
States/UTs must cooperate with the Central Government  so that a robust policy aimed 
towards alleviating the burden and mainstreaming the mental health issue can be 
implemented at the ground level.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
follow up the matter with the Institutes and the States/UTs to start different programs and 
submit proposals for release of funds.  

92 
 
Recommendation 
3.103 The Committee points out that Ministry did not launch any specific programs pertaining to 
mental health during Covid -19. According to WHO about 7.5 percent Indians suffer from some 
mental disorder and WHO predicted that by 2020, roughly 20 per cent of Indi a will suffer from 
mental illnesses. The Committee is of the view that unprecedented condition during the pandemic 
would have considerably increased the prevalence of depressive disorders and mental illness in 
the country. The Committee desires the Ministr y to conduct a study to assess the prevalence of 
mental illness, depressive disorders and suicide death rate in the country including the impact of 
the pandemic on the mental health of the population. 
(Para 4.83) 
Action Taken 
3.104 The Ministry has not launched any special Schemes under the National Mental Health 
Programme considering the increase in mental health issues due to COVID -19. However, 
realizing the impact that COVID-19 may have on the mental health of the people the Gover nment 
has taken a number of initiatives to provide psychosocial support during COVID -19. These 
initiatives include.  
a. Setting up of a 24/7 helpline in March,2020 itself, to provide psychosocial support, by 
mental health professionals, to the entire affected  population, divided into different target 
groups viz children adult, elderly, women and healthcare workers.  
b. Issuance of guidelines/advisories on management of mental health issues, catering to 
different segments of the society. 
c. Advocacy through various m edia platforms in the form of creative and audio -visual 
materials on managing stress and anxiety, and promoting an environment of supported and 
care for all.  
d. Issuance of detailed guidelines by the National Institute of Mental Health and 
Neurosciences (NIM HANS), Bengaluru -―Mental Health in the times of COVID -19 
Pandemic-Guidance for General Medical and Specialized Mental Health Care Settings.‖ 
e. Online capacity building of health workers by NIMHANS in providing psychosocial 
support and training through (IGOT)-Diksha platform. 
3.105   In addition to the above, the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) component of 
the National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) has been sanctioned for implementation in 692 
districts for which support is provided to States/UTs through the National Health M ission. 
Facilities made • available under DMHP at the Community Health Centre(CHC) and Primary 
Health Centre(PHC) levels, inter -alia, include outpatient services, assessment, counselling/ 
psycho-social interventions, continuing care and support to persons with severe mental disorders, 
drugs, outreach services, ambulance services etc. In addition to above services there is a 
provision of 10 bedded in-patient facility at the District level. 
Further Recommendations/Observations  
3.106 The Committee has time and again emphasized on the importance of mental health 
and the need of integrating mental health in the health policy of the Government. The 
pandemic brought about a significant increase in the number of people struggling with 
mental health issues. The Co mmittee is of the  considered view that the Ministry needs to 

93 
 
amplify its efforts in delivering mental health services to the masses. The Committee , 
therefore, reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must conduct a study to assess 
the prevalence of mental illness, depressive disorders and suicide death rate in the country 
including the impact of the pandemic on the mental health of the population.  
Recommendation 
3.107 The Committee is appalled at the shortage of mental health professionals in the co untry. 
As per WHO Mental Health Atlas 2017, India has only 1.93 mental health workers and 0·29 
psychiatrists per 100,000 populations, which is much below the global average. The Committee is 
also dismayed to note the lack of a centrally maintained data bas e on the number of clinical 
health professionals working in the field of mental health in the country. The Committee strongly 
recommends the Ministry to create a database on the number mental health professionals in the 
country so as to realistically assess their requirement. 
(Para 4.84) 
Action Taken 
3.108 With a view to augment the availability of trained manpower in the field of mental health 
in the country, the Government is implementing Manpower Development Schemes for 
establishment of Centres of Excellence and strengthening/ establishment of Post Graduate (PG) 
Departments in mental health specialties. Till date, support has been provided for establishment of 
25 Centres of Excellence and strengthening/ establishment of 47 Post Graduate (PG) Departm ents 
in four mental health specialties viz. (i) Psychiatry, (ii) Clinical Psychology, (iii) Psychiatric 
Nursing, and (iv) Psychiatric Social Work, in the country. This Ministry has, from time to time, 
emphasized to the respective State/UT Governments, the need for timely completion of work 
pertaining to the establishment of Centres of Excellence and strengthening/establishment of Post 
Graduate Departments in mental health specialties. The respective States/UTs have also been 
requested to furnish UCs for fun ds released, seek balance funds on reimbursement basis and 
complete the approved projects expeditiously. 
3.109 In addition to the Manpower Development Schemes of NMHP, the Government is also 
augmenting the availability of manpower to deliver mental healthcare services in the underserved 
areas of the country by providing online training courses to various healthcare service providers 
like medical officers, psychologists, social workers and nurses to deliver quality mental healthcare 
services throughou t the country through the Digital Academies established at the three Central 
Mental Health Institutes, namely, National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences, 
Bengaluru, Lokopriya Gopinath Bordoloi Regional Institute of Mental Health, Tezpur, Assam , 
and Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi. 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
3.110 The Committee recommends the Ministry to pursue the activities pertaining to 
mission of the establishment of Center of Excellence i n mental health specialties in  the 
States/UTs. The poor availability of mental health specialists in the  country is a matter of 
concern, especially, when the pandemic has significantly amplified the mental health issues 
around the world. The Ministry must make constant efforts to bring  about a change in the 
attitude towards mental health issues through awareness generation programmes and giving 
due impetus to effective implementation of Manpower Development Scheme . The 

94 
 
Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to work towards providing  mental health 
care services even at primary and community healthcare level. The Committee believes that 
the Ministry must address the shortage of mental health professionals in the country for 
ensuring availability of mental health care services to the ge neral public. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must create a database on the number of 
mental health professionals in the country so as to realistically assess their requirement.

3.139 The Committee takes into account the submission of the Ministry that utilization of AB -
PMJAY was adversely impacted with the onset of the COVID -19 pandemic, however, the

101 
 
21, Rs. 6400 crore were allocated which was again reduced to Rs.3100 crore. The Committee is

Action Taken 
3.140 National Health Authority concurs with the observation made by the Hon‘ble DRPSC. The 
utilization under AB-PMJAY was sub-optimal due to following reasons: 
o There was gradual uptake in the scheme in the initial two  years of implementation as 
States/UTs were putting in place the necessary mechanisms to operationalize the scheme. 
o A few States with nearly 20% of the eligible SECC beneficiary population haven‘t joined the 
scheme. 
o Certain States chose to join the scheme only from 2019 onwards. 
o Demand for services in in three States that account for 30% of the beneficiary base viz. Uttar 
Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar was muted in the initial phase. 
o It was expected that the demand under AB -PMJAY would pick up from 2020 onwards. 
However, the onset of COVID -19 had an adverse impact on the functioning of AB -PMJAY 
as evidenced by 
 (i) A 30% decline in the number of authorized hospital admissions during the period 
from March‘20 to August‘20 
 (ii) Potential shortfall of 1.20 Cro re Ayushman cards due to interruption in beneficiary 
enrollment activities 
 (iii) The performance of 79% empanelled private hospitals were negatively impacted   
during the period from Apr‘20 to Jun‘20. 
3.141 In this regard, NHA is undertaking various steps i ncluding measures to foster greater 
participation from SHAs.  
 A capacity development framework has been developed and shared with SHAs regarding 
the deployment of adequate human resources at State and District level. NHA shall ask 
SHAs, yet to fulfil the n orms of the framework to ensure strict compliance with respect to 
the same. 
 The ongoing Aapke Dwar Ayushman campaign has been designed to foster greater 
ownership from the SHAs. SHAs have risen to the occasion by using innovative methods 
including greater involvement of Panchayati Raj institutions, frontline healthcare workers, 
village level entrepreneurs from CSC and UTIITSL to achieve the targets under the 
campaign. 
 A new division called ―Provider Operations‖ has been established at NHA. One of the key 
objectives of this division is to strengthen the District Implementation Units (DIUs) across 
the country. An exercise in this regard has already been carried out in Bihar and 
Jharkhand.

continues to cause various human diseases and include Aflatoxins that have the potential to cause

acute exposure to high concentrations in food. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends

 The Committee understands that Ayushman Bharat aims to provide free access to 
health insurance coverage for the poor and improve accessibility of health services in the

related loopholes under the scheme that need to be addressed so as to provide universal 
coverage to the poor and the needy. The Committee, in this connection, wishes to fl ag the 
constraints related to non -updation of the list of beneficiaries, fraudulent practices at 
empanelled hospitals, incomplete operationalization of the Health and Wellness Centres.  
The Committee desires the Ministry to address these issues besides giv ing impetus to 
increasing the pace of implementation of the Scheme for the overall well being and good 
health of the economically weaker sections of the society. 
(Para 3.5 of 126th Report) 
 The Committee expresses its deep concern over the existing inter-state disparity on 
health infrastructure and the poor health indicators. The Committee believes that adequate 
budget allocation to health sector is concomitant to ensure robust implementation of health 
sector reforms in the States. Financially poor S tates lack adequate resources which result in 
poor healthcare delivery system. The Committee desires that the States must be incentivized 
for better performance on health matrix so as to ensure achievement of improved health 
outcomes. The Ministry must sup port and encourage the States/UTs so that they spend at -
least 8% of the total budget in the health sector and ensure that implementation of different 
Health Schemes are not hindered due to lack of funds. 
(Para 3.8) 
 The Committee finds that the Ministry ha s not taken any note of the 
recommendation of the Committee to consider the proposal of Rs. 5,97,906.56 crores made 
to the 15 th Finance Commission.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation 
and expects the Ministry to vigorously pursue its b udgetary requirements suggested by the 
Finance Commission.   
(Para 3.14) 
 The Committee is anguished to find that against total allocated amount of Rs. 29.00 
crores in 2020 -21 under RSBY, the actual expenditure is to the tune of Rs. 46, 32,366 only. 
The Committee has been consistently emphasizing upon increasing the budgetary outlay of 
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on various schemes. The Committee believes 
that the Ministry must follow a sound budgetary management policy wherein schemes with 
poor utilization trends are closely monitored. The Committee is of the considered view that 
the Ministry must make efforts to ensure that the funds allocated are utilized optimally to 
make the Scheme result oriented and achieve the Mission and objective of t he Scheme. The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry to frame guidelines on financial prudence in 
consultations with States and track the utilization under the Schemes so that utilization of 
funds is commensurate with the projected requirement and under -utilization of funds is 
avoided. The argument of the Ministry that increased outlay would lead to increase in 
proportionate share of the States does not look sound and convincing.  
(Para 3.20) 

111

liquidation of the pending UCs. The fact that Utilization certificates for funds amounting to 
Rs. 17342.54 crore and Rs. 22.30 crore are pending under Human Resources for Health and 
Medical Education and National AIDS & STD Control Progra mme respectively speaks 
volume of poor management and monitoring of allocated funds. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must start monitoring of UCs through the

(Para 3.23)

with UPSC and SSC so as to expedite the recruitment process for the vacant 349 posts of 
Medical Officer in GDMO sub cadre and all vacant posts from Gazetted staff re spectively 
for the smooth implementation of the scheme and continuation of assured healthcare 
services to the beneficiaries of the scheme.   
(Para 3.30) 
 The Committee desires that all generic AYUSH Medicine must be made available to 
the beneficiary at CGH S dispensary. The Committee finds that the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare has not furnished any information on the assured supply of allopathic 
medicines to the CGHS dispensary. The Committee would like the Ministry to take effective 
measures for en suring a continuous supply of allopathic medicines and develop a robust 
mechanism for delivery of medicines to all the CGHS dispensary.  
(Para 3.33) 
 The Committee is constrained to highlight a huge gap between the sanctioned 
strength (905) and the in -position strength (643) as 262 posts in different cadres are lying 
vacant in SJH and VMC. The Committee observes that the Institute is yet to 
formulate/amend the recruitment rules for some categories of Posts and approval for filling 
up some vacant posts are yet to be finalized. The Committee is anguished over the slow pace 
of recruitment process in such a reputed Institute and, therefore, strongly recommends the 
Institute to expedite the recruitment process and fill up the vacant posts so that the Institute 
can function at its full capacity.  
(Para 3.36) 

112 
 
         The Committee observes that most issues in Safdurjung Hospital and Vardhman 
Mahavir Medical College could have been resolved under a coordinated approach of the 
serving agencies. The Committee notes th at the hostel facilities and stack parking around 
newer blocks are yet to start and the Ministry must avoid further procedural delays. The 
Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to work out the proposals on redevelopment 
of staff colony and hostel facilities and ensure the completion of all the pending projects. The 
Committee also reiterates its recommendation that the Medical Superintendent of the 
hospital may be vested with the power to hire staff/faculty on contract as per the situational 
requirement of the Hospital. 
(Para 3.39) 
 The Committee expresses its anguish over delay in approval of Layout Plans for the 
infrastructure project in VMMC. The Committee calls upon the Ministry to expedite the 
process of granting necessary approvals to the project o n construction of proposed 
accommodation facilities. The Ministry must fix accountability for undue delays in 
completion of projects and ensure timely execution of all projects. The Committee also 
recommends the Ministry to follow up the pending proposals with the Ministry of Finance 
and ensure that adequate funds are earmarked for additional infrastructure projects. 
(Para 3.45) 
 The Committee is shocked to note the evasive reply of the Ministry on the progress of 
infrastructure projects in ABVIMS and Dr. R ML Hospital. The Committee finds that the 
scheduled date of completion of the two infrastructure Projects, undertaken by the Atal 
Bihari Vajpayee Institute of Medical Sciences (ABVIMS) and Dr. RML Hospital was 
14.09.2019, however, the date has now been ext ended to 14.03.2022. The Committee, taking 
note of the poor record of the Institute, recommends the Ministry to ensure that the 
construction activities are completed in the extended deadline without any further time and 
cost over-runs.  
(Para 3.48) 
LADYHARDINGE MEDICALCOLLEGE (LHMC) &SMT.S.K.HOSPITAL 
 The Committee desires the Ministry to assess the actual requirement of funds for 
LHMC and S.K. Hospital and take urgent corrective measures to mitigate financial liability 
under the Comprehensive Redevelopment  Plan of LHMC phase -I; alongwith incurred 
expenditure on procurement of Machinery and equipment, setting up of clinical skill lab and 
Operation and Maintenance (O&M).  The Committee expects the Ministry to furnish a 
status note on the project within one month of presentation of this report to Parliament. 
(Para 3.51) 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the vacant positions of 70 faculty and 804 
non faculty posts continuing in LHMC. The Committee is of the considered view that delay 
in seeking administr ative approval or any other procedural delays slows down the pace of 
recruitment process. The Committee underlines the need to fill up the vacant posts on a 
regular basis and within a specified period of time. The Committee also reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministry may delegate administrative autonomy to the Institute 

113 
 
for recruitment of non -faculty members and appointment of Assistant Professors on a 
contract basis. The Institute must also take measures to fill up the vacant posts on 
permanent basis to ensure continuity and smooth functioning of the institute. 
(Para 3.58) 
KALAWATI SARAN CHILDEN'S HOSPITAL 
 The Committee wonders that KSCH has not responded to the recommendation of the 
Committee over vacancy positions and status of the recruitment p rocess to fill up the vacant 
posts. The Committee observes that against the total sanctioned strength of 773 posts in 
various cadres, the in-position strength has further decreased to 666 and thus 107 posts still 
remain vacant. The Committee, therefore, wo uld like the Institute to expedite the 
recruitment process for filling up the vacant posts. 
(Para 3.61) 
 The Committee expresses its displeasure at the existing gap between the sanctioned 
strength and the in -position strength of the AIIMS like Institutions. The Committee opines 
that such a wide gap would impact the day to day functioning of the Institutes. Th e 
Committee, therefore, strongly desires the Ministry to take suitable measures to address the 
issue of shortfall of manpower in Project Cell, Faculty and Non faculty in these Institutes. 
The Committee further recommends for expediting the recruitment proc ess so that the 
AIIMS like Institutes excel in their envisaged goal and mission.  
(Para 3.66) 
OTHER HOSPITALS/ INSTITUTIONS 
DEVELOPMENT OF NURSING SECTOR 
 The Committee, in 126 th Report, had highlighted the shortage of nurses in the 
country which remains a grave concern; however the response of the Ministry, thereto, in its 
ATNs, is not tenable. The recruitment rules may vary from States to States but the Union 
Government must pla y a guiding role in ensuring that the nurse and patient ratio in the 
country is improved. The Committee observes that while the nursing sector is in need of 
reforms, the issues like poor career progression, low remuneration, high workload etc 
plague the sector. The Ministry in consultation with the States must make efforts to ensure 
that the working conditions of the nurses are improved and the profession gets the respect it 
deserves. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to take appropriate action on the 
recommendations of the Committee of Experts constituted under the chairpersonship of Dr. 
Bimla Kapoor. 
(Para 3.69) 
COVID-19 VACCINATION FOR HEALTH CARE WORKERS AND FRONTLINE 
WORKERS – NHM 
 The Committee observes that out of Rs. 35,000 crores earmarked in 2021 -22 for 
procurement of COVID vaccine, an expenditure of Rs. 19,675.46 crores has been incurred as 

114 
 
on 27th November, 2021 and funds to the tune of Rs. 15324.54 crores remain unspent despite 
due and cry for vaccine doses. The Committee takes into acco unt the concerns regarding 
issues of shortage of vaccines, raised by many States in the past few months rather some 
States claiming downsizing of the vaccines supply. Although, the Committee notes that the 
supply of vaccine doses to States is calculated on  a formula that weighs all the factors like 
population, efficiency, active case -load, etc. the Committee recommends that vaccine equity 
must be ensured for mitigation of Covid -19 on ground level.  The Committee also desires 
strict monitoring over proper utilization of the funds budgeted for procurement of Covid -19 
vaccine doses. With the threat of Omicorn variant looming large and the rising concerns 
around omicron variant escaping immunity, calls of administering the booster doses of 
vaccines have drawn the attention of all. Moreover, with the start of vaccination programme 
for children between the age group of 15 -18 years, the Ministry must accordingly assess the 
additional budgetary requirements to ensure uninterrupted procurement and supply of 
vaccines t o all the sections of the country. The Committee also desires that issue of 
administering booster dose/precaution dose to all must be estimated without delay and 
adequate availability of vaccines must be ensured.  
(Para 3.73) 
STATUS OF ON-GOING PROJECTS TAKEN BY AIIMS, NEW DELHI 
 The Committee notes with concern that the pace of completion of construction 
projects at AIIMS New Delhi has been very slow. Almost all the construction projects got 
delayed and the target date of completion for all the four projec ts has been extended. The 
Committee observes that the delay in the construction work was mainly due to non 
performance by the selected construction agencies and the lockdown imposed during the 
pandemic Covid-19. As per the submission of the Institute, all the projects should have been 
completed by now. However, the Committee finds undue delay in completion of projects in 
Surgical Block, New Paid Ward and Geriatrics Block due to variety of reasons as advocated. 
The Committee is assured that the Institute nee ds to adopt a stringent monitoring 
mechanism so that any remaining work is completed within the stipulated time limits. The 
Institute must put in place a robust assessment process for selection of the project 
development agency or contractor, taking into c onsideration its past track record so that 
such unnecessary additional costs and time extensions are minimized in future Projects and 
time lines are adhered to.  
(Para 3.76) 
REDEVELOPMENT OF RESIDENTIAL COLONIES OF AIIMS (AYURVIGYAN 
NAGAR & WEST ANSARI NAGAR) 
 The Committee notes that the approval of the construction of 3519 dwelling units 
were given by the Cabinet on 13.10.2016 and the units were expected to be completed within 
the span of 60 months. The timeline has already elapsed and the final approval from NDMC 
and SDMC is still awaited. The Committee is of the opinion that undue delay in the 
construction activities leads to unnecessary costs and time overruns.  Needless to say, factors 
like inflation, abrupt ending of contracts, arbitration cases, disputes etc. contribute to undue 
disruptions in completion of a project. The Committee recommends the Ministry to make a 
proper assessment before the beginning of any project and conduct regular review meeting 

115 
 
to track the progress of the project. This will ensure  timely completion of the ongoing 
projects and also help avoid time and cost overruns. 
(Para 3.82) 
IMPLEMENTATION OF MASTER PLAN OFAIIMS NEW DELHI 
POST GRADUATE INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES AND RESEARCH 
(PGIMER), CHANDIGARH 
 The Committee observes that th e delay in the Project of "Modernisation of Research 
Block A and B and Modernization of Nehru Hospital", PGIMER Chandigarh was mainly 
due to the non -performance by the selected construction agency. The Committee, therefore, 
desires that the remaining work which is now planned to be carried out departmentally 
must be monitored closely. For this to happen, stringent monitoring mechanism need to be 
put in place for timely completion of the work. The Committee, in this connection, 
recommends the Institute to ex pedite the review process and complete the Modernisation 
Project without further delay. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the status of 
the Satellite Centre of PGIMER, Chandigarh at Sangrur (Punjab).  
(Para 3.85) 
 The Committee is perturbed to note that despite the best efforts by Institute to fill up 
the vacant posts, there still exists a gap in the in -position strength and the sanctioned 
strength in various cadres of PGIMER Chandigarh due to continuing administration 
blockade. The Committee is of the view that the Institute must address the shortage of 
workforce at all levels and fill up the vacant posts at various levels without further delay. 
The Committee would also like to be updated on the application filed before the Supreme 
Court and t he litigation cases pending in the court pertaining to filling up of vacant posts 
through promotion.  
(Para 3.89) 
NATIONAL HEALTH MISSION 
Immunization 
 The Committee is aware of the fact that the National Immunization Schedule, vaccine 
doses and dosing int erval is decided based on the recommendations of National Technical 
Advisory Group for Immunization (NTAGI). The Committee is however concerned over 
other vaccines that are not part of the National Immunization Schedule. The Committee is 
of the view that t he vaccines administered outside the Immunization Programme must also 
have uniformity in doses and schedule. Vaccines for diseases that are endemic to a 
geographical area must only be administered in that particular area. The Committee further 
recommends t hat universal coverage be part of the National Immunisation Schedule that 
contains provision of booster doses as precaution dose to all as guard against emerging 
variants of Coronavirus.  
(Para 3.93) 

116 
 
Strengthening of State Drug Regulatory System 
  The Committee wonders as to why the State Government of West Bengal and UTs of 
Lakshadweep and Chandigarh are hesitant in signing the MoU with the Central Government 
under the Scheme of Strengthening of State Drugs Regulatory System despite persuasion by 
the Department of H&FW. The Committee also expresses its displeasure over the slow pace 
of activities under the Scheme of the Ministry which is aimed at upgrading and strengthening 
the States Drug's Regulatory structures. The Committee emphasizes that poor test ing 
infrastructure in the country poses a hindrance in ensuring safety and quality of drugs 
available for consumption.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Department, 
to coordinate with States/UT Government with a view to put in place a vibr ant, dynamic and 
effective regulatory regime for safeguarding the public from substandard drugs. The 
States/UTs also need to be persuaded for implementation of the Scheme. 
(Para 3.98) 
 National Mental Health Programme 
  The factors of poor utilization of b udget under the Scheme and the lack of proposals 
from the States /UTs jointly contribute to the prevalence of mental health issues in the 
country. Despite reports citing the prevalence of mental health illness among the Indian 
population, the very indiffer ence shown by the States reflects the continuing trivialization of 
the issue. Lack of awareness about the importance of redressal /treatment of mental health 
issues is one of the major hindrances in implementation of the Scheme.  
(Para 3.101) 
  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to incentivize the Institutes in 
carrying out activities under the revised funding mechanism and ensure that there is no 
delay in reimbursements to the Institutes. The Committee believes that the need of th e hour 
is to launch a awareness campaign based on a systematic understanding of the magnitude of 
mental health burden and assessing the trends and its prevalence for all the States/UTs. The 
States/UTs must cooperate with the Central Government so that a ro bust policy aimed 
towards alleviating the burden and mainstreaming the mental health issue can be 
implemented at the ground level. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
follow up the matter with the Institutes and the States/UTs to start dif ferent programs and 
submit proposals for release of funds.  
(Para 3.102) 
  The Committee has time and again emphasized on the importance of mental health 
and the need of integrating mental health in the health policy of the Government. The 
pandemic brought  about a significant increase in the number of people struggling with 
mental health issues. The Committee is of the considered view that the Ministry needs to 
amplify its efforts in delivering mental health services to the masses. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must conduct a study to assess 
the prevalence of mental illness, depressive disorders and suicide death rate in the country 
including the impact of the pandemic on the mental health of the population.  
(Para 3.106) 

117 
 
  The Committee recommends the Ministry to pursue the activities pertaining to 
mission of the establishment of Center of Excellence in mental health specialties in the 
States/UTs. The poor availability of mental health specialists in the country is  a matter of 
concern, especially, when the pandemic has significantly amplified the mental health issues 
around the world. The Ministry must make constant efforts to bring about a change in the 
attitude towards mental health issues through awareness generation programmes and giving 
due impetus to effective implementation of Manpower Development Scheme. The 
Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to work towards providing mental health 
care services even at primary and community healthcare level. The Comm ittee believes that 
the Ministry must address the shortage of mental health professionals in the country for 
ensuring availability of mental health care services to the general public. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must crea te a database on the number of 
mental health professionals in the country so as to realistically assess their requirement. 
(Para 3.110) 
National Programme  for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, 
Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke 
  The Committee i s of the view that coordination between the States/UTs and the 
Center is crucial for successful implementation of any Scheme falling under State lists. For 
this both, the Central and State Governments need to come forward to share the 
responsibility for completion of the Projects. The Committee also recommends the Ministry 
to persuade States/UTs Government to timely submit all the pending utilization certificates 
and requisite documents so that additional funds are released for executing the activities 
connected to the project. 
(Para 3.113) 
  The Committee is aware that the States are the main implementing agencies of the 
Center’s policies. For this, the Ministry must ensure that they maintain a regular 
consultations and understanding with the States so that  there remains no confusion on the 
directives of the Center to the States. The Ministry must work towards establishing a 
coordination channel between the Center and the States/UTs so that the ongoing projects 
are timely completed. The Ministry must work in  tandem with the States/UTs and chalk out 
a timeframe for the operationalization of all the SCIs/TCCC. The Committee observes that 
since most States lack the institutional framework for public health management and thus 
depend on the Center for capital as well as technical support, therefore, the Central 
Government must provide technical and logistical support to the States/UTs Government 
for annual and successful completion of all the 19 State Cancer institute (SCI) and 20 
Tertiary Cancer Care Centre (TCCC).     
(Para 3.117) 
 The Committee believes that Research on the trend, incidences of cancer burden, the 
survival rate etc can guide the Ministry's realistic assessment of funds and help in framing a 
futuristic policy for controlling the increasing number of cancer patients in India. The 
Committee further reiterates its recommendation for establishment of Cancer speciality 
Institute under PPP scheme with the mission of undertaking extensive cancer research 

118 
 
projects. The Committee believes that timely updati on of Cancer registry would be followed 
by use of the registry in various research applications.  
(Para 3.121) 
 The Committee observes with concern that the operationalization of the new campus 
of CNCI had been delayed; however, the Committee understands t hat the outbreak of 
Pandemic Covid -19 has acted as a deterrent factor. The Committee, nevertheless, 
recommends the Institute to expedite the recruitment process and fill up the vacant posts of 
all the categories of the staff so that the Institute is put up  in operationalization mode at the 
earliest.  
(Para 3.126) 
Human Resources for Health and Medical Education 
  The Committee recommends the Ministry to closely monitor the progress of all the 
Medical Colleges in the States that have been approved under Phas e II and III of the 
scheme. The Committee urges the Ministry to sort out all the pending issues with the 
remaining 16 colleges under Phase II that have not applied for letter of permission to start 
the academic courses. The Committee further recommends the  Ministry to continue the 
timely transfer of funds and regular review meetings with the State authorities. The 
Ministry must make concerted efforts to achieve the envisaged vision of expanding tertiary 
care in peripheral areas and making provision and annu al appointment of all adequate 
number of doctors/specialist in the newly established medical colleges under Phase II and III 
of the Scheme. 
(Para 3.130) 
  The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that the Scheme is aimed at 
creating 10,000 MBBS seats in Government Colleges across the country. The Committee 
believes that the Center along with States needs to make concerted efforts to actively utiliz e 
the existing healthcare resources along with creation of new health infrastructure. The 
different Schemes under "Human Resources for Health and Medical Education"  aim to 
achieve the same. The Committee is of the view that the States must also shoulder th e 
responsibilities along with the Center and expedite the release of their share of funds under 
the Scheme.  
(Para 3.133) 
  The Committee appreciates that the Ministry has increased its release of funds under 
different phases of the three centrally sponsor ed Schemes. However, funds to the tune of Rs. 
16,467.66 crore still remain unreleased. The Committee is concerned at the pending of 
utilization certificates involving the funds released and recommends the Ministry to strongly 
take up the matter of pending utilization certificates with the States/UT Government. The 
Committee believes that the Ministry must find out workable strategies to resolve the 
pendency issues so as to release the remaining amount of funds for assured implementation 
of Scheme within sti pulated timeframe. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to 
devise new monitoring modules for ensuring definite progress of the development activities 

119 
 
in the Health Sector with objective of upgrading the medical infrastructure and enhance the 
health workforce in the country. 
(Para 3.138) 
 The Committee has time and again raised concerns on the different issues that have 
been posing a hurdle in the smooth implementation of the AB -PMJAY. There is also the 
need to increase awareness regarding AB -PMJAY among all the stakeholders, especially, 
the beneficiaries and the empanelled hospitals. The Ministry must also work towards 
strengthening the grievance redressal mechanism under the Scheme. The Committee notes 
that the list of beneficiaries is based on the SECC data which leaves a large group of p eople 
out of the beneficiary list. The Committee, therefore, strongly reiterates its recommendation 
that the Ministry must make efforts to expand and update the beneficiary base. The 
Committee recommends the Ministry to develop a foolproof monitoring mecha nism to 
ensure that no eligible person is denied health care services under the Scheme. The 
Committee desires that the Ministry must set up a robust monitoring mechanism and 
conduct periodic audits and inspections so that any fraudulent practices are avoided.  
(Para 3.142) 
  The Committee emphasizes that setting up Medi -City can help in addressing the 
issues related to shortage of doctors in certain areas and strengthen the health 
infrastructure in the country. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recom mendation that 
the Ministry must explore the idea of establishing Medi -city on PPP Model in the country. 
The Central Government, in coordination with the States, must chalk out a plan for 
establishing Medi-Cities across the country.  
(Para 3.147) 
 The Comm ittee emphasizes that the Ministry along with States must continue 
implementation of incentivising Schemes for encouraging doctors to serve in rural areas. 
The Committee also points out that National Medical Commission has succeeded the 
Medical Council of India and, therefore, the use of MCI may be avoided.  
(Para 3.150) 
HEALTH MANAGEMENT AND BUDGETING BEYOND PANDEMIC COVID -19 
IMPASSE 
  The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry must work towards 
creation of an All India Medical Services on the lines of All India Civil Services such as IAS, 
IPS and IFS. The Committee recommends the Ministry again to take up the matter with the 
States on priority basis. The Committee is of the considered view that the All India Medical 
Service would enhance  the success rate of Healthcare Projects and trigger policy 
formulation and ensure effective implementation of the Scheme at the ground level. 
(Para 3.153)

CHAPTER – I 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1 The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare comprises of the following two 
Departments: 
(a) Department of Health Research; and 
(b) Department of Health and Family Welfare 
 
The Vision, Mission and Objectives of the Ministry of Health  and Family Welfare are 
indicated as under: 
Vision 
Attainment of highest possible level of health and well -being for all, through 
preventive and promotive healthcare and universal access to good quality health services 
without anyone having to face financial hardship as a consequence. 
Mission 
 To ensure availability of quality healthcare on equitable, accessible and affordable 
basis across regions and communities with special focus on under -served population 
and marginalized groups. 
 To establish comprehensiv e primary healthcare delivery system and well -functioning 
linkages with secondary and tertiary care health delivery system. 
 To develop the training capacity for providing human resources for health (medical, 
paramedical and managerial) with adequate skill mix at all levels. 
 To regulate health service delivery and promote rational use of pharmaceuticals in the 
country. 
Objectives 
 To improve health status of the people through concerted action. 
 To expand preventive, promotive, curative, palliative and rehabilitative services 
provided through public health sector with focus on quality. 
 To progressively achieve Universal Health Coverage. 
1.2 The Department of Health & Family Welfare is implementing various schemes, 
programmes and national initiatives to p rovide universal access to quality healthcare as per 
the commitments of the National Health Policy 2017.  Several statutory and regulatory 
bodies, Autonomous bodies/ institutes, Central Government Health Scheme etc. work under 
the Department.  
Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY)  
1.3 PMSSY has been launched with the objectives of correcting regional imbalances in 
the availability of affordable/reliable tertiary healthcare services and to also augment 
facilities for quality medical education in the country.  
1.4 Setting up of 22 new AIIMS have been approved under PMSSY, of which 6 AIIMS at 
Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Jodhpur, Patna, Raipur and Rishikesh are fully functional and the rest 

2 
 
are at different stages. Demand for new AIIMS / addition al AIIMS are also received from 
States from time to time. 
Central Government Health Services (CGHS) 
1.5 CGHS provides comprehensive medical facilities to Central Govt. employees and 
members of their families in addition to other specified categories like M embers of 
Parliament (MPs), ex -MPs, ex -Governors, ex -Vice-Presidents, Retired Judges of Supreme 
Court and High Court, Freedom Fighters and members of their family, etc. The facilities 
under this scheme include outpatient care through a network of allopathi c, ayurvedic, 
homoepathic, unani/siddha dispensaries/units and also provide comprehensive medical 
facilities to Retired Central Govt. employees. 
 
National AIDS Control Programme (NACO)  
1.6 The programme aims at providing healthcare, support and treatment to people living 
with HIV/AIDS and to control this disease through State/UT/Municipal health societies 
across the country. 
1.7 The Government of India has taken many steps to provide affordable healthcare 
services to the people. As part of Ayushman Bharat,  the Government is supporting States for 
strengthening Sub Centres and Primary Health Centres as Health and Wellness Centres for 
provision of comprehensive primary care. Further, under Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana 
(PMJAY) (the second component of Ayush man Bharat), the Government provides coverage 
upto Rs. 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization to over 10 
crore poor and vulnerable families (approx. 50 crore persons). This scheme covers poor and 
vulnerable families base d on deprivation and occupational criteria as per Socio Economic 
Caste Census data. 
 1.8 In addition, the National Health Mission (NHM) provides financial and technical 
support to States/UTs for accessible, affordable and quality healthcare, especially to the poor 
and vulnerable sections of the population, in both urban and rural areas. Under NHM, all 
States/ UTs are supported for providing a host of free services including for maternal health, 
child health, adolescent health, family planning, universal imm unization programme, and for 
major diseases such as Tuberculosis, HIV/ AIDS, vector borne diseases such as Malaria, 
Dengue and Kala Azar, Leprosy etc. Other major initiatives for which states are being 
supported include Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JS SK), Rashtriya Bal Swasthya 
Karyakram (RBSK), Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK), implementation of 
NHM Free Drugs and Free Diagnostics Service Initiatives, PM National Dialysis Programme 
and implementation of National Quality Assurance Framework

2.12 In a specific reply to a query regarding the challenges faced by the States in 
increasing their health spending, the Ministry submitted that Delhi and Puducherry have 
attained required  level of 8% of health budget in total State budget. Other States are also 
exhorted to increase their budgetary allocation in health in order to reach the required level of 
8% or more which was identified as one of the goals in the National Health Policy o f 2017. 
The Ministry further submitted that there are Inter -State differences in absorption capacity of 
funds at the State level. The states are not uniformly poised in terms of health infrastructure 
as well as human resources, as a result, some states with low level of health infrastructure and 
human resource are not able to use the fund effectively.  
2.13 The Committee is concerned at the existing wide inter -State and intra -State 
disparity in healthcare infrastructure across the country. Despite the much emphasized 
guidelines of the NHP, the States/UTs barring Delhi and Puducherry have not enhanced 
the share of health budget to more than 8% of the total State budget in the last 5 years. 
The Committee understands that States with poor financial resources and inefficient 
fiscal capacity have a herculean task ahead to overcome the situation of fragile health 
infrastructure vis -a-vis the demand of accessible and affordable healthcare facilities. 
The Committee is of the considered view that in order to maximise the benefits of 
economic, social and human capital, the States must invest in institutionalizin g a robust 
healthcare ecosystem that is capable of delivering adequate healthcare services to the 
masses on ground level especially in rural, urban and tribal region. The sooner the 
States realize the difference, a resilient and strong health system makes,  the better will 
be the outcome on all social as well as economic indicators. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the States/UTs to emulate the UTs of Delhi and Puducherry and increase 
the share of health spending in their States Budget.  The Committee in  this regard 
recommends the Department of Health and Family Welfare to persuade the State 
Governments to achieve the budgetary health expenditure to 8%. 
2.14 The Committee noted that health has always remained an underperforming 
sector and despite funds al location many States are not performing well  on several 
health parameters. Many States lack the adequate absorption capacity to judiciously 
manage the allocated funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Union 
Government to incentivise the States/UTs to make ground assessment of the efficacy of 
the health policies and help the States design policies suiting the needs of the respective 
region. The Union Government must coordinate with the States to maximise the output 
under the Central Sector as well as Centrally Sponsored Schemes.  
2.15 The Committee  is also of the opinion  that robust health policies and judicious 
allocation of funds under different Schemes is fundamental for the optimal performance 
of the States/UTs. The Committee notes that healthcare  services remain highly 

9 
 
fragmented that further aggravates the problem of high OOPE in the country. The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends the Ministry to make efforts in developing a 
better healthcare financing mechanism and ensuring the delivery of quali ty healthcare 
services.

months and the Direct Recruitment vacancies within a year and to avoid increase in

Committee also feels that there should be a transparent transfer policy for the MOs & 
the staff so that no one person should occupy a policy position for a long period.

consider opening of treatments through yoga at all the Ayush dispensaries and also

3.21 The Committee notes that against the total allotted funds of Rs. 110.14 crore at 
BE 2021 -22 under the total Capital Head, funds to the tune of Rs. 68.08 crore were 
spent leaving a balance of Rs. 42.06 crore. The Committee further notes that under 
Capital Head "Machinery and Equipments", 55.27% of funds allocated in RE 2021 -22 
have been spent. Against the allocated funds of Rs. 1435.64 crore under the revenue 
head, funds to the tune of Rs. 1181.47 crore only have been spent thus leaving a balance 
of Rs. 254.17 crore. Considering the Utilisation trend in previous years, the Committee 
notes that the budgetary utilisation of the Institute has been satisfactory. However, the 
Committee notes that many construction projects are in pipe line in the Institute. The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends the Ministry to assess the budgetary 
requirements of the Institute and in case of any shortage of funds, the Institute may be 
allocated additional funds at the supplementary demand stage. The Co mmittee, 
however, recommend the balance funds under the Capital Head i.e. to the tune of Rs. 
42.06 crore should be optimally utilized for the indented purpose.  The Committee 
desires that the Institute must ensure that the funds are spent judiciously so as  to 
achieve the originally conceived objective within stipulated timeframe.

3.26 The Committee is dismayed at the slow pace of construction activities at the 
SJHVMC. The Committee notes that such unnecessary delays due to procedural and 
administrative hassles result in time and c ost overrun. The Committee emphasizes that 
all these issues could have been avoided through better monitoring and timely 
submission of the required receipts and documents by the Institute. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Institute to re -submit t he proposal regarding the 
redevelopment of staff colony and the DIB Note with revised cost for the redevelopment 
of hostel facilities. The Ministry must coordinate with the Institute and make efforts to 
adhere to the timeline for all the pending projects. The Committee is of the view that the 
inordinate delay in the Dwarka Project reflects poor management and poor planning on 
behalf of the Institute as well as the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Ministry to set realistic timelines for the  completion of the projects and make 
consistent efforts to adhere to the timelines.

specialized healthcare workforce. The Committee further notes that many measures 
have been taken up to fill up the vacant posts, nevertheless, the high vacancies in faculty 
and non -faculty in the Institutes necessitates concerted efforts to expedite the 
recruitment process. The Committee notes that AIIMS Patna and Raipur have the 
lowest faculty strength among all the new AIIMS established under Phase I o f PMSSY.

The Committee also observes that in AIIMS Raipur, 27 faculty posts have been filled up 
on contractual basis whereas in AIIMS Bhubaneshwar and Patna no faculty is working 
on contract.

highlighted the gross shortage of Professors/Additional Professor/Ass ociate

many important Departments such as Cardiology, Medical Oncology and Haematology, 
Neonatology, etc were just functioning with one doctor in the new AIIMS. The 
Committee understands that the shortage of doctors and specialists in the country is a 
major concern. However, the Ministry must make constant and concerted efforts to 
improve the faculty and student ratio in the Institutes and offer special 
packages/incentives and explore alternative such as paid research collaboration, better 
working hours etc to fill the vacant posts in the Institutes.

have been filled up on a regular bas is. The Committee expresses its concern and

posts.

roadmap for providing the necessary infrastructure, faculty and para -medical staff to 
all the 22 AIIMS functioning and scheduled to be operationlised in the next three years.

faculty and para -medical staff, besides the proper infrastructure most of the AIIMS

medical staff by providing specialised training or encourage institution involved in such

SOTTOs need to strengthen their institutions,   streamline their functioning for effective 
outcomes and devise an annual action plan.

34

States/UTs, namely, Telangana, Arun achal Pradesh, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh, Manipur,

3.85 The Committee note d that the Ministry has not been able  to utilize allocated  
funds under the National Organ Transplant Program (NOTP). The Committee observes 
that organ donation rate in the country is very low when compared to other countries 
and there is a huge lack of awareness among the public. The Committ ee feels that India 
has a vast potential of organ donations and demand due to its population but the 
Ministry needs to make concerted efforts to develop such feelings amongst its citizens. 
NOTP aims to promote organ donation and transplantation across all States/Union 
Territories in the country. However, the Committee notes that performance of the 
program has been very poor which is reflected by huge underutilisation of funds under 
the Scheme. The Committee notes that the Scheme was allotted Rs. 30.50 crore  in BE 
2021-22 which was slashed to Rs. 6.39 crore in RE 2021 -22 which is a 79% decrease 
with respect to BE 2021 -22. The Committee further notes that the program has been 
allotted a total of Rs. 15.00 crore in BE 2022-23.  
3.86 The Committee appreciates th at the program has been continued  for next five 
years i.e. 2021-22 to 2025 -2026 with a total outlay of Rs. 94.92 crore. The Committee, 
nevertheless, believes that cooperation and coordination among the States/UTs and the 
Union Government is crucial for the success of the program. The Committee wonders as 
to why 14 States have not forwarded their proposals for setting up of SOTTOs and the 
Ministry has received only few proposals for infrastructure up gradation from existing 
ROTTOs and SOTTOs. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to follow 
up with the States that are yet to submit the proposals for SOTTOs and convince them 
to come forward. The Ministry may take the matter with the States urgently and make 
consistent efforts to achieve the objectives of setting up of State Organ and Tissue 
Transplant Organisations (SOTTOs) in each State/UT, setting up of National/ 
Regional/State Bio-material centres and other envisaged targets under the program for 
successful achievement of cherished objectives of the program.  
3.87 The Committee also recommends the M inistry to share the findings of the 
assessment undertaken by the third party with the States/UTs. The Ministry must 
monitor the progress made by the States/UTs and issue guidelines regarding timely 
release of budgetary, allocation and expediting recruitme nt process etc. The Committee 
also notes that green corridors are also crucial for expediting organ transplantations. 
However, establishment of green corridor requires active coordination and 
participation from different agencies across the country. The Co mmittee, accordingly, 
recommends the Ministry to make consistent efforts to ensure development of such 
corridors and make efforts to engage all the stakeholders. The Committee also 
recommends the Ministry to explore usage of drones and modern technologies to 
minimise wastage of donor organs and ensure quick delivery of organs across the 
country.

registered street vendors.  The Committee notes that the Scheme of Indigenous Food 
Streets is a way forward to regulating the highly unorganised food sector and uplifting 
the safety and hygiene standards of street vended foods. The Committee strongly 
believes that the Street Food Ve ndors need to be trained in quality control, hygiene 
practices, safe handling, waste management etc. The Committee accordingly 
recommends the Ministry to approve the Central Sector Scheme and provide adequate 
budget for the Scheme so that a cleaner healthi er and safe street food culture can be 
established in the country. 
2. Strengthening of Food Testing System in the Country Including Provision of 
Mobile Food Testing Labs:  
ESSAI is implementing a Central Sector Scheme for "Strengthening of Food Testing Sys tem 
in the Country Including Provision of Mobile Food Testing Labs" (SOFTeL) with a total 
outlay of Rs. 481.95 Crore. The time frame for implem entation of the Scheme was 2016 -17 
to 2018 -19. MoH&FW vide letter dated 11.08.2021 had granted approval of the ex isting 
scheme for financial years 2019 -2020 and 2020 -2021 and extension of the scheme for a 
period of two years from FY 2021 -22 to 2022-23 with the modified scheme components and 
financial outlay of Rs. 241.34 Crore. 
The scheme would enable the States/UTs to analyse the regulatory and surveillance samples 
drawn by the FSO within the shortest possible time frame; to analyse the safety parameters in 
food samples such as Heavy metals, Pesticide residues, Antibiotic and drug residues and 
Naturally occurring tox ic substances along with Microbiological tests; to ensure compliance 
of FSSAI standards on food; to enable the laboratory to achieve NABL accreditation within 2 
years from the date of release of final installment; to become a resource point for training an d 
facility up-gradation for other existing Government / Public Food testing laboratories in the 
State; and to introduce online laboratory data management system through Laboratory 
Information Management System (LIMS).

4.1 The Department of Health and  Family Welfare submitted that the National Health 
Mission (NHM) is Department's flagship health systems  reform programme that provides a 
robust platform for implementation of a range of interventions   focused on primary and 
secondary health care in rural and urban areas. The National Health Mission (NHM) aims for 
attainment of universal access to equitable, affordable and quality health care services, 
accountable and responsive to people's needs, with effective inter -sectoral convergent action 
to address the wider social determinants of health.

infrastructure, augmentation of human resource, enhanced service delivery and 
decentralization of planning and implementation to district level to facilitate context specific 
& need based interventions & improved intra and inter -sectoral convergence for effective 
utilization of resources.
