CCH year after year, elections could not be co nducted. The Committee is not satisfied with the 
justification for delay given by the Department. It seems that the process of notification for 
election and appointment of Returning officers is  a very cumbersome procedure as it has taken 
more than two years to complete this exercise. Wh at is more disturbing is that elections still 
remained to be conducte d, reason being non-ma intenance/updation of State Registers of 
Homoeopathy by the States. The Committee takes a serious view of this. The Committee fails to 
understand the lack of initiative on the part  of the CCH/Department in getting the State 
Registers updated well in time. The Committee is of  the view that the Department should take 
the required steps for streamlining the election procedure for CCH. (Para 3.4) 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee has been given to understand th at maintenance of Central Register of 
Indian Medicine and updati ng of the same is a continuous pr ocess. The Committee, however, is 
constrained to note that out of the eighteen States having State Boards, as on 31.03.05, Gujarat 
is the only State whose state Re gister is updated upto January, 2005 . In the case of rest of the 
States, pendency ranges from March 1983 in J&K to August 2004 in Delhi. Pendency in the 
State Registers has an adverse effect on the maintenance of Central Register. The Committee 
would therefore like to impress upon the Depart ment to vigorously pursue with the State 
Government the updation of the State Registers. 
 With regard to Central Register of Homoeo pathy, CCH is required to get renewed the 
registers after every eight years. The Committee fi n d s  t h a t  i n  r e s p e c t  o f majority of States, 
renewal has become due but it seems no action has been initiated so far. The Committee urges 
upon the Department to take the required action without any further delay. The Committee also 
observes that Central Register of Homoeopathy cannot be cons idered updated in any respect. It 
covers varying period from 1982 to 2004 in respect of different states. It seems Gazette 
Notifications are also being issued after al ong time-gap. Procedural formalities may be 
responsible for such a situation.  The Committee is of the firm op inion that entire procedure of 
maintenance and updation of both State and Central Regist ers for Indian Medicine and 
Homoeopathy needs to be reviewed so as to ensure its timely publication. (Para 3.5) 
Comments of the Committee 
 Committee had drawn the attention of the Department to there being no check on practice 
by non-qualified doctors and quacks. Reply of the Department, however, does not give any idea 
about the existence of any monitoring mechan ism either at State or Central level. The 
Committee would like to reiterate that there is an urgent need for taking an initiative by the 
Department in this area. Such a move would go a long way in curbing the unauthorized practice 
by AYUSH doctors and also increasing the faith of  general masses in the traditional system of 
medicine. (Para 3.6) 
VII. CENTRAL COUNCIL FOR RESEARCH INSTITUTE OF UNANI MEDICINE, NEW 
DELHI 
Comments of the Committee 

 Committee’s attention has been drawn by the ve ry slow progress made in the construction 
work of the building of the Re gional Research Institute of Unani Medicine, Srinagar. The 
Committee understands that disturbances in the valley and shortage of funds are primarily 
responsible for this situation. The Committ ee is, however, not fu lly convinced by the 
justification given in this regard by the De partment. The Committee finds that not much 
progress seems to have been made in the constr uction of the building of RRIUM, Srinagar. The 
Committee had made a specific query about the orig inal estimate and the actual expenditure on 
the project. The Committee has been given to understand that against an original estimate of Rs. 
6.08 crore submitted by CPWD, total estimated expenditure now stands at Rs. 4.87 crore for the 
construction of the building undertaken by the Kashmir University. An amount of Rs. 4.37 crore 
has been released so far. The Committee’s speci fic query about the actual expenditure on the 
project remains unanswered. The Co mmittee is still not aware abou t the present status of the 
buildings of RRIUM, Srinagar. The Committee would like to be apprised in this regard. (Para 7.1) 
X.  SURVEY ON “USAGE & ACCEPTABILITY OF AYUSH’’ 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 The Committee has been info rmed that following two surv eys have been conducted by 
ICMR during the Tenth Plan- 
- Survey on ‘Usage and Acceptability of ISM& HD- final Report submitted in August, 2003 
- Survey on’ AYUSH beneficiaries covered under CGHS and selected Teaching hospitals 
attached to AYUSH Medical Colleges- draft report approved by the Department and final 
Report awaited.  
 The Committee was given to understand that  delay in submission of Reports was 
primarily due to involvement of a number of Stat es and other field agencies in the survey work. 
The Committee would like to be a pprised about the follow-up action taken, if any, on the first 
survey mentioned above. (Para 10.4) 
XI. ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF AYURVEDA, NEW DELHI 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee has been commenting on the sl ow progress being made in the project for 
construction of building of All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi. Latest feedback received 
from the Department indicates that during 2005- 06 also uptill now, only procedural formalities 
are being completed, real construction is yet to start. The present status is that draft EFC Memo 
along with Detailed Project Report has been se nt to the Planning Co mmission and Department 
of Expenditure on 24.6.05. Since then, Department is awaiting th eir comments, after receipt of 
which, EFC meeting would be held. The Comm ittee does not have much faith in the 
Department’s expectation of the project being completed within the anticipated cost of Rs. 
325.00 crore. The Committee re iterates that the Department should vigorously pursue the 
completion of all procedural formalities requi red for commencing the construction of the 
building of All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi. (Para 11.1) 
XII. EXPANSION OF AYUSH DISPENSARIES IN CGHS 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is dismayed to note the very  slow progress being made in making AYUSH 
dispensaries in CGHS functional. Out of the seven dispensaries sanctioned in 2003-04, only three 
can be made functional. The Committee is not in clined to accept the claim of the Department 
that the three AYUSH dispensaries at Trivandr um, Guwahati and Delh i are now functional. 
Deployment of medical officers from the existing  strength of CGHS dispensaries can only be 

considered as a stop-gap arrangement. It seems that proce ss of new recruitment and revival of 
old posts continues to be im peded by procedural formalit ies. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should take some concrete steps to make AYUSH dispensaries 
functional at the earliest so as to increase the usage and acceptability of AYUSH system. (Para 12.1) 
XIV. NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is constrained to observe th at not much progress has been made in 2005-
06 so far with regard to creation of posts for th e National Medicinal Plants Board. Creation of 
three posts and outsourcing of three posts for the Board agreed to by the Department of 
Expenditure is yet to get the formal  sanction. Latest position in this regard is that comments of 
concerned Departments on the EFC note for sa nction of requisite posts are awaited. The 
Committee is not aware whether the Board could be made fully functional with the approved six 
posts which includes one post of  Driver and Messenger also. Th e Committee reiterates that the 
Department should expedite the process for crea tion of six posts. The Department may also 
make an assessment about the actual requirem ent of manpower for the Board and pursue the 
same with the Planning Commission-Department of Expenditure. (Para 14.2) 
XV.  STRENGTHENING  OF  PHARMACOPOEIAL  LABORATORIES 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee views with serious concern the state of affairs in both the Labs; i.e. HPL 
and PLIM. The Committee was given to unders tand that the buildings for HPL and PLIM 
would be ready by Februa ry, 2005. However, the date for comp letion again shifted to June-July 
-2005 and as per the latest info rmation, the buildings were to be  ready in all respects with all 
mandatory certificates by October, 2005. The Committee is not aware about the latest status but 
hopes that targets must have been achieved. Also , as regards the proposal for creation of posts, 
the Committee opines that the Depa rtment should not only submit the modified proposal to the 
Department of Expenditure at the ea rliest but also pursue the same so  as to get it arrive of the 
logical conclusion. All efforts should be made to get the post of Director, PLIM and HPL filled 
up urgently. The Committee hopes that the De partment would work towards removing all 
bottlenecks in the whole process beca use the objective of these Labs i.e. laying down the 
standards for drugs of AYUSH and also for their te sting/analysis is of immense importance for 
users. (Para 15.2 to 15.5) 
XVI. DRUGS QUALITY CONTROL 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is happy to note that two st atutory bodies under the Drugs and Cosmetics 
Act, i.e. Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani Drug, Technica l Advisory Board a nd Ayurveda, Siddha, 
Unani, Drug Consultative Committee have been  constituted by the Department. ASUDCC will 
be meeting every six months, with all the State Drug Controllers participating. This Committee 
will take care of all aspects of ASU (Ayurveda,  Siddha and Unani) drugs and will also initiate 
preventive/deterrent action whenever required. Th e Committee hopes that these two statutory 
bodies will be activated at the earliest. (Para 16.5) 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is given to understand that dr ug quality control is the responsibility of the 
Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) and the state licensing authorities. The Committee 
would however like to point out that as per th e Annual Report of the Department for 2004-05 

Drug Control Cell in the Department is also in volved in the control of  misbranded/adulterated 
and spurious drugs of AYUSH, besides other ma tters. It seems that this Cell has not been 
handling the cases of misbranded/a dulterated and spurious drugs so  far. If not, the Committee 
would like to be apprised about the work done by the Cell during last two years. The Committee 
notes that the Department now proposes to get the post of Additional Drug Controller (AYUSH) 
and four Drugs Inspectors (AYUSH ) revived and filled up to assist  the DCGI in the task of 
quality control of AYUSH drugs. The Committee emphasizes that the Department should take 
all the required steps to implement the proposal at the earliest. (Para 16.6) 
Comments of the Committee 
 The report of scientists of USA mentioning the presence of metals in Ayurvedic/Herbal 
Medicinal products more than permissible limits is directly related to the efficacy and credibility 
of Ayurvedic medicines. The Committee appreciates  that the Department has initiated a study 
to see the toxicity/safety profile of metal base d bhasmas. A project to estimate the presence of 
various metals in normal habita t in raw drugs and classical Ay urvedic formulations has also 
been started. The Committee feels that findings of the study/project wo uld be available after 
some time only. However, it seems that Ha rvard Medical Associatio n has not been kept 
informed about the follow-up action taken by th e Department. If that be so, the Committee 
would impress upon the De partment to do so without any fu rther delay. Feed back from the 
manufacturing companies should also be expedited. (Para 16.7)

CHAPTER–I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
1.1 Inter-State and intra-State disparity in healthcare infrastructure 
Recommendations/Observations  
1.1.1 The Committee is concerned at the existing wide inter -State and intra -State disparity 
in healthcare infrastructure across the country. Despite the much emphasized guidelines of 
the NHP, the States/UTs barring Delhi and Puducherry have not enhanced the shar e of 
health budget to more than 8% of the total State budget in the last 5 years. The Committee 
understands that States with poor financial resources and inefficient fiscal capacity have a 
herculean task ahead to overcome the situation of fragile health in frastructure vis-a-vis the 
demand of accessible and affordable healthcare facilities. The Committee is of the considered 
view that in order to maximise the benefits of economic, social and human capital, the States 
must invest in institutionalizing a robus t healthcare ecosystem that is capable of delivering 
adequate healthcare services to the masses on ground level especially in rural, urban and 
tribal region. The sooner the States realize the difference, a resilient and strong health system 
makes, the bett er will be the outcome on all social as well as economic indicators. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the States/UTs to emulate the UTs of Delhi and 
Puducherry and increase the share of health spending in their States Budget.  The Committee 
in this reg ard recommends the Department of Health and Family Welfare to persuade the 
State Governments to achieve the budgetary health expenditure to 8%. 
(Para 2.13 of 134th Report) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2     The NHM expenditure, which is shared by both the Union and States will induce the 
State to further increase their budgetary allocation on health. As per the expenditure data of 
the union budget for 2018 -19 and 2019 -20 expenditure on NHM is more than 50 % clearly 
indicating the purpose of the union government. Apar t from the overall allocation, around 
20% of the allocation is kept under the NHM conditionality framework. This framework 
incentivizes the State to perform better on various health parameters and also penalizes the 
States for not meeting the targets. This  is a step toward s result-based financing and nudges 
the States towards improving their efficiency and the better performing States get more 
budgetary support. 
 
1.2 Health and Underperforming Sector  
Recommendation 
1.2.1 The Committee noted that health has always remained an underperforming sector and 
despite funds allocation many States are not performing well on several health parameters. 
Many States lack the adequate absorption capacity to judiciously manage the allocated 
funds. The Committee, therefore,  recommends the Union Government to incentivise the 
States/UTs to make ground assessment of the efficacy of the health policies and help the 
States design policies suiting the needs of the respective region. The Union Government must 

2 
 
coordinate with the St ates to maximise the output under the Central Sector as well as 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes.  
(Para 2.14) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 The performance and the absorption capacities vary across the States. There are 
various reasons for this including capacities as well as governance issues which are beyond 
health sector. Under NHM, States are encouraged to take up assessment of efficacy of  
various health sector policies and schemes and dedicated budget lines are there to budget 
such activities. In order to focus on the outcomes, the MoHFW has decided an output 
matrix for the biennial PIPs. In discussion with the States, the level of achievement has been 
decided which would be monitored on a quarterly basis with the help of PMS and HMIS 
portal. 
1.3 Robust Health Policy and Judicious Allocation of Funds 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 The Committee is also of the opinion that robust health policies and judicious 
allocation of funds under different Schemes is fundamental for the optimal performance of 
the States/UTs. The Committee notes that healthcare services remain highly fragmented t hat 
further aggravates the problem of high OOPE in the country. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Ministry to make efforts in developing a better healthcare financing 
mechanism and ensuring the delivery of quality healthcare services.  
(Para 2.15) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 The Government is striving towards comprehensive care for all. In this direction, it 
has initiated the following programs which will have an impact on reducing Out of Pocket 
expenditure in the country and provide quality health care to the population: 
(i) Health and Wellness Centre under Ayushman Bharat is an attempt to move 
from a selective approach to health care to deliver a comprehensive range of 
services spanning preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative 
care. It has two components that are complementary to each other. Under its 
first component, 1,50,000 Health & Wellness Centres (HWCs) will be created 
to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care, that is universal and free to 
users, with a focus on wellness and  the delivery of an expanded range of 
services closer to the community.  
(ii) HWC is envisaged to deliver an expanded range of services that go beyond 
Maternal and child health care s ervices to include care for non - 
communicable diseases, palliative and r ehabilitative care, Oral, Eye, and ENT 
care, mental health and first -level care for emergencies and trauma, including 
free essential drugs and diagnostic services 
(iii) Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM -JAY): The second component is the 
Pradhan Mantri J an Arogya Yojana (PM -JAY) which provides health 

3 
 
insurance cover of Rs. 5 lakhs per year to over 10 crore poor and vulnerable 
families for seeking secondary and tertiary care. 
(iv) Free Drugs Initiatives: In 2015, under National Health Mission the 
government of India launched the Free Essential Drugs initiatives. Under this, 
free drugs are provided to all citizens in different levels of public health 
facilities.  
(v) Free Diagnostics Initiatives: The government of India under the National 
Health Mission (NHM ) launched the Free Essential Diagnostics in 2015. 
Under this initiative, a limited number of essential diagnostics at different 
levels of public health facilities are provided free to all citizens of India. 
(vi) Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Program: T his initiative was rolled out in 
2016 as part of NHM wherein quality dialysis services are provided „Free‟ to 
BPL patients and at nominal costs to others through Public -Private 
Partnerships. 
(vii) Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), wherein all servic es including, 
drugs, diagnostics, transport, diet, and blood transfusion (if necessary) are 
provided free to all pregnant women and children up to the age of one year.  
(viii) Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) wherein financial incentives are provided to 
mothers who underwent institutional deliveries. 
(ix) Free Treatment for TB under RNTCP: Under this scheme, free treatment 
services are available for TB at all Government hospitals, Community Health 
Centres (CHCs), and Primary Health Centres (PHCs). 
(x) Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK): RBSK was launched in 2013 as 
a new initiative aimed at screening over 27 Crore children from 0 to 18 years

Recommendation 
1.15.1 The Committee notes that the Scheme of Strengthening of Food Testing System in the

Authorities are the main implementing agency for the enforcement of the FSS Act. The

plan for overcoming the shortage and expanding the pool of technical workforce.  
(Para 3.94) 
Action Taken 
1.15.2 The recommendations of the Committee have been noted and the following steps have 
been taken in this connection: 
(i) Central Sector Scheme for “Strengthening of Food Testing System in the Country 
Including Provision of Mobile Food Testing Labs” (SOFTeL) is already a PAN 
India Scheme which includes strengthening/setting up of 43 State Food Testing 
Labs with least one food testing laboratory in each State and two in larger States. 
Till date, a grant of Rs. 326.49 Crore has been sanctioned/released for 41 State 

10 
 
Food Testing Laboratories (SFTLs) from 30 States/UTs for the upgradation/setting 
up.

task of evaluation of the Central Secto r Scheme „S OFTeL‟, being implemented 
through FSSAI during Feb -March, 2020 by Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare. Based on the outcome review of the third party evaluation conducted by 
NIHFW, the scheme was extended up to FY 22 -23 with few modifications in the 
previous scheme (e.g.  provision of 2 additional manpower in each lab being 
upgraded with High End Equipment (HEE) was included). 
(iii) There is an Empowered Committee (EC) headed by the Chairperson, FSSAI, to 
guide and over see the implementation of the scheme. The Committee meets 
regularly to oversee the implementation of the scheme.  7
th meeting of empowered 
Committee was held on 17.11.2021. Additionally, FSSAI has conducted Gap 
Analysis in State Food T esting Laboratories (SFTLs) & National Food 
Laboratories (NFLs) through a third party contract during 2021 -22 with an 
objective to strengthen the Food testing Laboratories in India. Gap analysis of 76 
laboratories (74 SFTLs and 2 NFLs)  was conducted by the third party. The report 
submitted was examined by FSSAI and most of the recommendations in the report 
for the identified gaps are being implemented by FSSAI including infrastructure, 
equipment, manpower, certified reference materials (CRMs), NABLs cope etc. 
Accordingly, instruments and manpower requiremen ts for different FTLs are 
considered in the MoUs being finalized with the States to extend necessary 
financial assistance. 
 
(iv) FSSAI is also disbursing the funds to States/UTs from the funds allocated by 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare through MOUs being signed with States as 
per the terms & conditions agreed by the State for strengthening of food safety 
ecosystem since FY 2020 -21. The year 2022 -23, is the third year of the funds 
disbursement through MOUs. The funding under MoUs with States is being done 
as Central: State share, as agreed by the States during execution of the respective 
work plans. The funding patterns being followed under MOUs are as follows: 
 
 60:40 (60%FSSAI:40%State), 
 90:10 (90%FSSAI: 10%State), 
 100 % FSSAI (75% retention of license & registration fees by FSSAI) to 
the states, & 
 100%FSSAI share for  the UTs without legislation). 
 
(v) As regards the need of technical workforce and filling up of gaps of technical 
manpower, wherever necessary and crucial for the functioning of the testing 
laboratories, FSSAI is providing 03 technical manpower along with each of the

of one technical person per equipment for a period of 7 years from the date of 
installation of the equipme nt. Further, a grant -in-aid for 2 additional technical 
manpower is also being provided for FY 2021 -22 & 2022-23 under CSS. Besides, 
FSSAI is also providing the funds for technical and non -technical work force 
required for the smooth functioning of State fo od testing laboratories on 
contractual basis from the funds allotted by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
other than CSS since FY 2020-21 as per the demand of the States/UTs. Training of

technical personnel in State Labs and Inter Lab Comparisons, Prof iciency Testing

2.2 Policy intervention to bridge infrastructure gaps 
Recommendation 
2.2.1 The Committee notes that in 2021-22, the country was engulfed by a deadly pandemic 
Covid-19 wave and the delivery of healthcare services was largely hampered. The pandemic 
brought forth in open the poor state of health infrastructure and necessitated Government's 
focus and Policy intervention to bridge infrastructure gaps to strengthen the healthcare 
facilities. It was anticipated that the ravages of t he pandemic will bring the attention of the 
Government to the rural -urban divide in the healthcare services and its delivery. However, 
just a 0.2 % increase in the BE of 2022 -23 in comparison to RE 2021 -22 reveals the 
reluctance of the Government in addres sing the immediate need of increasing public 
investments in the health sector. 
(Para 2.5) 
Action Taken 
2.2.2 It may be stated that in comparison to BE 2021 -22 of Rs. 71238.77 Crore,  the  RE 
2021-22 was enhanced due to  primarily one time Grant of Rs. 15728.22 Crore to combat 
CoVID-19 pandemic. With regard to 0.2 % increase in BE 2022 -23, Department of Health & 
Family Welfare have been allocated Rs. 83000.00 Crore in BE which is 16.50 % mo re than

the previous year (BE) Budgetary allocation. However, there has been a consistent effort in 
increasing the Budgetary outlay of the Department of Health and Family Welfare. 
2.2.3 In order to bridge infrastructure gaps to strengthen the health care f acilities in both

(PM-ABHIM) with an outlay of Rs. 64,180 crores over 5 years has been launched on 25th 
October-2021. In the current financial year, Rs. 5155.71 crore ha s been allocated for the said 
scheme. The scheme would develop capacities of primary, secondary, and tertiary care health 
systems, strengthen existing national institutions, and create new institutions, to cater to 
detection and cure of new and emerging diseases. 
2.3 Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS)  
Recommendations 
2.3.1 The Committee observes that the actual fund expenditure under the CGHS Scheme 
over the past few years has been higher than the allocation at BE stage. The Committee notes 
that a substantial part of the expenditure under the Budget is attributed to Pensions and 
Other Retirement Benefits (PORB). The Ministry must take special note of the budgetary 
expenditure and demands under the Scheme and ensure that adequate funds are allocated to 
the Scheme. The Committee is also of the view that all the CGHS beneficiaries should be 
provided with the cashless treatment facility at the empanelled hospitals and diagnostic 
centres.  The Committee has also come to know that many empanelled hospitals  avoid 
admitting CGHS beneficiaries stating that their bills are settled by the Ministry after a long 
time. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to prepare a time schedule for payment 
to the empanelled hospitals and ensure that there is no delay in p ayment to empanelled 
hospitals due to any shortage of funds under the budgetary head.  At the same time the 
Ministry must also ensure that the beneficiaries of CGHS get standard treatment at private 
hospitals and empanelled diagnostic centres. 
(Para 3.4) 
Action Taken 
2.3.2 Budget Estimates of CGHS are formulated based on the trend of expenditure in 
previous financial years. Payment of bills of empanelled private hospitals and diagnostic 
centres and also reimbursement to pensioner beneficiaries is made from Pension and other 
Retirement Benefits (PORB) Head. Shortfall, if any, is met from the enhanced allocation at 
RE stage. 
2.3.3 As per extant scheme guidelines, cashless treatment facility is provided only to certain 
specified categories of CGHS beneficiaries . Medical Reimbursement claims of serving 
central government employees are settled by the concerned Ministry/ Department from its 
own Budget Head. As the system of settlement medical reimbursement claims of serving 
employees is decentralized, it may not be  feasible to provide cashless facilities to the serving 
beneficiaries. 
2.3.4 Government has taken several measures to address the delay in settlement of the 
hospital bills as under, Bill processing has been shifted to NHA IT Platform for online 
settlement of hospital bills in a transparent and eco-friendly paperless mode.

3.3 Budgetary Allocation of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
Recommendation 
3.3.1 The Committee also notes that the budgetary allocation of Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare accounts f or 2.1% of the total BE 2022 -23 whereas the allocation for 
Ministry of Defence is 13.3% of the total budgeted expenditure of  the Government in 2022 -
23. The Committee realizes that for a country like India with limited State and Central 
Government funds, mobilization of resources poses a big cha llenge. However, this should not 
deter the Governments from increasing its health expenditure and according less priority to 
the health sector.   Health is one sector that can drive people to poverty and disrupt the 
economic conditions of families. Attenti on of the Committee has also been brought to the 
Tracking universal health coverage: 2017 Global Monitoring Report by WHO and World 
Bank that states, "Average 4.16 % of the population annually slips into poverty due to 
catastrophic health expenditure". The Committee reemphasizes that the importance of health 
sector must not be ignored and health must be given priority in terms of budgetary allocation. 
(Para 2.4) 
Action Taken 
3.3.2     India being a signatory to the SGD goals, achieving Universal Health coverage is one 
of the important targets. The National Health Policy also espouses similar sentiment as it has 
set a target of increasing government health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP to e nsure affordable 
and accessible health services to all. Report by WHO and World Bank has identified that 
around 4.6% of the population falls below poverty line due to excessive health expenses. The 
recent NHA estimates for out –of – pocket expenditure (OOPE) on health (which might lead 
to financial vulnerability) and Government health expenditure do suggest that there has been 
a positive development in the country. The government health expenditure as a share of GDP 

31 
 
has increased from 1.15% in 2013 -14 to 1.35% in 2017-18. For the same period, the share of 
OOPE has declined from 64.2% to 48% 
Further Recommendation 
3.3.3     The Committee keeps into consideration the submission of the Secretary while 
giving his presentation to the Committee on DFG (2022 -23) th at as per the WHO's 
Global Health Expenditure Database 2018, the Government Health Expenditure as 
percentage of Current Health Expenditure is only 27% and the Out of Pocket 
Expenditure as percentage of the Current Health Expenditure is 62.7%. India ranks 
158 out of 196 countries in GHE as percentage of CHE and 176 out of 196 countries in 
OOPE as percentage of CHE . Expressing concern over the factual statement of the 
Secretary, Committee recommends the Department to approach Ministry of Finance to 
earmark budgetary allocation, at last 2.5% of GDP, as per target of National Health 
Policy to ensure affordable and accessible health services to all and also reduce the 
share of Out–of– Pocket Expenditure (OOPE).   
 
3.4 National Health Accounts Data  
Recommendations  
3.4.1 The Committee takes into account the National Health Accounts data submitted by the 
Ministry and notes that there has been a gradual increase in the Government Health 
Expenditure as a percentage of GDP ranging from 1.2 to 1.35. However the Committee is not 
happy with the slow trend of increase in the share of health budget.  
(Para 2.9)

and States/UTs. According to the NHA 2017-18, the share of the Union government is 40.8%

majority of allocation on health comes from the States and health is also a State subject, 
that‟s the primary responsibility of the State to finance the health.  
3.4.3    In that direction, the NHP - 2017, has already mentioned that States should spend 
more than 8% of their general expenditure on Health. As per the State Finance: Study of 
Budgets of 2021 -22, the average of actual expenditure by States (Including UTs with 
legislature) for the year2019-20 was 5.1%. 
3.4.4 The government is continuously making efforts to increase the allocation to health. 
The 15 th FC has allocated special health grants of Rs.70,051 crores to local bodies. Apart 
from that, Government has also initia ted PM -ABHIM amounting to Rs.64,180 crore and 
ECRP-II with the allocation of Rs.23,123 crores. All these initiatives are directed toward 
building a robust health infrastructure in the country. The target of 2.5% by 2025 National 
Health Policy is based on t he premise that this target will enable universal health coverage 
in the country.  
3.4.5 To provide affordable and quality tertiary health care facilities, Government is 
setting up new AIIMS and upgrading Government Medical Colleges under the Pradhan 

32 
 
Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana. State Governments are also supported for setting up of 
new medical colleges as well as for increasing UG and PG medical seats.  
Further Recommendation 
3.4.6    The Committee recommends Ministry to approach the Ministry of F inance and 
the State Government to ensure allocation of Union Budgetary grant to the tune of 
2.5% of GDP and 8% States budget, respectively on Health Sector as per target of NHP 
-2017 to enable Universal Health Coverage.  The Committee takes into account 1 5th 
Finance Commission allocation to the tune of Rs. 70,051 crores as special health grants 
to the local bodies, allocation of fund to the tune of Rs. 64,180 crore and Rs. 23,123 
crore under ECRP-II.  The Committee hopes that with all these investment the Ministry 
will be in position to build a robust health infrastructure in the country.  
 
3.5 Vacancy Position of CGHS 
Recommendations 
3.5.1 The Committee takes note of the fact that out of the sanctioned strength of 1531 
Medical Officers, 287 posts are l ying vacant. The Committee fails to understand the reason 
behind the huge vacancy in the Gazetted staff where out of the sanctioned 36 posts, almost 32 
posts are lying vacant. The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to follow up with 
the concerned authorities for expediting the recruitment of Medical Officer, Gazetted as well 
as Non -Gazetted Staff in the CGHS dispensaries to ensure proper functioning of the 
dispensaries.  The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should prepare a roadmap 
for streamlining the recruitment process to ensure that at no point of time there is a vacancy 
of more than 5% of the sanctioned strength.  The Committee feels that the promotional 
vacancies may be filled within six months and the Direct Recruitment vacancies within a year 
and to avoid increase in backlogs the Ministry should initiate the process of recruitment in 
anticipation of the vacancies.   
(Para 3.10) 
Action Taken 
3.5.2 Following measures have been undertaken to streamline the process of recruitment of 
Medical Officers and other staff in CGHS: 
i. Regular reporting of vacancies of GDMOs is done by CHS Division of the Ministry to 
UPSC for filling up through Combined Medical Services Examination held annually 
by UPSC. 
ii. The process of compilation of vacancies of  other staff has been streamlined by 
making it zone-wise at the level of Additional Directors as against the earlier practice 
of city-wise compilation thereof. 
iii. Additional Directors of CGHS have been directed to hold regular meetings of 
Departmental Promotion Committees (DPCs) to fill up promotional posts. 
iv. Additional Directors of CGHS have been directed to firm up vacancies and intimate 
the same in the online portal / window of Staff Selection Commission (SSC) as soon 
as it is opened for the purpose. Further , any follow -up action in the recruitment 
process, as desired by SSC, is to be taken promptly by them. 

33 
 
3.5.3 Regular training programmes are organized at Institute of Secretariat Training and 
Management (ISTM) for Office Superintendents to familiarize them  with various recruitment 
related formalities, so that they can assist Additional Directors in their discharge of 
administrative duties and to fast-track the process of recruitment.    
Further Recommendation 
3.5.4 The Committee observes that the Ministry m ore often than not, counts on 
plethora of steps taken to fill up the vacant posts, still the position of vacant posts 
continues to remain static year after year and so is the case with CGHS having 287 
Medical Officer vacant posts, out of sanctioned strengt h of 1531, 32 vacant posts  of 
gazetted staff other than Medical Officer indicating out of sanctioned 36 post and 1537 
non-gazetted posts out of 4728 sanctioned posts.  The Committee, therefore, does not 
approve the plea of the Ministry taking series of action for filling up vacant posts but to 
the understanding of the Committees are of no avail.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to adhere to measure of Human Resource For ecasting 
Management Model and streamline the recruitment process to fill up  the position of 
vacancy status against the sanctioned strength.

3.13 National Organ Transplant Program (NOTP) 
Recommendation  
3.13.1 The Committee noted that the Ministry has not been able to utilize allocated  funds  
under the National Organ Transplant Program (NOTP). The Committee observes that organ 
donation rate in the country is very low when compared to other countries and there is a 
huge lack of awareness among the public. The Committee feels that India has a va st potential 
of organ donations and demand due to its population but the Ministry needs to make 
concerted efforts to develop such feelings amongst its citizens. NOTP aims to promote organ 
donation and transplantation across all States/Union Territories in the country. However, the 
Committee notes that performance of the program has been very poor which is reflected by 
huge underutilisation of funds under the Scheme. The Committee notes that the Scheme was 
allotted Rs. 30.50 crore in BE 2021 -22 which was sla shed to Rs. 6.39 crore in RE 2021 -22 
which is a 79% decrease with respect to BE 2021 -22. The Committee further notes that the 
program has been allotted a total of Rs. 15.00 crore in BE 2022-23.  
(Para 3.85) 
Action Taken 
3.13.2 One of the important objectiv es of National Organ Transplant Programme (NOTP) is 
to improve awareness about organ donation among the public. Towards this end the NOTTOs 
and SOTTOs have been conducting awareness activities on an ongoing basis right through 
the year. These awareness act ivities have led to increased pledging from the people. Most of 
these activities are pro bono activities at the level of the  
NOTTO/SOTTOs. Underutilization of IEC funds is mostly due to these being conducted on 
pro bono basis. 
3.13.3 NOTP is a central sect or continuing scheme. The scheme has been evaluated 
externally and found to be giving positive results in terms of increased awareness about organ 
donation, increase in number of deceased organ donations and establishments of organization 
for organ procure ment and distribution. The organ donation rate i.e. number of persons 
donating organs per million populations has increased from around 0.16 in 2012 to 0.52 in 
2019. Further, based on the feedback and past experience, to make the programme more 
effective and bridge the gap between demand for and supply of the organs for transplantation, 
some new components have been introduced in the programme such as support in facilitating 
medical education of doctors and staff of medical colleges/institutions (both Gover nment and 
Private) doing transplant activities or willing to start organ transplantation activities, training 
for transplant teams (surgeons, physicians, anaesthetists, nurses, technicians and perfusionists 
(in cases of heart and lung transplants) in India  or Abroad, setting up of 4 skills centres in 
NOTTO and medical colleges in the country, 10(ten) Regional/State Biomaterial Centres, 

42 
 
setting up of State Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisations (SOTTOs) in each State, 
developing new/strengthening existing  retrieval and transplant centres, and support to 
retrieval centres. The SOTTOs are encouraged to send proposals to optimize utilization of 
funds for all the components of the programme. 
Further Recommendation  
3.13.4 The Committee appreciates that despite lower allocation of budget to NOTP and 
underutilization of IEC fund the organ donation rate has increased from 0.16 in 2012 to 
0.52 in 2019 due to enhanced impetus to organ donation awareness  campaign.  
However, the Committee observes that to make NOTP mo re effective and bridge the 
gap between demand and supply of the organs for transplantation , various new 
components have been incorporated in the programme viz. Medical Education for doing 
transplantation, training to transplants teams, setting up of 4 skills centers in NOTTO, 
10 Regional/State Bio-material centre, setting up of SOTTO in each State, strengthening 
existing retrieval and transplant centre etc.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
Ministry to assess whether the continuing quantum of budge tary grant would be 
sufficient to meet the expenditure involving on various activities enshrined in new 
components of NOTP.

3.18 Ayushman Bharat Health-Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) 
Recommendation 
3.18.1 The Committee observes that the expenditure profile of all the initiatives under NHM 
has been satisfactory, however, there has been re-appropriation of funds from one pool to the 
other due to the pandemic Covid -19. The Committee notes that Ayushman Bharat Health-
Wellness Centres (AB -HWCs) is aimed at providing Comprehensive Primary Health Care 
(CPHC) to the masses. However, the Committee believes that along with increasing the 
number of these HWCs, the Ministry must also work towards enhancing the quality o f 
healthcare service delivery at these Centres. The Committee strongly recommends the 
Ministry to complete operationalization of the remaining HWCs and achieve the target of 
setting up of 1,50,000 functional HWCs by December 2022. The Ministry must also wo rk 
towards augmenting the Health care facilities by including tele -medicine, Yoga and mental 
health care services in these HWCs.  
(Para 4.19) 
Action Taken  
 
3.18.2 The National Health Policy 2017 envisages the goal of attainment of the highest 
possible lev el of health and well -being, through a preventive and promotive health care 
orientation, and universal access to good quality health care services without anyone having 
to face financial hardships as a consequence. To progressively achieve Universal Health  
Coverage, Ayushman Bharat – Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) was 
launched in 2018 to deliver Comprehensive Primary Healthcare Services. With a target of 

46 
 
1,50,000 Health and Wellness Centres by December, 2022, the existing Sub -Health Centres 
(SHC), Primary Health Centres (PHC) and Urban Primary Health Centres (UPHC) are being 
transformed into AB -HWCs to deliver Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC) that 
includes preventive, promotive, curative, palliative and rehabilitative services which is 
universal, free, and close to the community. As on 30th June, 2022, total 1,20,112 AB -HWCs 
which includes 92,470 SHCs, 22,915 PHCs and 4,727 UPHCs, have been operationalized 
throughout the country against the operationalization target of 1,50,000 AB -HWCs by 
December, 2022. 
 
3.18.3 The measures undertaken for the approved centres to be recognized as functional AB -
HWC are: 
 
1) HR - availability - To improve the delivery mechanism, a new cadre of healthcare 
providers are introduced at the mid -level with educational back grounds such as 
B.Sc in Community Health or a Nurse (GNM or B.SC) or an Ayurveda 
Practitioners with due certification in public health. These Mid -Level HealthCare 
Providers are designated as Community Health Officer (CHO). The CHO at SHC -
HWC carry out publ ic health functions, ambulatory care, and management and 
provide leadership at the Sub-Health Centre-Health and Wellness Centres. 
 
2) Infrastructure - All AB -HWCs are provided with sufficient space for outpatient 
care, for dispensing medicines, diagnostic services, adequate spaces for display of 
communication material of health messages, including audio visual aids and 
appropriate community spaces for wellness activities, including the practice of 
Yoga and physical exercises. 
 
3) Availability of Free Medicines  - Number of essential medicines at PHC -HWCs 
have been increased to 172 and at the SHC -HWCs, these have been increased to 
105. The CHO at the SHC -HWCs dispense medicines based on treatment plans 
initiated by the medical officer at the PHC-HWC. 
 
4) Availability of Free Diagnostics -Number of essential diagnostic tests have been 
increased to 63 in PHC -HWCs and 14 in SHC -HWC. Completion of CBAC 
enumeration for NCDs and CDs - Community-Based Assessment Check list is 
administered by the ASHA for each individual abo ve 30 years at the household 
level. This captures the risk for various illness and also enables screening by MPW 
and referral to the nearest Ayushman Bharat – Health and Wellness Centre (AB -
HWC). 
 
6)    Capacity building of primary healthcare team on expanded  package of services - 
The MO, ASHAs and ANMs have been trained in the 7 basic services. The  
Community Health Officer undergone 15 days Expanded Induction training after 
their posting at SHC -HWC. This training covers sessions on RMNCHA+N, 
Communicable diseases, non-communicable diseases, and Jan Aarogyasamiti. 
 
7) Expanded Service Delivery- The existing package of Primary Health Care services 
is being expanded to go beyond Reproductive and Child Health and 
Communicable Diseases to include comprehensive primary health care services for 
non-communicable diseases, Mental Health, ENT, Ophthalmology, Oralhealth, 
Geriatric and Palliative healthcare and first level care for emergencies and traumas 

47 
 
well as Health promotion and wellness activities like Yoga. About 1.18 Cr 
Wellness Sessions, including Yoga, has been conducted at AB -HWCs & 60.46 Cr 
Screenings for NCDs (Hypertension/ Diabetes/ Oral, breast & cervical cancer) has 
been done as on 10.06.2022. 
 
8)    Robust IT system- AB-HWC portal and app has been developed and being used by 
the States/UTs to capture progress on AB -HWC operationalization. Tablets are 
being provided at AB -HWC for operationalization and digitization of the health 
information. Total Teleconsultation sundere-Sanjeevani is 3.90 crores (as on 
30.06.2022). E-Sanjeevani HWC is operational at 94,599 Spokes & 10,709 Hubs 
(including Spoke cum hubs). 
 
9) Financing/provider payment reforms -Performance linked payment is being 
provided to CHOs and primary healthcare team at HWC. 
 
10)    Community mobilisation and health promotion through activities like Fit Health 
Worker Campaign, Eat Right India movement, Annual health calendar for 
promoting wellness related activities. 
 
3.18.4 Additionally, to ensure an in tegrated approach of primary healthcare, various 
community platforms, namely Jan Arogya Samiti (JAS), Village Health, Sanitation and 
Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) and Mahila Arogya Samiti (MAS) are being created and 
engaged the level of community and AB-HWCs. 
 
Further Recommendation 
3.18.5 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in operationalizing 
a total of 1,20,112 AB-HWCs throughout the country against the target of 1,50, 000 AB-
HWCs by December, 2022. The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry 
will make all out effort to achieve the target of op erationalizing 1,50,000 AB -HWCs in 
order to provide Comprehensive Primary Healthcare Services across the country.  T he 
Committee further recommends that all these centre must have adequate human 
resource with 4 technical expertise and latest tools and techniques, diagnostic kits, 
medicines to provide quality healthcare service and standard treatment.  The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry should popularize tele -consultation Sundere-
Sanjeevani in rural areas.

to keep vigil on Institute’s construction consultant M/s HSCC to ensure that 04 
remaining buildings out of 12 buildings are also completed within revised timeframe i.e 
September, 2022. 
(Para 3.17.3) 
AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH-WELLNESS CENTRES (AB-HWCS) 
 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in operationalizing 
a total of 1,20,112 AB-HWCs throughout the country against the target of 1,50, 000 AB-
HWCs by December, 2022. The Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry 
will make all out effort to achieve the target of opratinalizing 1,50,000 AB -HWCs in 
order to provide Comprehens ive Primary Healthcare Services across the country.  The 
Committee further recommends that all these centre must have adequate human 
resource with 4 technical expertise and latest tools and techniques, diagnostic kits, 
medicines to provide quality healthca re service and standard treatment.  The 
Committee also recommends the Ministry should popularize tele -consultation Sundere-
Sanjeevani in rural areas.   
(Para 3.18.5) 
MERGER OF POOLS UNDER NHM 
 The Committee understands the merger of flexible pools will end ow greater 
flexibility to States and UTs for appropriation of funds on various component of the 
scheme as per the instant requirement, however, the Committee desire to be apprised of 
the achievement of physical target as a result of release of funds agains t various 
components/activities approved in SPIP and subsequent improvement in health 
indicators. The Committee further desires to know as how the scheme incesstinize 
States/UTs with poor health track record on health indicators. The Committee notes 

65 
 
various mode of keeping track on the financial utilization of fund and progress 
thereupon, however, such monitoring mechanism must oversee the transformation of 
healthcare delivery system at ground level , that is the ultimate measurement of success 
of the scheme.  
(Para 3.19.5) 
PENDING UTILIZATION CERTIFICATE UNDER NHM 
 
The Committee desires that the pending 136 utilization certificate amounting to 
Rs. 629.69 crore with respect to the Central grants released upto  financial year 201 -20 
need to be liquidated at the earliest.  The Committee further hopes that the Ministry 
will apprise the current pending UCs involving the total amount and steps taken to 
liquidate the pending UCs.  
(Para 3.20.4) 
DRUG MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY 
 The Committee is of the considered view that vibrant, dynamic strengthened 
drug testing laboratories is concomitant efficient and effective drug regulatory 
mechanism to avert the prevalence of sub -standard drugs, therefore, the Ministry 
should instruct and guide the State Governments to strengthen State Drugs Regulatory 
System.  Moreover, the Committee wants to be informed of the response of State 
Governments of Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka to the 
Ministry’s perusal for submitting the project proposals matching the i ndicative amount 
of each State. U nderstandably the Ministry will continue to monitor optimal utilization 
of fund earmarked for the scheme. 
(Para 3.21.7) 
NATIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME 
 
 The Committee desires to know the status on opening the S ingle Nodel Agency 
Account (SNA) by the Institution for further release of funds under NMHP.  The 
Committee hopes that facilities available under DMHP at CHC and PHC level w ould 
ensure successful exe cution of NMHP in direction of reducing the Mental Health 
burden in the country.  The Committee further wishes to know the fund allocated to 
IEC for awareness generation activities in the school, workplaces and community.  
Besides that the Ministry may apprise the Committee about the measures undertaken to 
reduce the Mental Health burden in the country.  
(Para 3.22.5) 
 
ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW MEDICAL COLLEGES 
 The Committee notes that out of 157 sanctioned medical colleges 72 medical 
colleges have become functional.  The Committee, however, desires to know the status of 
the Letter of Permission submitted by 36 new medical colleges to NMC for commencing 
the courses from academic session 2022 -23.   The Committee further recommends the 
Ministry to incentivize State Government to invite proposal for upgrading the 
educational infrastructure in existing medical colleges so that quality education could be 
imparted in those medical colleges.  The Committee also hopes that the Ministry would 

66 
 
take up the matter of op erationasation of remaining sanctioned medical colleges at the 
earliest.  
(Para 3.23.3) 
MEDICAL EDUCATION STANDARDS AND PROFESSIONAL COMPETENCE 
 The Committee is of the view that in order to ensure medical education standard 
and professional competence in medical colleges, the provision for human resources and 
technical expertise be made at the time of sanctioning of operationalization of medical 
colleges, itself so that quality of education imparted is not compromised. The Committee 
hopes that po sting the status of construction projects alongwith release of fund  on the 
dashboard would strengthen the monitoring mechanism besides making the system 
more transparent, result oriented and avoidance of time and cost overruns.  
(Para 3.24.3) 
 
PRADHAN MANTRI AYUSHM AN BHARAT HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE 
MISSION (PM-ABHIM) 
 The Committee aspires to know the total actual expenditure incurred on various 
components of PM -ABHIM since the commencement of the scheme and the physical 
target achieved so far.  The Ministry may apprise the Committee for appropriation of 
total outlay of Rs. 64,180 crore on various components of scheme; financial year wise 
and the physical target set under the scheme.  The Committee hopes that the successful 
execution of PM -ABHIM the health infrast ructure and consolidation of healthcare 
services.  
(Para 3.25.5)

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
1.1  Vision of the Department 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.1.1 The Committee recognizes the vision of the Department of Health Research and 
acknowledges the objectives set by the Department to achieve the set vision. However, the 
Committee is of the strong opinion that with changing times and fickle nature of the health 
emergencies, the Department needs to continuously evaluate its objectives and approach and 
recalibrate it, if the need arises. The Committee also believes that no objective can be achieved 
in its entirety if the Department functions in isolation or in association with research based 
institutes only. The Committee, therefore, recommends that to realize its vision, DHR must 
work in synergy with various departments and Ministries of the Central and State Governments 
as well as the leaders in healthcare industry in the private sector. 
(Para -1.3 of 135th Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The Department of Health Research along with ICMR is working in tandem with various 
Departments and Ministries of the Central and State Governments as well as private sector. 
ICMR has launched consortiums in the area of high priority areas like TB, Malaria and  Cancer. 
The aim is to bring together all major national players (with international collaborators) to 
address overarching scientific questions to tackle these health issues in a mission mode.  
 
1.1.3 In battle against COVID -19, ICMR worked in coherence wi th centre and state health 
departments, other S &T agencies and private partners like Bharat Biotech & Zydus Cadilla to 
bring out various solutions ranging from ramping up the testing infrastructure to developing 
diagnostic kit for national serosurveillance to developing a fully indigenous vaccine. 
 
1.1.4 ICMR-DHR-Centre of Excellences (CoE) for fostering MedTechinnovations was 
established at seven IITs viz., IIT -Bombay, IIT -Delhi, IIT -Guwahati, IIT -Hyderabad, IIT -
Kanpur, IIT-Kharagpur and IIT -Madras. These centres of excellence for Medical Device and 
Diagnostic development have been set up with an aim to develop the products/technologies in 
synergy with the requirements of the National Health Mission, Ayushman Bharat and Public 
Health Programs of the Government of India for their potential deployment. 
 
1.1.5 ICMR works in  collaboration with national pro grammes like NV BDCP, NACO etc. to 
generate new evidence to eliminate the communicable diseases like lymphatic filariasis, 
kalazar, AIDS, leprosy etc. As per the recommendation by eminent members of the committee, 
DHR-ICMR will work towards further strengthening the inter -departmental, inter sectoral 
collaborations to bring out logical solutions to health challenges of the nation. 
 
 
 
 

3 
 
1.2  Data and Projection Models 
   
 Recommendation 
 
1.2.1 The Committee recommends Department of Health Research to work with independent 
experts and statistical organizations to ensure that it has the best possible data and projection 
models to inform their thinking. 
(Para 2.12 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.2.2 ICMR has a full-fledged institute, National Institute of Medical Statistics (NIMS) that has 
contributed immensely in the area of AIDS, COVID -19 etc. The projections in the demand for 
COVID-19 realted essential supplies for the whole country were also handled under the 
leadership of ICMR-NIMS. ICMR is planning to recruit biostatiscians in mission mode and is 
also working in the capacity building programmes to create a talent pipeline of skilled 
biostatisticians. 
 
1.2.3 As suggested by committee, Department will develop a framework and identify 
independent experts from different statistical organisations to work on data and disease 
modelling. Recently, ICMR collaborated with IITs and Imperial College, Lo ndon to carry out 
modelling in the area of COVID-19. 
 
 
1.3  Ramping up testing capacity 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.3.1 The Committee agrees that India did ramp up its testing capacity exponentially since the 
pandemic began in January 2020. Yet; it's true that as c ompared to several other countries with 
high case load, India's testing numbers remained low under whelming. 
(para 2.24 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.3.2 In terms of cumulative numbers, India is second highest in COVID -19 testing in the 
world with more than 86 crore tests done till now. India made sure to optimally use its testing 
capacity as per the requirement through calibrated testing approach. As per WHO guidance a 
140 tests per million population per week were recommended. However, India’s average 
testing remained close to 900 -1000 tests per million population per week. Besides, the total 
testing numbers at the peak of 2 nd and 3rd wave were higher than many developed nations like 
USA and UK. 
 
1.4  Establishment of VRDLs 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.4.1 The Department has submitted that till date 132 VRDLs have been established across 25 
States and 5 Union Territories. These Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) 

4 
 
are established in a three -tier mode, viz., Regional, State and Medical College L evel. Regional 
level VRDLs are equipped with serology, RT-PCR, virus isolation, sequencing and fluorescence 
microscopy; State Level labs are equipped with serology, RT - PCR, fluorescence microscopy 
and sequencing, while Medical College Level are equipped w ith serology and Rt -PCR. These 
VRDLs are intended to cover the entire country for timely diagnosis/identification of viruses 
during outbreaks of epidemics, generation of data about viral diseases for facilitating quick 
deployment of adequate resources and measures to save the human lives during outbreaks. 
(Para 3.2 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.4.2 As on April 2022, a total of 136 VRDLs have been setup across the country spread over 
25 States and 5 UTs. The VRDL network is a three tiered system comprising of regio nal level, 
state level and medical college level laboratories designated as top level, middle level and 
lower level respectively. During the subsequent expansion of the VRDL network, equal 
geographic coverage of the country has been ensured.  
 
1.4.3 The VRDLs are equipped with state -of-art laboratory infrastructure, capable to diagnose 
more than 25 viruses of public health importance. Further impetus has been given to strengthen 
the VRDL network by implementing coordinated research activities on advance dia gnosis, 
robust surveillance mechanism for various virus diseases, epidemiological studies, outbreaks 
detections etc. 
 
1.4.4 Each laboratory has linkage with local health authorities and are being supplied field 
samples of any outbreak cluster with the help  IDSP and their sentinel sites. The data with 
respect to outbreak investigations and diagnosis is being uploaded on real -time basis to the 
dedicated data mining center operational at ICMR -NIE, Chennai. The interpretation/analysis of 
the data is parallel reported to the respective health authorities at Central and State level.   
 
1.5 Establishment of 3 tier VRDLs 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.5.1 The Committee observes that since Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories  (VRDLs) 
are established in a three -tier mode, viz., Regional, State and Medical College Level. VRDLs 
can be established in Sikkim and Nagaland as well at regional and state level even if there is no 
Medical College in these two States. The Committee notes that the States of Sikkim and 
Nagaland had highest fatality rate among st all the North -Eastern States.  Non-availability of 
testing facility could have been one of the reasons for high causality. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends DHR to work in associati on with the State Governments of North -Eastern Region 
and establish VRDLs in any government run research centre or any government hospital. 
(Para 3.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.5.2 As per the scheme norms, VRDLs can be establish in government medical 
colleges/research institutions/army hospitals. Due to unavailability of medical colleges in the 
State of Sikkim and Nagaland, the VRDLs could not be setup. However, DHR will explore the 
potential sites in the mentioned States.  

5 
 
 
1.5.3 Besides that, a viral diagnostic laboratory is functional at STNM Hospital, Gangtok, 
Sikkim since 2015 with financial support from ICMR. The said lab is equipped with all 
necessary infrastructures and trained human resources. The lab is catering whole Sikk im region 
efficiently. 
 
1.6  Establishment of MRHRU 
 
 Recommendation 
 
1.6.1 The Committee, therefore recommends DHR to work assiduously in establishing MRHRU 
in each state and UT of the country considering the poor state of health technology in almost 
all Indian States. The Committee also recommends the Department to approve and establish 
more such units in the rural part of country and accordingly the Department must seek 
adequate funds for the scheme at the RE stage and in subsequent years. 
(Para 3.27 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.6.2 The Department also has the target of establishing 01 MRHRU in each State and Union 
Territory. Accordingly, the recommendation of the Committee has been noted for guidance and 
compliance. 
 
 1.7  Capacity Building and Skill Development 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.7.1 The Committee takes note of the efforts put by DHR for capacity building and skill 
development of the human resource. However, the Committee believes that the major problem 
now-a-days in medical research is its sub -standard quality. Poor quality medical research 
leads to almost no or little impact in clinical practice. The Committee takes note that in India, 
faculties and scientists in medical institutions, are largely engaged in teaching and clinical 
care and there is very little number of scientists interested in medical research. 
(Para 3.37 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.2 In order to promote quality research, the subject specific calls with well -defined research 
questions have been initiated upon brainstorming discussions with the biomedical experts. 
 
1.8  Quality of Medical Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.8.1 The Committee is of the strong view that quality of medical research can only be 
improved by inviting large no. of scientists, who can devote specific time for research f rom 
medical institutions especially in the field of diseases engulfing the country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends utilizing college facilities having specific and exclusive time for 
research activities. The Committee also recommends that there shoul d be added incentives for 

6 
 
researchers for conducting high-quality and viable medical research that can be translated into 
action in treatment of life threatening diseases. 
(Para 3.38 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.8.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is no ted and will work towards implementing 
them.  
 
1.9  Basic Objective of HTAIn 
 
 Recommendation 
 
1.9.1 The Committee acknowledges the basic objective of HTAIn i.e. to analyse the health 
technologies viz. medicines, devices and health programmes  for its cost- effectiveness, clinical-
effectiveness and equity issues by means of Health Technology Assessment (HTA), and in turn 
helping in decision making for an optimal utilization of allocated health budget. The Committee 
believes that HTAIn scheme an d the scheme of establishing Model Rural Health Research 
Units (MRHRU), if operated in consonance & conjunction to each other can greatly aid in 
improving the overall health infrastructure, particularly in rural and semi -urban areas. The 
Committee, believes that adequate budgetary allocation and subsequent optimal utilization of 
allocated funds under this scheme would also help in minimizing the cost for healthcare by 
reducing the out of pocket expenditure that still remains enormous. The Committee notes th at 
out of the 17 Resource Centres of HTAIn only one such centre is in NE region and none in the 
UT of J&K and Ladakh. The Committee, therefore, recommends DHR to work towards setting 
up at least one such centre in J&K/Ladakh and one more in NE region. 
(Para 3.44 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.9.2 Resource Centre is available at Indian Institute of Public Health (IIPH), Shillong in NE 
Region. However, the recommendation of the Hon’ble Committee to constitute a centre in UT 
of Jammu &Kashmir and Ladakh will be consid ered and the recommendation of the Hon’ble 
Committee regarding HTAIn and MRHRU schemes working in conjunction and consonance 
with each other for improving the overall health infrastructure has been noted for compliance. 
 
1.10  Specialized Cancer Centre in NER 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.10.1 The Committee understands that North -Eastern states have the highest incidence of 
Cancer in India, for example Mizoram has the highest incidence of stomach cancer, Meghalaya 
has big number of esophageal cancer cases and Nagaland reports high Nasopharyngeal cancer 
cases, but due to unavailability of specialized facilities, patients often visit other cities of India 
for diagnosis and treatment. Thus, specialized cancer centre for screening, early diagnosis and 
treatment of cancer within the region needs to be  established. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends DHR to fast track setting up of oncopathology labs in NE region. 
(Para 3.47 ibid) 
 

7 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.10.2 The DHR ICMR advanced Molecular oncopathology diagnostic services have been set 
up in Cachar Cancer I nstitute in Silchur and RIMS, Imphal. The suggestion of the Hon’ble 
Committee regarding Mizoram will also be considered as and when a proposal is received from 
Mizoram. 
 
1.11  Allocation of Fund to ICMR 
  
Recommendation 
 
1.11.1 Considering the pivotal role of Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) in the field 
of bio -medical and health research in India, the Committee is deeply concerned to note the 
large gap in funding of ICMR when compared with health research institutions of countries like 
US, UK, France and China. What worries the Committee more is that the allocation of fund to 
ICMR and subsequent utilization of funds by ICMR has always been less than the projected 
demand, even in the Covid -years, where the need for adequa te funds and optimal utilization 
was call of the hour. The Committee believes that the budgetary allocation to ICMR in 2022 -
23, is grossly inadequate keeping in view the mandate of the ICMR. However, the Committee is 
also aware that the utilization trends of ICMR over the years don‟t present a justified reason 
for increase of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends ICMR to improve the absorption 
capacity of its scheme implementing agencies. The Committee recommends ICMR to provide 
more money for researc h projects, joint -research projects with national and international 
bodies, establish net work of labs for diagnosis of Communicable and Non - Communicable 
diseases, extensively fund research projects, provide trainings/ international exposure to 
researchers, develop programmes to encourage youth to take up research, scheme to develop 
inclination towards health-research in students of higher-secondary and senior secondary. 
(Para 4.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.11.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. Some more centers under ICMR like 
Center at Nagpur, Jabalpur, Chandigarh, Bangalore & Dibrugarh are under Construction. These 
Centers will cater the enhanced need of the Country and will also increase the absorption 
capacity of ICMR. 
 
1.12  Dual-Use Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.12.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends DHR -ICMR to formulate regulations and 
national policy for oversight of dual -use research - which refers to experiments that are 
conducted for peaceful purposes but can be modified or altered to cause harm. The Committee 
further recommends DHR/ICMR to conduct trainings and develop strict and exhaustive 
guidelines on bio-safety and bio-security. 
(Para 4.11 ibid) 
 
 
 

8 
 
Action Taken

Also a high level BSL -4 expert committee has been notified and is operational now. ICMR has

1.13  Lack of public confidence in Healthcare 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.13.1 The Committee, however, believes that there is a general lack of public confidence in

confidence might pose a hurdle in conducting clinical trials. The Committee recommends 
ICMR to work in cohesion with the pharmaceutical industry to regain trust of the general

and inform patients and the society at large about the benefits of engaging in clinical research 
and allowing authentic collection of patient data. 
(Para 4.15 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.2 The Communications Unit of ICMR is working continuously to bring mass awareness 
regarding the procedure of drug/vaccine development and also tackle the vaccine hesitancy

1.14  Projects taken by ICMR 
 
Recommendation  
 
1.14.1 The Committee takes note of the projects under taken by ICMR along with different 
organizations of the Ayush . The Committee is of the view that Ayurveda, Homeopathy, Siddha, 
Unani and herbal medicines have wide socio cultural acceptance with large chunk of 
population subscribing to the alternative mode of treatment, but the Committee believes that 
scientific research is needed, so that these regimens can be incorporated as standard treatment 
regimens. Research on Ayush preparations must be conducted scientifically so that it is in line 
with the modern patenting system. The Committee, therefore, recommends ICMR to  work 
towards linking various disciplines of Ayush with each other and also with modern system of 
medicine, as it may lead to a possible convergence of various disciplines for global benefit. 
(Para 4.17 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.14.2 ICMR through its institut e ICMR -National Institute of Traditional Medicine (ICMR -
NITM) has envisioned to influence public health outcomes by integrating Traditional Medicine 
(TM) with Modern Health System, through Research, Human Resource Development and 
 

9 
 
Outreach. ICMR -NITM is wor king on developing evidence -based, affordable, traditional 
medicine solutions for public health concerns, which may be further integrated with modern 
healthcare systems. More than 1500 TM formulations from 750 TM practitioners involving 
1200 species of pla nts has been documented.  The scientific evidences are being created 
through (i) Pharmaco -epidemiological studies on utility of TM practices (ii) Robust 
observational studies (iii) Pre-clinical evaluations through in silico, in vitro and in vivo studies 
of the selected practices (iv) Clinical evaluation of the selected preparations/ practices that 
include Model Rural Health Research Units as rural sites (v) Implementation research & 
development of policies and recommendations on models of integration. ICMR -NITM created 
a database on ethnomedicinal plants of Western Ghats (http://nitmmedplantsdb.in), successfully 
validated the TM practice for osteoarthritis, filed provisional patent on TM formulation for 
COVID-19.  ICMR -NITM aims to provide an interface of Mo dern Healthcare System and 
Traditional Healthcare System by recommending use of validated traditional medicine, training 
to create a cadre of integrative health care researchers and professionals and human resource 
development and developing policies and g uidelines. Thus, its activities are not limited to 
drug/product development but to ensure integration of already validated traditional medicine, 
skill-sets and knowledge-base to the existing healthcare system. 
 
1.15  Funding Health Research Institutions 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.15.1 Analysing the data from the 2016 evaluation the Committee observes that, there is wide 
gap in funding between health research institutions of countries like US, UK, Australia, China 
and Brazil and ICMR. The Committee further observes  that though annual output (in terms of 
paper published) of ICMR has continued to grow with respect to its 2005 output and in2014, 
ICMR produced 108% more papers than it did in 2005, however, the Committee believes that 
this won't be a just comparison with  NIH (National Institute of Health, US) as NIH is already 
working at a very high output, and given a larger base, it's rate of growth (in terms of paper 
published) cannot be as high as ICMR. The Committee further notes that just the number of

Recommendation

2.11  Establishment of BSL-IV and BSL-III Labs 
 
Recommendation 
 
2.11.1 The Committee notes the establishment of 2 new BSL-IV and three new BSL-III labs. The

understands that the two new BSL -IV labs would co ver the East and West part of India, 

16 
 
however, the North and South India still don‟t have BSL -IV labs. The Committee believes that 
in the absence of well -equipped and high -tech labs, samples have to be transported over long 
distances to the nearest lab. this causes delay in diagnosis often leading to serious 
repercussions over result of diagnostic test. The Committee is of the strong opinion that lack of 
adequate number of BSL -3 and BSL -4 labs would greatly hinder India's chances of defeating

Committee, therefore, recommends ICMR to establish one BSL-IV lab in each of the four zones.

benefits of research if it meets ethical, considerate and smart policymaking. 
(Para 4.10 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
2.11.3 Operationalization and maintenance of BSL -4 labs is highly demanding and complex. 
Besides, BSL-4 is not needed routinely for outbreak investigation. BSL -4 labs are required for 
animal experiments, growing viruses and undertaking animal challenge studies. These 
specialized research functions are undertaken in BSL -4 as the inoculums of the pathogen 
generated for these experiments is very high, thus increasing vulnerability of the laboratory 
workers to become infected. Besides, the high risk viruses stored in these labs nee d to be 
maintained with utmost caution as any leakage from these labs can lead to havoc in the country. 
Constructing too many BSL -4s is not advisable due to biological threats. The BSL -3 labs are 
more than adequate for handling high risk pathogens and unde rtaking investigation of 
pandemics/epidemics. As of now, there are 18 BSL -3 labs operational/ under construction 
within the ICMR/DHR network. Also ICMR/DHR has developed a mobile BSL-3 lab in public 
private partnership. This lab is operational and will take pandemic preparedness to next level as 
it can be driven to the outbreak site and made operational within 24-48 hours. 
 
 2.12  Challenges faced by the ICMR 
 
Recommendation 
 
2.12.1 The Committee takes note of the challenges faced by the ICMR in operationalising 
clinical trials in India during the COVID -19 pandemic and commends for its efforts to carry 
out clinical trials in the face of such difficulties. The Committee also appreciates ICMR for 
developing a pan -India clinical trial network (Indian  Clinical Trial and Education Network -
INTENT) which will provide a single, ready platform for conducting rapid but good quality 
randomized clinical trials. 
(Para 4.14 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.12.2 ICMR is grateful to the committee for acknowledging the chal lenges faced in 
operationalizing clinical trials. INTENT would prove to be a very beneficial ready resource for 
conducting clinical trials in the country.
