CHAPTER–III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE  
 
3.1  Rapid Response Teams (RRT) 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.1.1  The Committee recommends DHR - ICMR to establish and manage Rapid Response 
Teams (RRT)  consisting of epidemiologists, immunologists, virologists, experts of infectious 
disease, physicians and other relevant scientific and clinical staff to counter any emergency 
situations developing due to disease Outbreaks. 
(Para1.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.1.2 During COVID-19, ICMR convened National Task Force (NTF) consisting of eminent 
epidemiologists, public health experts, physicians, virologists & other clinical scientists to 
deliberate on various aspects of disease outbreak including Diagnostics, Epi demiology & 
Surveillance, Operational Research (OR) & Clinical Research.  
 
3.1.3  At present, a multidisciplinary team of epidemiologists, virologist and immunologists 
does exist in ICMR Institutes, involved in outbreak investigation. Besides, each Institute of 
ICMR has relevant linkages with clinical experts.  
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.1.4  The Committee appreciates the existence of the multi -disciplinary team consisting 
of epidemiologists, virologists and immunologists at ICMR. The Committee, however, 
intends to convey the Government that the Rapid Response Team (RRT) must be at the 
alert mode to meet any eventualities of Biological and Chemical weapons/warfare, besides 
combating the challenges posed by the outbreak of endemic or pandemic. Such oversight 
body should not only have relevant linkages with clinical operational and clinical research 
institutes but also integrated co -ordination with national decision making body viz., NITI 
Aayog, PMO and Cabinet Secretariat to ward off or keep vigil against any possible 
biological or chemical warfare so that appropriate decision is taken with out delay even of 
an hour. The Committee understands that the Government needs to incorporate the 
component of biological/chemical, deterrence in its national security strategy. 
 
3.2  Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) 
  
Recommendation 
 
3.2.1 The Committee has noted that Pradhan Mantri Ayushman  Bharat Health Infrastructure 
Mission (PM-ABHIM) which was launched in October last year has yet not seen the light of the 
day. The Committee feels that the PM ABHIM is to be implemented from 2021 -22 to 2025 -26 

18 
 
i.e. for 5 years, thus non -utilization of fun ds allocated for the very first year casts serious 
doubts over the scheme achieving its intended targets. The Committee desires to know the 
reasons for the delay and hopes that the said scheme will be commenced soon. The Committee 
recommends that the Depar tment should give more impetus in implementing this scheme as it 
aims to bridge gaps in public health infrastructure, mainly in critical care facilities and 
primary care, both in rural and urban areas. 
(Para 2.15 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.2.2  As per approval of Cabinet for the PM-ABHIM scheme is to be implemented from 2021 -
22 to 2025-26 i.e. for 5 years. RE 2021 -22 under PM-ABHIM was Rs.140 Crores against which 
amount of Rs.116 Crores incurred during the F.Y. 2021 -22 under PM-ABHIM Scheme. Further, 
Rs.690 Crores has been earmarked for the F.Y. 2022-23 under PM-ABHIM scheme. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.2.3  The Committee endows due credence to PM -ABHIM in bridging gaps in public 
health infrastructure especially focused in critical care facilities and primary healthcare. 
The Committee, in this regard, would like to be apprised of appropriation of Rs. 140.00 
Crore during financial year 2021-22 and Rs. 690.00 crore in financial year 2022 -23 and the 
achievement of physical target against the actual expenditure during the said financial 
years.  
 
3.3  Funds for Covid-19 to ICMR 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.3.1 The Committee feels that adequate funds for Covid-19 to ICMR in BE 2022-23 should have 
been allocated. With newer variants of Covid -19 expected and questions over efficacy of 
vaccines with respect to newer variants, research work like genome analysis, efficacy studies o f 
vaccines over newer variants, efficacy of vaccines on lactating mothers etc is bound to suffer due 
to non-allocation of funds. Keeping in view the fact that Covid-19 is still not over, the Committee 
strongly recommends the Department to seek funds from M inistry of Finance under Covid -19 
head. 
(Para 2.16 ibid)  
 
Action Taken 
 
3.3.2 The funding for health research has continuously being increased over last few years 
including by budget allocation under PM -ABHIM. An amount of Rs.690.00 crores  has been 
allocated for the year 2022 -23 which includes Rs 323.00 crores for  Covid-19 during the F.Y. 
2022-23 under PM -ABHIM Scheme. However, as per the need and with development of 
national level mission mode research programmes, Department will seek addi tional budget 
from the Ministry of Finance. 
 
 
 
 

19 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.3.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry of Finance must 
allocate DHR at least 0.1% of GDP for health research in the next five years and earmark 
at least 5% of total health budget for health research for next year, to start with, towards 
combating any future outbreak of disease and meeting health exigencies.  
 
3.4  Emergency Epidemic Preparedness and Response 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.4.1 The Committee observes that in 2020 -21, out of the Rs. 1,275.00 crores released to 
ICMR, actual expenditure was only 1,236.30 crores. Similarly, in 2021-22 out of the total funds 
allocation of Rs. 526.28 crores the ICMR spent Rs. 232.72 crores only. The Co mmittee 
expresses its serious concern over partial utilisation of fund allocated under Emergency 
Epidemic Preparedness and Response. The Committee does not agree with the Department's 
version that less utilization of the allocated funds, did not affect in any way the physical 
achievements both in terms of procurement of testing kits, setting up of testing labs and 
creating the testing capacity in the country. Contrary to Department's reflection, the deadly 
second wave overwhelmed India's Covid -19 testing in frastructure. The second wave scores of 
people with symptoms of the disease could not get themselves tested, since labs were fully 
booked and test reports were significantly delayed. In many places, this delay in delivery of 
reports meant that seriously il l patients in dire need of comprehensive treatment couldn't get 
hospitalized and as a result scores of people died too. 
(Para 2.23 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.4.2  ICMR has prepared the budget for Covid -19 during the F.Y. 2020 –21 on the basis of 
anticipated requirement for the Covid -19 testing kits for all over India with the anticipated 
prices as on May – June 2020. However, Government has decided in September 2020 that  
States will procure the kits themselves which resulted less number of procurement by ICMR.     
The rates of kits have been also reduced too much as compared to March – April 2020 to post 
September 2020. During the second wave of infections, some labs where the case load was high, 
had an exceeded in-turnaround time (> 48 – 72 hours) in a proportion of cases due to very high 
demand for testing. 
 
3.4.3 Besides, many States and Offices (Private & Government Organizations) imposed a 
demand for testing of even healthy individuals, during inter-state travel or attending Office. This 
was not as per the National Covid -19 Guidelines of ICMR and Ministry of Health & Family 
Welfare and this resulted in overwhelming of labs un-necessarily. 
 
Further Recommendation  
 
3.4.4 The Committee is not in agreement with DHR’s plea of partial utilization of fund 
allocated under Emergency Epidemic Preparedness and Response. The delayed delivery of 
investigation reports & long waiting in queue of patients at hospital corridors & gates 
resulting into more than 5 lakh death during Second Wave of Pandemic Covid -19 are 
testimony to the fact of exhibiting mismanagement of Pandemic Covid-19. All Government 

20 
 
machinery reached to the point of grinding halt. The Committee understands the 
limitation of DHR over its anticipating capacity in the situation of unpredicted and 
unprecedented global health emergencies. However, the Committee recommends ICMR to 
enhance its professional pursuit and operational efficiency to meet any future health 
eventualities of this magnitude or more than this . The Committee further recommends 
ICMR to undertake project to make in -depth research/studies to predict/pre -hand 
revelation of possible outbreak of Pandemic by adopting the sewage sample test etc.  
 
3.5  Diversion of manpower and other resources 
 
Recommendation 
  
3.5.1 The Committee observes that the Department had to divert manpower and other 
resources in the Department of Health Research (DHR), ICMR and Medical Colleges for 
Covid-19 Management and ramping up the t esting labs both in 2020 -21 and 2021 -22. The 
Committee recommends that now with the experience of three waves, the Department should 
formulate a contingency plan to tackle such situation more skillfully. 
(Para 2.29 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.5.2 DHR-ICMR has r ecruited staff specifically for dealing with COVID -19 testing. The 
strength is kept according to the situation of COVID -19 in the country. The VRDL network is 
being strengthened along with addition of four NIVs in the country. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.5.3  The Committee recommends DHR to formulate the Contingency Plan to combat 
Covid-19 like national health emergencies viz. outbreak of ‘Monkeypox’ for timely and 
effective management of its menace. The DHR may appprise the Committee about steps 
taken in matter.  
 
3.6  Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.6.1 The Committee is pleased to note that the scheme for establishing Viral Research and 
Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) has been extended for another  five years i.e. till 2026. The 
Committee observes that out of the 132 VRDLs established across 25 States and 5 Union 
Territories in the country, only 80 VRDLs are functioning. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends DHR to facilitate for trained manpower and  work on other administrative 
procedures for swift commencement of operations in all the VRDLs. The Committee believes 
that for catering to the testing needs of a vast country like India, the spread/network of testing 
labs must be expanded. The Committee, therefore, recommends that, DHR must aim towards -
"One VRDL in each District" by 2026. The Committee hopes that increasing the spread of 
VRDLs would help in reducing the turnaround time from the present 24-48 hours. 
(para 3.6 ibid) 
 
 

21 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.6.2 As on April 2022, a total of 136 VRDLs have been setup across the country and while 
approving the expansion of the VRDL network, equal geographic coverage of the country has 
been ensured. Reporting of testing data indicates about the lab status whether fun ctional/non-
functional. As on date, 112 out of 136 VRDLs are reporting non -COVID 19 diagnoses and 
outbreak investigation data on the dedicated data mining centre at ICMR -NIE Chennai. The 
other VRDLs approved during last one and half year are in the process  of becoming fully 
functional. DHR is monitoring the same regularly.  Three consecutive trainings have been 
conducted for the VRDLs on the data reporting and technical aspects in the past four months. 
  
3.6.3 As per the present scheme norms, setting -up of V RDLs in each District may not be 
possible, since the VRDLs can be funded in government medical colleges/research 
institutions/army hospitals only. The scheme has specified yearly targets with defined budget 
outlay. However, during the COVID -19 Pandemic, l arge n umber of molecular diagnostic 
laboratories have been setup at district level, that can server the purpose.  
  
3.6.4 The DHR/ICMR is doing handholding of the VRDLs with the help of resource centers 
(NIV-Pune & NIE Chennai) by providing trainings on adv ance tools of diagnosis, 
standardization and developing S OPs for various testing procedures, enabling lab quality 
systems, sampling & transportation to further reduce the turnaround time from 24-48 hours. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.6.5 The Committee, notes that the DHR/ICMR is doing handholding of the VRDLs with 
the help of resource centers (NIV -Pune & NIE Chennai) by providing trainings on 
advance tools of diagnosis, standardization and developing S OPs for various testing 
procedures, enabling lab quality s ystems, sampling & transportation to further reduce 
the turnaround time from 24 -48 hours. The Committee, however, recommends DHR to 
ensure setting up of VRDLs in each district as a long term goal. The Committee is of the 
firm view that expansion of network  of testing quality labs throughout the country would 
definitely reduce the transportation time having a bearing on the turnaround time. 
 
3.7  Setting realistic targets 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.7.1 The Committee believes that targets should always be challenging  and commensurate to 
its capacity and requirements. The Committee recommends DHR to set targets keeping in mind 
the size of the country and its population so as to cover the remote and rural areas of the 
country which are devoid of quality testing infrastructure. 
(Para 3.11 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.7.2 The Department has targeted to establish 14 New VRDLs during the year 2022 -23. The 
VRDLs are approved taking into account the coverage of the Scheme and geographical 
distribution of VRDLs across the country. 
 

22 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.7.3 The Committee gives impetus to the need of a network of quality testing 
infrastructure in the country to map the various health index of the whole population to 
the extent of last miles of the country. The committee, therefore,  recommends DHR to 
expand the scope of VRDL scheme to cover the remote rural and tribal areas of the 
country. The Committee further recommends the Ministry of Finance to allocate higher 
allocation to the said scheme and extend its period of time years for implementation till 
achievement of its ideal objective of setting up of one VRDL in each district. 
 
 3.8  Establishment of MRUs 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.8.1 The Committee has been given to understand that so far, 92 MRUs are approved in the 
country and the Department's target was to set up 6 MRUs in 2021 -22. The Committee 
observes that like in 2021 -22, the MRU scheme has been allocated Rs. 60 crores only for t he 
same target of setting up 6 MRUs in 2022 -23. The Committee recommends DHR to set higher 
targets every year and seek more allocation for the scheme to increase the spread/network of 
MRUs in the country as there are no MRU in several states and the States  like Bihar and 
Chhattisgarh don‟t have MRUs in commensurate to the population of States. 
(Para 3.19 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.8.2 Targets for setting up new MRUs in a year are decided on the basis of past trends, 
requirements and availability of funds. All t he States and Union Territories are addressed 
regularly to send proposals for setting up of MRUs in Medical Colleges.  The MRU scheme 
approved for 2021-22 to 2025-26 envisages establishing of 30 MRUs, i.e. 06 MRUs every year. 
However, against the target of  establishing 06 MRUs in 2021 -22, 11 MRUs were actually 
approved. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.8.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation to DHR to seek allocation for the 
scheme to increase the spread/network of MRUs in the country as there are no MRU in 
several states and the States like Bihar and Chhattisgarh don’t have MRUs in 
commensurate to the population of States. 
 
 
3.9  Setting up MRUs in NER 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.9.1 The Committee has observed that no MRU has been established in Sikkim, Nagaland, 
Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh. Given the increasing Cancer cases in north-eastern States, 
the Committee is of the considered view that the Department must work in tandem wit h the 
respective State Governments and set up MRUs in these States at the earliest. The Committee 
believes that good clinical research infrastructure at the local level in the State can help boost 

23 
 
country's fight against Cancer and severe non - communicable diseases like Hypertensions and 
cardio-vascular diseases. 
(Para 3.20 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.9.2 MRUs in Govt. Medical colleges are established on the basis of proposals received from 
State Governments.  MRUs in the State of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Mizoram and Nagaland 
have been established under the MRU scheme of ICMR. Now, these have been taken over by 
DHR. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.9.3 Keeping in view the geographical landscape of NER, the Committee recommends for 
intensive network of MRU for ens uring basic infrastructure of clinical investigation and 
research work for region specific study of Biology of Diseases. The Committee is of the 
considered view that only better research infrastructure would provide adequate facilities 
for treatment of can cer and other life threatening communicable and non -communicable 
diseases viz. Hypertension and cardio -vascular disease. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation for setting up of MRUs in Sikkim and Meghalaya.  
 
3.10  Operationalisation of MRUs 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.10.1 The Committee also observes that though 92 MRUs are approved in the country but all 
the MRUs are not functional, the Committee finds no point in just announcing and approving 
MRUs if there is not enough manpower and infrastructure at the ground level. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends Department to reduce the delay between the dates of the announcement 
of approval and the actual operationalisation of MRUs at the ground level. 
(Para 3.21ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.10.2 The Time lag between the initial sanction of an MRU and the subsequent 
operationalization of that MRU is generally due to the time taken in awarding contracts for 
Civil Works and procurement of equipment and the recruitment of staff.  These functions in 
State Govt. Medical Colleges are regulated by the rules/instructions of the respective State 
Governments.  Process in these activities is, however, monitored regularly through periodical 
progress reports and virtual review meetings. The recommendation of the  Parliamentary 
Committee has, however, been noted for guidance and compliance. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.10.3 The Committee feels that DHR should take concrete steps for reducing the time lag 
between sanctioning of an MRU and operationalization of MRU uni t. The Committee 
does not approve the procedural delay in awarding civil works and procurement of 
equipment. The DHR, therefore, should have effective supervision and monitoring over 
the progress of the MRU projects. To avoid the delay, the Committee recom mends DHR 

24 
 
to get the technical and human resource strength sanctioned at the time of sanctioning of 
the project, itself.  
 
3.11  Objective of the MRHRU Scheme 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.11.1 The Committee notes that the objective of the MRHRU scheme is to transfer  modern 
technology for tackling the disease burden in rural India. The Committee is of the view that 
considering the havoc caused by Covid-19, particularly the second wave of Covid-19, there is a 
dire need to beef up health infrastructure in the rural India. The modern healthcare equipments 
and technologies which are generally limited to urban centres should be taken to the rural 
healthcare facilities as well. The Committee observes that despite the year -on-year increase in 
the budget of the scheme, the tar get to set up MRHRUs is decreasing from 7 in 2019 -20 to 2 in 
2021-22. For 2022 -23 also the target is to set up 2 MRHRUs only. The Committee further 
observes that there is no MRHRU in the vast state like Uttar Pradesh and also the UT of 
Ladakh. 
(Para 3.26 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.11.2 The targets are decided on the basis of past trends, proposals received from State 
Governments and available resources.  State Governments, ICMR, Directors of ICMR 
Institutes are regularly addressed to send their proposals. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.11.3 The Committee recommends DHR for taking pro -active steps in incentivizing the 
State Government to prepare proposal on setting up of MRHRU in rural areas. Extensive 
and equitable distribution of MRHRU would ensure the facility  of understanding Biology 
of various diseases in tribal and remote rural areas and thus ensure access to affordable 
treatment. The DHR, therefore, need to work in tandem with State Government and seek 
enhanced budgetary allocation from the Ministry of Fina nce for laying out network of 
MRHRU for ensuring availability of Modern tools, methods, equipments and technologies 
in rural healthcare system.  
 
 
3.12  Proposal for fellowship/training 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.12.1 The Committee observes that over the past three years the reason for under - utilisation 
of the allocated funds has been same i.e. due to receipt of less number of proposal for 
fellowship/training. The Committee understands that unless there is adequate bud getary 
allocation followed by optimal utilization of allocated fund, the objective to create a large pool 
of trained and skilled medical researchers would not be realized. The Committee is not 
satisfied with Department repeating the same reason for less nu mber of proposals for 
fellowship/training for under-utilisation of the allocated funds. The Committee desires to know 
the concrete steps taken by DHR to increase the number of proposals for fellowship/training. 

25 
 
The Committee strongly feels that there is no  dearth of talent in our country, hence the DHR 
should work on establishing institutional mechanism to attract scientists for submitting more 
proposals for fellowship under the schemes of DHR. 
(Para 3.33 ibid) 
 
3.12.2 The Committee observes that over the past 9 years, DHR's efforts to encourage Indian 
health research personnel serving abroad and coming back to India has paid little dividends as 
in these 9 years only 10 persons have availed this offer. The Committee ther efore, recommends 
that the Department must analyse the programme and find out the reasons as to why the scheme 
has few takers. The Committee also recommends that DHR must develop a conducive 
environment and offer lucrative prospects to Indian researches se rving abroad, so that they are 
encouraged to come back to their country of birth and serve their country. 
 
(Para 3.34) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.12.3 Following initiatives have been taken by the DHR in order to attract scientists for 
submitting more proposals with better research quality: 
 
1. For wider publicity the scheme was advertised in the national daily newspapers 
and social media platforms. 
 
2. Monthly stipend and research grant has been enhanced. 
 
3. Evaluation of the proposals, for those projects which are weak and require 
modification, the experts committee members provide the guidance and 
opportunity to modify the proposals. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.12.4  The Committee considers the need for creation of poo l of trained and skilled 
medical researchers in various fields to eliminate/eradicate various diseases in the country 
through in depth study, understanding Biology of Disease and find out solution for 
eradication in a time -bound manner. The Committee, ther efore, emphasizes the need for 
establishing institutional mechanism and simplification of procedures for inviting larger 
number of proposals for fellowship under the scheme governed by DHR. 
 
 
3.13  Human Resource Development for Health Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
3.13.1 The Committee observes that over the years there has been gross underutilization of the 
funds allocated and like in the case of Human Resource Development for Health Research 
component, the reason for under-utilization is same for all the years. The Committee notes that 
during last three years i.e. 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22, RE allocation has significantly been 
reduced, thereby implying that DHR did not get enough viable research projects to be 
undertaken and appropriation of alloc ated fund thereon. The Committee recommends DHR to 

26 
 
make serious efforts to identify research projects which have potential for treatment of diseases 
and therefore rational utilisation of allocated funds could be made. The Committee, strongly 
suggests DHR t o promote research and encourage researchers to undertake research for the 
benefit of public health. The Committee also recommends that in view of the increasing 
biological threats, the DHR should put more emphasis on research related to biological 
weapons to ensure that in the eventuality of biological attacks, the country is safeguarded 
against any biological warfare. 
(Para 3.41 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.13.2 The observation of the Hon’ble  Committee is noted and efforts will be made to identify 
research projects having potential for treatment of diseases and utilization of allocated funds. 
Following initiatives have been taken by the DHR in order to attract scientists for submitting 
more proposals with better research quality: 
 
1. For wider publicity the scheme was advertised in the national daily newspapers and social 
media platforms. 
 
2. Evaluations of the proposals, for those projects which are weak and require modification, 
the experts  committee members provide the guidance and opportunity to modify the 
proposals. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.13.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that DHR should encourage and 
emphasize on research relating to surveillance over biological weapon s and chemical 
warfare which have been equally threatening as nuclear weapons. The Committee, cautions 
the Government for chalking out counter strategy to guard the country against possible 
Biological and Chemical attack and therefore, feel the need and ur gency of strengthening 
defence mechanism from the point of Biological and Chemical Weapons.

CHAPTER–IV 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH FINAL REPLIES 
OF THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
4.1  Need for more skilled manpower in future 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.1.1 The Committee is contended to note that the Department is well aware of the need for 
more skilled manpower in future and bringing in more professionalism in its working for 
realizing the objectives of bio-safety and bio-security as well as to deal with diseases identified 
for elimination like TB, Malaria, Filariasis within a definite timeframe. However, the 
Committee, feels that Department should take action to fill the posts of scientific professionals 
so that crucial research work is  not delayed. The Committee recommends Department to fast -
track recruitment processes of skilled and scientific professionals. The Committee further 
recommends DHR to create a work culture and environment which attracts highly skilled 
professional shaving great scientific acumen. The Committee believes that offering lucrative 
career prospects along with a good work -life balance and liberty to carry out world class 
research would definitely attract best scientific brains to ICMR. 
(Para 1.11 ibid) 
Action Taken  
 
4.1.2 As on date, the total sanctioned strength of regular Government employees in the 
Department is 42 out of which 06 sanctioned posts are for Scientist C, D and E. These posts are 
to be filled on Deputation (ISTC) basis. The recruitment p rocess of Scientist C, D & E (02 
posts each) is at advanced stage in consultation with Union Public Service Commission 
(UPSC). 
 
4.1.3 DHR is concerned about intake of trained manpower and has been advertising and 
recruiting scientific positions in mission mode. In last 2 -3 years more than 100 scientists have 
been recruited in ICMR. Recently, scientists posts in the area of Entomology, An imal Resource 
Facility & Hemoglobinopathies Centre. Regular training is imparting in the area of Bioethics & 
Biosafety and Biosecurity. These activities will be strengthened further. 
 
 
4.2  Adequate Funds to Health Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.2.1 The Committee observes that for DHR, BE 2021 -22 allocation was Rs. 2663.00 crores 
which was increased to Rs. 3080.00 crores in RE 2021 -22 and the allocation for BE 2022-23 is 
Rs. 3200.65 crores only. The Committee further notes that while the increase in b udget from 
BE 2021-22 to RE 2021-22 is almost 16%, the increase from RE2021 -22 to BE 2022-23 is just 
3.92% only. The Committee further observes that while countries like UK and USA are 
allocating budget of around 2% of their GDP to health research, India w hich faces humongous 
burden of diseases which lead to poverty inducing out -of-pocket health expenditure by its 
population, allocates only 0.02% of its GDP for health research. 
(Para 2.6 ibid) 

28 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.2.2  The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. 
 
4.3  Higher Budgetary allocation for Health Research 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.3.1 The Committee is of the view that the increase in health research budget, year on year is 
very meager and is not commensurate with the tasks DHR -ICMR are entr usted to deal with. 
Thus the allocated budget is grossly insufficient to meet the existing and future healthcare 
challenges. The Committee feels that higher budgetary allocation for health research will 
result in more research based findings which in turn would help in devising more informed 
affordable and practical plans/methodologies for diagnosis and treatment of both 
communicable and non -communicable diseases. Higher allocation for health research would 
also make the country better prepared for tackling  any future outbreaks and health exigencies. 
The Committee, in its 127 th Report on Demand for Grants had recommended Government to 
allocate 5 percent of the budget of the Department of Health & Family Welfare to DHR. The 
Committee further reiterates its recommendation to allocate 5% of the total health budget for 
health research in the next two years. The Committee also recommends that considering global 
standards with respect to investment in health research, the Government must invest at least 
0.1% of the GDP in the next five years. Here the Committee also advances its support to DHR 
for seeking higher budgetary allocation from Ministry of Finance. 
(Para 2.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.3.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. The matter will be pursed with 
Ministry of Finance based on requirements during the RE stage. 
 
4.4  Boosting the absorption capacity of the implementing agencies 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.4.1 The Committee is pleased to observe that the percentage of shortfall/variation as 
compared to "Projected demand" is decreasing year -on-year. Therefore, the Committee is 
hopeful that the Department will continue to improve its fiscal performance by projecti ng 
realistic estimate each year to the Ministry of Finance. However, the Committee feels that that 
on the one hand the Secretary DHR demands 5% of total health budget for health research, on 
the other hand the Department's Projected Demand is nowhere close  to 5% of total health 
budget (Rs. 83,000 crores in BE 2022 - 23). The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends 
that DHR must work towards boosting the absorption capacity of the implementing agencies 
which are tasked with running its schemes across different regions of the country. 
 (Para 2.9 ibid) 
 
 
 
 

29 
 
 
Action Taken  
 
4.4.2 Department is working closely with the implementing agencies by providing training and 
hand holding to improve the quality of proposals received. Along with media advertisement for 
increasing awareness about the schemes. These efforts will ensue boosting in the absorption 
capacity of the implementing agencies and recently, PM-ABHIM schemes has been approved for 
next 5 years covering new activities / centers which are going to start w ithin the ambit of this 
Scheme which will boost the absorption capacity of ICMR. 
 
4.5  Enhance funds absorption capacities 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.5.1 The Committee, over the years, has recommended higher allocation to DHR, including 
for financial year 2022-23. After observing continuous under-utilisation of allocated funds, the 
Committee is of the opinion that seeking higher allocation by the department is not justified 
until the Department and its sister organizations and scheme implementing agencies don‟t 
enhance their funds absorption capacities. The Committee, therefore, urges DHR to boost fund 
absorption capacity of the implementing agencies and all organizations associated with it. The 
Committee also recommends that higher budgetary allocation would be jus tified only if the 
Department hires more skilled, experienced and scientific staff and undertakes more research 
projects of significance having impact on health and well being of Indian population. 
(Para 2.27 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.5.2 Continuous efforts are being made by the Department to increase research work in 
VRDLs, MRUs, MRHRUs thereby enhance their absorption capacity.  So far, 136 VRDLs, 97 
MRUs and 30 MRHRUs have been established and proposals for setting up more such units are  
under process.  Due to diversion of resources and staff for COVID -19 duties to augment the 
COVID testing capacity of the country lead to under utilization of funds. With the COVID 
pandemic on decline, research activities of are expected to increase, resul ting in more 
absorption capacity. The implementing agencies are also being pursued constantly by holding 
review meetings and workshops to expedite the utilization of funds. 
 
4.5.3 Taking into account the pandemic situation, some more centers of ICMR like O ne Health 
Center Nagpur, NIV Units at Chandigarh, Bangalore, Jabalpur & Dibrugarh are under 
construction. These Centers will cater the enhanced need of the Country and will also increase 
the absorption capacity of ICMR. 
 
 
4.6  Allocation as per originally conceived plan 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.6.1 The Committee believes that appropriate expenditure as per originally conceived plan by 
ICMR-DHR would make a good case for seeking higher budgetary allocation at the RE stage 
and BE 2023 -24 as it is well established t hat only through the in -depth health research, the 

30 
 
country can be saved from the life-threatening non-communicable and communicable diseases. 
 
(Para 4.6 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.6.2 Guidance of Committee is noted. Also, at the time of RE 2022 -23, an analysis  of last six 
months expenditure figures will be done and based on actual expenditure incurred, RE 2022 -23 
& BE 2023-24 will be demanded. 
 
4.7  Performance evaluation of ICMR 
 
Recommendation 
 
4.7.1 The Committee notes that the external evaluation and analysis conducted by Thomson 
Reuters for ICMR wherein ICMR was compared to similar organizations of US, UK, Australia, 
China and Brazil was done six years ago. Considering that since then the world has seen 3 
waves of Covid-19 pandemic, the Committee believes that now is an opportune time for another 
similar external evaluation. The Committee recommends ICMR to conduct such an evaluation 
wherein ICMR is compared to other competitors on parameters like, trends in budgetary 
allocation and utilization, compar ison between public and private investment, utilization 
avenues and research work under taken, health research infrastructure and its development, 
numbers of scientific professionals and clinical researchers, patents filed, number of 
fellowships and grant for research and future outlook. 
(Para 4.19 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
4.7.2 The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted for compliance. 
 
 
  

31 
 
RECOMEMNDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS- AT A GLANCE 
 
RAPID RESPONSE TEAMS (RRT) 
 
The Committee appreciates the existence of the multi -disciplinary team consisting 
of epidemiologists, virologists and immunologists at ICMR. The Committee, however, 
intends to convey the Government that the Rapid Response Team (RRT) must be at the 
alert mode to meet any eventualities of Biological and Chemical weapons/warfare, besides 
combating the challenges posed by the outbreak of endemic or pandemic. Such oversight 
body should not only have relevant linkages with clinical operational and clinical research 
institutes but also integrated co -ordination with national decision making body viz., NITI 
Aayog, PMO and Cabinet Secretariat to ward off or keep vigil against any possible 
biological or chemical warfare so that appropriate decision is taken without del ay even of 
an hour. The Committee understands that the Government needs to incorporate the 
component of biological/chemical, deterrence in its national security strategy. 
 
(Para 3.1.4) 
 
PRADHAN MANTRI AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE 
MISSION (PM-ABHIM) 
 
 The Committee endows due credence to PM -ABHIM in bridging gaps in public 
health infrastructure especially focused in critical care facilities and primary healthcare. 
The Committee, in this regard, would like to be apprised of appropriation of Rs. 140.00 
Crore during financial year 2021-22 and Rs. 690.00 crore in financial year 2022 -23 and the 
achievement of physical target against the actual expenditure during the said financial 
years.  
        (Para 3.2.3)  
 
FUNDS FOR COVID-19 TO ICMR 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry of Finance must 
allocate DHR at least 0.1% of GDP for health research in the next five years and earmark 
at least 5% of total health budget for health research for next year, to start with, tow ards 
combating any future outbreak of disease and meeting health exigencies. 
 
        (Para 3.3.3)  
  
EMERGENCY EPIDEMIC PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE 
 
The Committee is not in agreement with DHR’s plea of partial utilization of fund 
allocated under Emergency Epidemic Preparedness and Response. The delayed delivery of 
investigation reports & long waiting in queue of patients at hospital corridors & gates 
resulting into more than 5 lakh death during Second Wave of Pandemic Covid -19 are 
testimony to the fact of exhibiting mismanagement of Pandemic Covid-19. All Government 
machinery reached to the point of grinding halt. The Committee understands the 
limitation of DHR over its anticipating capacity in the situation of unpredicted and 
unprecedented global health emergencies. However, the Committee recommends ICMR to 

32 
 
enhance its professional pursuit and operational efficiency to meet any future health 
eventualities of this magnitude or more than this. The Committee further recommends 
ICMR to undertake project to make i n-depth research/studies to predict/pre -hand 
revelation of possible outbreak of Pandemic by adopting the sewage sample test etc. 
 
       (Para 3.4.4)  
 DIVERSION OF MANPOWER AND OTHER RESOURCES 
 
The Committee recommends DHR to formulate the Contingency Plan to combat 
Covid-19 like national health emergencies viz. outbreak of ‘Monkeypox’ for timely and 
effective management of its menace. The DHR may appprise the Committee about steps 
taken in matter.  
 
       (Para 3.5.3)  
 
VIRAL RESEARCH AND DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORIES (VRDLS) 
 
The Committee, notes that the DHR/ICMR is doing handholding of the VRDLs 
with the help of resource centers (NIV -Pune & NIE Chennai) by providing trainings on 
advance tools of diagnosis, standardization and developing SOPs for various testing 
procedures, enabling lab quality systems, sampling & transportation to further reduce 
the turnaround time from 24 -48 hours. The Committee, however, recommends DHR to 
ensure setting up of VRDLs in each district as a long term goal. The Committee is of the 
firm view that expansion of network of testing quality labs throughout the country would 
definitely reduce the transportation time having a bearing on the turnaround time. 
 
       (Para 3.6.5)  
SETTING REALISTIC TARGETS 
 
The Committee gives impetus to the need of a network of quality testing 
infrastructure in the country to map the various health index of the whole population to 
the extent of last miles of the country. The committee, therefore, recommends DHR to 
expand the scope of VRDL scheme to cov er the remote rural and tribal areas of the 
country. The Committee further recommends the Ministry of Finance to allocate higher 
allocation to the said scheme and extend its period of time years for implementation till 
achievement of its ideal objective of setting up of one VRDL in each district. 
 
      (Para 3.7.3)  
ESTABLISHMENT OF MRUS 
 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation to DHR to seek allocation for the 
scheme to increase the spread/network of MRUs in the country as there are no MRU in 
several states and the States like Bihar and Chhattisgarh don’t have MRUs in 
commensurate to the population of States. 
      (Para 3.8.3)  
SETTING UP MRUS IN NER 
 
Keeping in view the geographical landscape of NER, the Committee recommends 
for intensive network of MRU for ensuring basic infrastructure of clinical investigation 

33 
 
and research work for region specific study of Biology of Diseases. The Committee is of the 
considered view that only better research infrastructure would provide adequate facilities 
for treatment of cancer and other life threatening communicable and non -communicable 
diseases viz. Hypertension and cardio -vascular disease. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation for setting up of MRUs in Sikkim and Meghalaya.  
 
        (Para 3.9.3)  
OPERATIONALISATION OF MRUS 
 
The Committee feels that DHR should take concrete steps for reducing the time 
lag between sanctioning of an MRU and operationalization of MRU unit. The Committee 
does not approve the procedural delay in awa rding civil works and procurement of 
equipment. The DHR, therefore, should have effective supervision and monitoring over 
the progress of the MRU projects. To avoid the delay, the Committee recommends DHR 
to get the technical and human resource strength sa nctioned at the time of sanctioning of 
the project, itself.  
    (Para 3.10.3)  
OBJECTIVE OF THE MRHRU SCHEME 
 
 The Committee recommends DHR for taking pro -active steps in incentivizing the 
State Government to prepare proposal on setting up of MRHRU in rur al areas. Extensive 
and equitable distribution of MRHRU would ensure the facility of understanding Biology 
of various diseases in tribal and remote rural areas and thus ensure access to affordable 
treatment. The DHR, therefore, need to work in tandem with State Government and seek 
enhanced budgetary allocation from the Ministry of Finance for laying out network of 
MRHRU for ensuring availability of Modern tools, methods, equipments and technologies 
in rural healthcare system.  
    (Para 3.11.3)  
 
PROPOSAL FOR FELLOWSHIP/TRAINING 
 
The Committee considers the need for creation of pool of trained and skilled 
medical researchers in various fields to eliminate/eradicate various diseases in the country 
through in depth study, understanding Biology of Disease and find out solution for 
eradication in a time -bound manner. The Committee, therefore, emphasizes the need for 
establishing institutional mechanism and simplification of procedures for inviting larger 
number of proposals for fellowship under the scheme governed by DHR. 
      (Para 3.12.4)  
 
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT FOR HEALTH RESEARCH 
 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation that DHR should encourage and 
emphasize on research relating to surveillance over biological weapons and chemical 
warfare which have been equally threatening as nuclear weapons. The Committee, cautions 
the Govern ment for chalking out counter strategy to guard the country against possible 
Biological and Chemical attack and therefore, feel the need and urgency of strengthening 
defence mechanism from the point of Biological and Chemical Weapons.  
 
                              (Para 3.13.3)

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
1.1    Budgetary Allocation of Ministry of Ayush 
Recommendation 
1.1.1 The Committee notes that the allocation of Ministry of Ayush is 3.69% of the Health Budget 
in 2022-23 as against 4.17% of the Health Budget in 2021-22. Instead of a gradual increase over 
the years, this year has witnessed a marked reduction in allocation for the Ministry of Ayush 
compared to the allocation for Ministry  of Health & Family Welfare. The Committee is not 
happy with this reduction in allocation compared to Health Budget and would like to point out 
that the budget of Ministry of Ayush is still lower to 5% of the Health Budget. The Committee is 
of the consider ed view that Ministry of Ayush, intending to embark on a journey of AYUSH 
revolution, must be adequately funded and schemes meticulously executed so as to realize the 
full potential of AYUSH Systems. The importance of Ayush Systems, particularly in Covid t imes, 
is highly appreciated with rising popularity of these systems and their increasing acceptability as 
an economical and effective system of medicine. The Committee in its 128 th Report had 
emphasized upon appropriate financial support and had also recommended that 10% of the 
Health Budget should be given to Ministry of Ayush from 2022 -23 onwards. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends that Ministry of Finance maybe approached to allocate atleast 8% of 
the Health Budget to Ministry of Ayush in RE 2022 -23 and 10% of the Health Budget from next 
financial year. 
(Para 2.10 of 136th Report) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2 The projected demand for the financial year 2022 -23 is Rs. 3139.53 crore against which an 
amount of Rs. 3050.00 crore has been allocated. Since projected demand is low due to the reasons 
explained in para 2.2 & 2.4 above, therefore, the allocation for Ministry of Ayush budget comes 
to only 3.67% of Health Ministry‟s budget. How ever, additional fund if any, will be demanded at 
RE stage after due examination. The recommendation of the Committee is noted and the ministry 
is actively considering the concern of the Committee. 
1.2    Realistic assessment of its funds requirement 
 Recommendation 
1.2.1 The Committee, while referring to „Meeting the targets through enhanced allocation of 
budget in the document proposal to 15 th Finance Commission of India on Promotion of AYUSH 
Services & Strengthen the Healthcare Delivery in the country, recommends the Ministry of Ayush  
to have a realistic assessment of its funds requirement keeping in view the larger objectives of the 
Ministry on holistic wellness based on the principles of prevention o f diseases and promotion of 
health with enhanced investment which will in turn reduce the out of pocket expenditure and 
financial burden on the population.  
(Para 2.13 ibid) 
 

3 
 
Action Taken 
1.2.2       Union Cabinet has approved Rs. 3399.35 Crore ( Rs. 2209.58 Crore as Central Share 
and Rs. 1189.77 Crore as State Share) for operationalization of  12,500 Ayush Health and 
Wellness Centres (HWCs) under Ayushman Bharat in a phased manner by from the year 2019 -20 
to 2023 -24.  The objective of AYUSH Health and  Wellness Centres (HWCs) is to establish a 
holistic wellness model based on AYUSH principles and practices, to empower masses for “self -
care” to reduce the disease burden, out of pocket expenditure and to provide informed choice to 
the needy public. The li fe style changes have been also targeted through operationalization of 
12,500 AYUSH Health Wellness Centres. Further, 7553 AYUSH HWCs have been approved 
from 2019 -20 to 2021 -22. Out of this, 3313 AYUSH HWCs have been made functional under 
progressive category. The recommendation of the Committee is noted and the ministry is actively 
considering the concern of the Committee. 
1.3    Construction Projects 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 The Committee observes with concern that except for NIH, Kolkata, Phase II, all the 
remaining construction projects are incomplete. The physical progress as on 31 st December,

3.1    Key Initiatives   
Recommendation 
3.1.1 The Committee takes cognizance of the growing importance and emergence of AYUSH 
systems in public healthcare system. The Committee notes that with a wide functional area and 
proper institutional support of research councils, educational institutes, regulatory bodies etc, it 
is evident that the Ministry is treading towards establishing itself as a strong alternative system 
of medicine with growing number of people reposing their faith in its efficacy. The Committee 
appreciates that the National Health Policy (NHP) 2017 had strongly advocated  mainstreaming 
the potential of AYUSH within a pluralistic system of Integrative healthcare and re -emphasizing 
the need for integrating AYUSH in the National Health Mission, research and education. The 
Committee, therefore, believes that the Ministry has a  very important mandate to strategize and 
devise ways to galvanize the AYUSH system with a definite roadmap for quality education, 
quality healthcare delivery system, safety and efficacy of AYUSH drugs, promotion to exports 
etc. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Ministry to lay focus on the implementation of 
its schemes, maintaining high standards of education and research and regulation and control 
over quality and safety of AYUSH drugs. 
 
(Para 1.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
3.1.2 The recommendation of the committee has been noted. The Ministry of AYUSH has 
implemented a new Central Sector Scheme namely AYURGYAN during FY 2021 -22.  The 
main aim of the Scheme is to support Education, Research & Innovation in AYUSH by 
providing academ ic activities, training, Capacity Building etc. The Scheme has 02 sub -
components viz. Capacity Building and Continuing Medical Education (CME) in AYUSH and 
Research and Innovation in AYUSH. The scheme has been designed to encourage AYUSH 
personnel to under go need-based professional training and bridge the knowledge gaps; and t o 
encourage R & D activities in priority areas so that the research findings lead to validation of 
claims and acceptability of the AYUSH approach and drugs. 
 
3.1.3 The Ministry of Ayush is implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of National 
AYUSH Mission (NAM) in the country for promotion and development of AYUSH system of 
medicines through States/UTs. Grant-in-aid is provided to the States/UTs as per the proposals  
submitted through State Annual Action Plans (SAAPs). The Mission inter -alia makes provision

Recommendation 
3.7.1 The Committee observes that in the 36 States/UTs, a total of 487 AYUSH Co -located

focused attention is given to making Ayush healthcare facilities available through co -location 
facilities in order to provide an alternative system of medicine which is effective and

that with adequate fund allocation by the Government and concerted efforts of the Ministry, the

3.24.1 Since the time the Ministry of Ayush emerged as an independent Ministry, focused

efficacious line of treatment. The growth and popularity of Ayush Systems rose tremendously 
during the pandemic Covid -19 with high demand for  immunity booster med icines and mass 
following of the guidelines and advisories issued by the Ministry to manage Covid -19. Ayush 
systems gained popularity and recognition not only in the country but abroad too.

growing. The Ministry, therefore, strive towards accelerated growth of the Ayush systems by 
strengthening its regulatory system, infrastructure, enhanced budgetary investment, ensuring 
the accessibility of Ayush services in un -served and far flung rural, urban slum and tribal

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
Against the estimation of Ministry of Ayush the Committee does not find 
considerable increase in release of grants i.e. Rs. 50.56 Crore, Rs. 47.58 Crore and Rs. 
44.765 Crore during 2020 -21, 2021-22 and 2022 -23, respectively, to CCRS to achieve the 
short term and long term goals as envisaged in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 
and Na tional Health Policy 2017. The Committee understands that there would be 
quantum jump in recurring and non -recurring expenditure once the institutes gets status 
of 'Deemed to be University' and permission to start UG Course, PF, PG -Diploma is 
granted to the Institute. The Committee, therefore, recommends that pending application 
for grants of demand to be university is granted to CCRS without delay and adequate 
budgetary grant should be allocated CCRS to meet the recurring and non -recurring 
expenditure. The Committee further desires to know the physical achievement in regard 
to strengthening of infrastructure facilities research and outreach activities as done by 
CCRUM to prepare the Unani System of Medicine as economical and alternative system 
of medicine.  
(Para 3.4.14) 
The Committee further desires to be informed about the outcome of steps taken in 
regard to Ayush Public Health Programme under NAM during last two years viz. 
Integration of Ayush with NPCDCS,  VAYO Mitra, Ayush Geriatric Services, morbidity 
management and disability prevention. The Ministry may also furnish the details of 
objective of establishment of Ayush Grid, its intended institutional structure and proposed 
functions.  
(Para 3.4.15) 
MERGER OF ERSTWHILE SCHEMES IN NEW SCHEMES 
The Committee appreciates that the Ministry, subsequent to the completion of the 
procedural formalities, has finalized the components of 'AYURGYAN' & 
'AYURSWASTHA' Yojna. The Committee, however, desires that the new scheme 
guidelines are formulated without  further delay so that the actual 
operationalization/execution of the scheme takes place on the ground level and the said 
targets of the scheme are achieved within stipulated timeframe. The Committee hopes that 
the Ministry may inform about the operational ization and outcome of execution of 
AOUGSY. The Committee further feels that the Ministry should approach the Cabinet 
Secretariat urging that the Cabinet Note on PM -VAY stands withdrawn and a fresh 
Cabinet Note is required to be placed to give a flying start to the PM-VAY.   
(Para 3.5.5) 
 
SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY 
The Committee recommends the Ministry to furnish details of appropriation of 
amount out of earmarked fund to the tune of Rs. 800.00 cr. in BE 2022 -23 to National 

79 
 
Ayush Mission and achievement thereo f against the set physical target vis-à-vis each 
component of the Mission. The Committee hopes that judicious and optimal utilization of 
funds would yield desired result of the scheme on the ground level.   
(Para 3.6.6) 
The Committee takes into account the  fact that State/UT Governments have 
demanded more fund to strengthen the AYUSH health facilities, therefore, more funds 
are required for better access to AYUSH Services through increase in number of AYUSH 
Hospitals and Dispensaries, AYUSH HWCs and impleme ntation of different AYUSH 
Public Health Programmes. The Committee, accordingly recommends the Ministry to 
approach the Ministry of Finance to earmark the requisite fund to the scheme for its 
successful implementation. 
(Para 3.6.7) 
AYUSH CO-LOCATED FACILITIES 
 The Committee believes that Ayush co -located facilities at all three levels of 
healthcare viz. Public Health Centre (PHC), Community Health Centres (CHC) and 
District Hospitals  (DHs) in all States/UTs is essential for popularizing and propagating 
Ayush System as viable alternative system of medicine among common masses. Being 
economical and effective the Central Government should incentivize and encourage 
State/UTs Government to give flip to the Ayush co -location facilities having adequ ate 
technical facilities and human resources. The Ministry may emphasis on even distribution 
of Ayush location facilities in all States/UTs. 
(Para 3.7.3) 
OPERATIONALIZATION OF AYUSH HWCS 
 The Committee is of the considered view that the operationalization of Ayush 
Health and Wellness Centers (HWCs) would definitely accelerate in post pandemic covid -
19 phase as the situation arising of pandemic is gradually moving towards normalcy. The 
Ministry has already granted Rs. 230.66 cr. in third quarter of the year 2021-22 for 
upgradation of 3048 health facilities in 27 States/UTs. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry to monitor the completion of operationalization of Ayush HWCs within stipulated 
timeframe. 
 
(Para 3.8.5) 
PRADHAN MANTRI VRIKSH AYUSH YOJANA 
 
  The Committee stipulates that ones the PM -VAY is finalized, approved and 
implemented and the network of the 'Aushdhi Dhams' is evenly expanded across the 
country there would be increase in cultivation of medical plants. The Committee believes 
that the Cou ntry would become a hotspot for 'Medical Tourism' for foreigners willing to 
have treatment through Ayush System.   
(Para 3.9.3) 
 

80 
 
CREATION OF 24 POSTS FOR NMPB 
 
 The Committee expects the Ministry to furnish the details regarding the duration 
since when the  proposal of creation of 24 posts for NNPB is pending in E -Coord.-I of 
Department of Expenditure. The Ministry may again approach the Department of 
Expenditure to obtain green signal to the proposal. The Ministry may apprise to the 
Committee that response of the Department of Expenditure in the matter. 
(Para 3.10.4) 
 
 
INDIA AS EXPORTER OF MEDICINAL PLANTS, HERBS, SPICES 
 
 The Committee wants the Ministry of Ayush to proactively execute the scheme for 
encouraging export of herbal medicines and spices to usher Global Ayush Revolution led 
by India. The Committee reiterates its recommendation to the Ministry to examine an 
experiment with Odisha Model of livelihood assessment called Baithrani as an intervention 
for enhancing the production of high quality herbal raw material and enhancing the profit 
making herbal growers.  
(Para 3.11.4) 
CULTIVATING MEDICINAL PLANTS 
 The Committee understands that PM -VAY, that aims to promote cultivation of 
medical plants, post harvest management and marketing support, need to be approved and 
effectively implemented without further procrastination. The Committee believes that it 
would be appropriate for the Ministry and more specifically the NMPB to work in tandem 
with farmers and Ayush industry to encourage cultivation of medical plants. In the 
estimation of the Committee, the provision of financial assistance to the farmers to 
encourage farming/cultivation of medical plants should have continued under the centrally 
sponsored scheme. 
(Para 3.12.4) 
QUALITY CONTROL OF AYUSH DRUGS 
The Committee is of the firm view that assured quality control of AYUSH drugs is 
vital for global recognition  and acceptance of AYUSH system of medicine. The Committee 
is however, constrained to express its displeasure over dilly dallying approach of the 
Ministry in taking final and firm decision on strengthening of its regulatory framework i.e. 
adequate staffing of CDSCO. The Committee advises the Ministry that ad -hoc and interim 
arrangement would not be capable of strengthening the Ayush regulatory mechanism, 
therefore, the Committee recommends the Ministry to fill up 9 vacant posts in CDSCO, 05 
regulatory posts  including one post of Deputy Drugs Controller, four posts of Assistant 
Drugs Controllers (one each for Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs) 
without further delay so that the quality of the Ayush drugs is assured. 
(Para 3.13.4) 
 

81 
 
AYUSH VERTICAL CDSCO 
 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation to the Ministry to expedite the 
recruitment process to fill up 09 Posts in CDSCO on regular basis to complete institutional 
Ayush Vertical CDSCO so that Central Drugs Controller for Ayush can play pivotal role. 
(Para 3.14.3) 
PHARMACOVIGILANCE CENTRE 
 
The Committee recommends that the network of Pharmacovigilance centre should 
be evenly distributed across the country, of course, keeping in view the population and 
number of the Ayush drugs manufacturers and number of misleading claims and 
advertisement. The Committee believes that such consideration and adherence to the 
measure would definitely assure the quality control of Ayush drugs.  
(Para 3.15.3) 
SHORTAGE OF MANPOWER IN PHARMACOVIGILANCE CENTRES 
  The Committee takes into account that, as per the scheme guidelines of AOGUSY 
there is scope and requirement of two technical program officer and one Data entry 
operator (DEO) at NPVcC one Program Associate and one DEO at each IPVcC one 
Program Assistant at each PPVcC. The Committee, accordingl y, recommends the Ministry 
to consider the proposal for adequate manpower at each Pharmacovigilance Centre to 
ensure the achievement of cherished objectives of AOGUSY. 
(Para 3.16.3) 
NABH ACCREDITATION 
The Committee understands that the significance of NABH  accreditation for health 
institutions as the same endorse goodwill to the quality and competency of the institute in 
the delivery of the services. In this regard, the Committee recommends Sidha Central 
Institute Chennai to acquire the technical and instit utional standard as the same condition 
is pre-requisite to obtain NABH accreditation. The Committee observes that CCRH is also 
required to complete documentation process, sensitization programme and NABH Ayush 
Assessor Training Programmes to obtain NABH ac creditation for its three institutes. The 
Committee recommends the NEIAH, NEIAFMR, CCRAS to take requisite steps 
immediately to obtain NABH accreditation for its institutes. The Committee expresses 
concern over undue delay in grating adequate funds for con struction of building and 
acquirement of other physical, technical and trained manpower to obtain NABH 
accreditation.  
(Para 3.17.14) 
 
 
VACANT POSTS IN THE FIVE RESEARCH COUNCILS 
 
 The Committee is not ignorant of outcry of unemployed youth in the country on the 
one hand but unfortunately on the other hand the Committee finds it ironical that 
numerous posts in 5 Ayush council stands vacant. In CCRAS, out of total sanctioned 

82 
 
strength of 287 posts a total of 116 posts are vacant while in CCRH out of sanctioned 460 
posts the number of vacant posts stands to be 189. In CCRAS the proposal for revival of 
472 posts hangs fire pending under consideration of the Government. A number of posts 
are vacant in CCRUM and the Ministry has directed CCRYN to fill up the vacant posts. 
The Committee, therefore, urges the Ministry to closely monitor the recruitment process in 
Ayush 5 research councils.  
(Para 3.18.8) 
RESEARCH MANAGEMENT INFORMATION SYSTEM (RMIS) 
The Committee appreciates that CCRAS and CCRH have adopted the CTMS for 
better management of research projects. The Committee, however, desires that CCRS and 
CCRUM should also adhere to CTMS to promote objectivity, transparency and sharing of 
R&D outcomes. Other research councils should also follow the suit of CCRAS in regard to 
drug development, safety evaluation, clinical research, besides adopting to the good clinical 
practices (GCP).   
(Para 3.19.7) 
GRAND VISION OF THE MINISTRY 
Keeping in view the short term, medium term and the long term course of action 
pertaining to vision @ 2047 of the Ministry of Ayush, especially SGoS4 and SGoS8, the 
Committee considers urgent need of quantum increase in the Budgetary Allocation of the 
Ministry for overhauling the strategic areas of research, education and capacity building, 
healthcare manufacturing and services. The Committee, therefore, recommends for 
realistic assessment of budgetary requirement of the Ministry and urges the Ministry of 
Ayush to approach the Ministry of Finance for obtaining the budgetary grant as per the 
requirement.  
         (Para 3.20.3) 
 
SWEARING IN PROCESS BY DOCTORS 
The Committee is not happy with the response of the Ministry in regard to the 
suggestion of the Committee for taking up the matter to the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare to resolve the burning question relating to the swearing in process by doctors 
wherein there is confusion whether the AYUSH doctors would take the Hippocratic Oath 
or the Charak Oat h. The Committee finds that the Ministry is retorting that suggestion of 
the Committee has been noted and necessary step shall be taken in consultation with the 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare to resolve the issue. The Committee, therefore, 
believes th at the Ministry of Ayush in tandem with the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare would remove the confusion of the Ayush medical practitioners at the earliest.  
(Para 3.21.6) 
 
 

83 
 
VACANT POSTS IN VARIOUS AYUSH INSTITUTES 
 The prevalence of large number of vacant posts in various Ayush Institutes viz. 57 in 
NEIAH, 47 in NIA, revival of 470 posts in CCRAS, 189 posts in CCRH, 7 posts in NIS and 
likewise vacancy in other Ayush institutes are matter of concern to the Committee. The 
Committee feels that had the Ministry lend its support to the institute and monitored the 
recruitment process in various Ayush Institutes for filling up the vacant posts, there would 
have not been so much procrastination in filling up the vacant posts.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Ministry to coordinate with the Ayush Institutes and resolve the 
administrative stumbling block or whatever challenges come across over the recruitment 
process.  
(Para 3.22.12) 
LEGISLATION ON YOGA AND NATUROPATHY 
 The Committee expresses its concern over undue procrastination in bringing forth the 
necessary legislation to regulate the Yoga and Naturopathy. The Committee, therefore, 
reiterates its recommendation suggesting the Ministry to make concerted efforts for 
expediting the said legislation keeping in view with the fact that the said legislation would 
be a game changer in the regulation of Yoga and Naturopathy due to increasing acceptance 
and popularity of the Yoga and Naturopathy in changing the lifestyle and a s the mode of 
preventing the disease.   
(Para 3.23.3) 
TAP THE HUGE POTENTIAL OF AYUSH SYSTEMS 
The Committee appreciates 3 days GAIIS at Gandhinagar, Gujarat - Global Ayush 
Investment and Innovation Summit, from 20 -22 April, 2022, that collected Letter of 
Interest (LoI) over 9000 crore, 70 MoUs signed between countries, research institutes, 
farmer groups and industry. The Committee recommends that investment and MoUs so 
gathered must be optimally and opportunistically utilized in reviving the traditional Ind ian 
medicine and popularizing the same amongst countrymen as well as foreign health tourists. 
Besides, the enhanced budgetary grant, the Government should organize such Ayush 
Global Summit more frequently for inviting heavy investment in Ayush Sector for i ts 
assured promotion and propagation on the basis of rendering quality healthcare services. 
(Para 3.24.5)

Annexure-III 
VISION DOCUMENTS 
1. Vision Document  of CCRAS  envisages to develop scientific evidence in Ayurvedic 
Principles, drug therapies by way of integrating ancient wisdom with modern technology and to 
bring Ayurveda to the people through innovations related diagnostics, preventive, promotive as 
well as trea tment methods and also introduce scientific research for sustained availability of 
quality natural resources, to translate them into products and processes and in synergy with 
concerned organizations to introduce these innovations into public health systems.  
2. The main features  are Translation of research outcome into clinical practice through 
commercialization of new drugs developed by CCRAS through translational research for making 
them accessible to the public; Mainstreaming of Ayurveda therapies throu gh integration and 
including them in a National Health Programme;  Integration of Ayurveda in National 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme  by developing evidence based Ayurvedic 
interventions for Ante Natal, Post Natal and Child Health Care; Development of new 
drugs/combinations based on the leads from classical literature and also from local health 
traditions on different conditions to meet the demand of unmet medical needs;Development of 
safe /effective products for diseases of national and global impo rtance as add -on/ adjuvant 
therapies and also for standalone management for improvement of quality of life;Generation of 
scientific evidence on safety of Ayurvedic formulations and therapies; Development of the 
Directives addressing different research needs  viz. i. Drug development (addressing issues of 
quality, shelf life, safety issues and other requirements), ii. Safety evaluation (pre -clinical) and 
iii. Clinical research for AYUSH interventions; Validation of Fundamental principles of 
Ayurveda including Ayurveda biology; Development of comprehensive, pragmatic, adaptable an 
Ayurvedic user‟s friendly format for clinical diagnosis and clinical examination for utilization 
among health care professionals and its validation;  Development and validation of Clini cal 
Decision Support Systems and HIMS and e -management; Development of Standard Ayurvedic 
terminologies and its publication in different volume in a phased manner; Occupational Health  
such as Generalized Anxiety Disorder/Stress etcAnd Outreach programmes f or extending health 
care and documentation and institutional linkages with reputed institutes such as CSIR and 
ICMR collaboration 
 
3. The Council has strived to actualize research in most of the areas envisaged in the Vision 
Document 2030 . The Council has  validated Ayurveda classical formulations in identified 
disease conditions to generate tangible evidence on their clinical safety and efficacy and 
undertaken drug development in various identified disease conditions such as Ayush PJ -7 in 
Dengue, Ayush SL in chronic lymphedema, Ayush D in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Carctol S in 
Ovarian Cancer, Ayush HR &Ayush M3 in  Essential Hypertension, C1 oil for wound healing, 
Ayush Manas in Cognitive deficit etc which are under different phases of drug development. The 
Council developed Ayurveda formulations viz.AYUSH  64 , Ayush SG (ShunthiGuggulu) , 
Ayush 82 and transferred their technology through NRDC for making them accessible to the 
public. Also, AYUSH 64 was repurposed for the management of asymptomatic, mild to 
moderate COVID -19 based on the tangible evidence generated through robust studies and made 
available to the public through technology transfer. The Council has also undertaken studies to 
evaluate the clinical efficacy of Ayurveda formulations in Occupatio nal stress in IT 
persons/Nurses. 

95 
 
4. Envisioning the integration of Ayurveda into the National Reproductive and Child Health 
Programme, the Councilha simplemented a collaborative projectin association with Govt. of 
Maharashtra to  see the feasibility of intr oducing Ayurvedic interventions in Reproductive and 
Child Health (RCH) through integrative health care services in 30 selected PHCs of Gadchiroli 
district of Maharashtra,which is ongoing. 
5. The Council brought three general guidelinesfor (i)Drug development  (ii) safety /toxicity 
evaluation and (iii) Clinical evaluation of  Ayurvedic formulations/interventions. 
6. The council developed Standard Ayurvedic terminologies through consultation and 
published the document and  also hosted National AYUSH Morbidity and Standardized 
Terminology Electronic Portal (NAMASTE) for uniform centralized collection of AYUSH 
morbidity statistics.For validation of fundamental principles, the Council developed and 
validated the “Prakriti Assessment Scale” and designed a user frie ndly web portal namely 
“AYUR Prakriti Web Portal” for Prakriti assessment, validated Ayurveda diagnostic tools are 
also being developed for identified disease conditions, Swasthya Assessment Scale (SAS) to 
assess the Health status of a person through a val idated questionnaire for use by Ayurveda 
physicians.Also implemented A-HIMS in its institutes engaged in OPD/IPD services 
7. Council is also delivering health care services through different ongoing outreach 
programmes viz. THCRP, AMHCP (SCSP), RCH & NE. I n which health care services are being 
provided through OPD (Camps).  
8. Collaborative research projects were undertaken with reputed institutes such as ICMR. 
CSIR, AIIMS New Delhi, IIT New Delhi , IIT-Guwahati etc.

CHAPTER I 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1 India is on its path to become the most populated country in the world, therefore, 
access to affordable and quality healthcare services is crucial for optimizing the productivity 
of human resources in National economic growth and development. The National Health 
Policy-2017 recognized the pivotal importance of UN Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs) and envisaged the attainment of the highest possible level of health and wellbeing for 
all, at all ages, as its goal. As India steps into a post -COVID world, policy makers and project 
implementing agencies must realize the importance of UN SDGs in improving health 
indicators and establishing an equitable and resilient health system.  
1.2 The pandemic years brought the world to a standstill and threw a new set of 
challenges to health sector. It also brought to the forefront the lack of robust health 
infrastructure and the urgent need for investment in health sector. Frugal investment over the 
years in health related research and the limited availability of genome t esting facilities in the 
country further attributed to the late identification of other mutant variants of COVID -19 that 
severely impacted the mortality rate. The pandemic also highlighted the need of a strong 
primary health care infrastructure especially when the rural, slums and many urban areas are 
still devoid of basic healthcare facilities. Shortage of healthcare workforce, medical 
equipments, and medicines at PHC/CHC keeps a major chunk of population out of the ambit 
of affordable healthcare services.  The disruption in the available Primary Health Care 
Services due to COVID-19 further widened the gap between health care and its delivery. In a 
post pandemic world, therefore, the momentum gained in digitization of healthcare services as 
well as the investment in the health sector must be sustained and further enhanced.  
1.3 In the Union Budget 2023 -24, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been 
allocated budgetary funds to the tune of Rs. 89,155 crore. The Finance Minister in her budget 
speech had inter-alia announced that one hundred and fifty -seven new nursing colleges will 
be established in co -location with the existing 157 medical colleges. A Mission to eliminate 
Sickle Cell Anaemia by 2047 will also be launched along with a number of other ini tiatives. 
The Committee in this Report will examine the budgetary allocation and the utilisation trend 
of various Schemes and initiatives under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and 
accordingly give recommendations on the Demands for Grants of the Ministry.

tackling a sudden public health crisis.

2013-14 to 48.2% in 2018 -19. However, the Committee notes that a 48.2% of OOPE in 
health is still a major deterrent to quality health care. As per the Global 
Multidimensional Poverty In dex 2022 Pre -pandemic data, India is home to 
approximately 228.9 million poor people, which is the highest in the world. With such a 
major chunk of population that remains deprived of basic amenities, Government health 
spending is the only means to gain ac cess to affordable healthcare. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Union as well as the State Government to make consistent 
efforts to decrease the OOPE. The Committee recommends the Government to follow 
the examples of High -Income Countries (HIC) w here almost 70% of the expenditure on 
Health is borne by the Government.

Finance-A Study of Budgets 2021 -22 Report" wherein as per RBI, Statement indicate that 
only the UT Delhi and Puducherry has fulfilled the criteria of incurring at least 8% health 
expenditure out of their budgetary expenditure.

population ratio still remains skewed in many cities that are covered under CGHS. The 
Committee accordingly r ecommends the Ministry to assess the requirement of doctors 
in CGHS dispensaries across the country and ensure that adequate doctor to population 
ratio is maintained in all the CGHS cities. The Committee further recommends the 
Ministry to expedite the recr uitment of 340 candidates selected through Combined 
Medical Examination for filling up vacancies including the vacancies under CGHS.

but the Wellness Centres are still running from rented buildings, however, even after 
one year, the completion certificates have not been obtained from CPWD. Accordingly, 
the Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Mi nistry must obtain the 
completion certificate from CPWD and shift the Wellness Centres to the new buildings

medicines in CGHS dispensaries, delay in clearance of the dues owed to the private 
hospitals, viability of the CGHS rates, poor  experience of the beneficiaries etc persist in 
the CGHS ecosystem. Issues of basic medicines been indented in some CGHS 
dispensaries have also been noted. The Committee recommends the Ministry to ensure 
consistent supply of medicines under CGHS through Sc hemes like the Pradhan Mantri 
Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP). The Committee further observes that 
empanelling top private hospitals for providing comprehensive tertiary care is 
challenging under the present CGHS rates. The Committee accordingly recommends 
that a grading system for hospitals may be devised where CGHS rates are standardised 
for each category of hospitals. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to make an 
assessment on the budget required for expanding the pool of empanelled hospitals under 
the Scheme. The Committee has observed that CGHS rates for treatment and diagnosis 
have not been revised for many years and therefore, recommends that it may be revised 
keeping in view the present market rates.

3.40 The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) aims to make quality healthcare

tune of Rs. 200 crore was allocated in BE 2022-23 which was decreased to Rs. 140.00 crore at
